Facts of the case of the plaintiff, in short, inter alias, are that on 8-10-1995 plaintiff was appointed as Lecturer of Economics in the said college, namely, Kanchipara College and was drawing her salary and Government allowances as per MPO approved by the Government. She was married and became pregnant for the first time in November, 1997 and used to suffer from sickness time and again due to the same. She became seriously sick in July, 1998 due to pre-delivery complications making it difficult to continue taking classes regularly. She verbally informed the same to defendant No. 1 and ultimately, submitted applications on 12-7-1998 to him for maternity leave and went to Dhaka and got admitted in the clinic under Dr Niky Akhter situated at Section 10, Mirpur, Dhaka and gave birth to a boy on 3-9-98. The boy became sick and was admitted to Shishu Hospital, Dhaka on 4-9-98 and stayed there till 12-9-98 for treatment attended by her. She returned to her home at Gaibandha on 14-9-98. Consequently, she could not take her classes from 12-7-1998 to 14-9-1998. She went to the college to resume her duties on 15-9-98 but the defendant No. 1 refused to accept her joining letter informing her that she has been dismissed from her service and the order of her dismissal has been published on 2-9-1998 in a local daily. "Sandhan" as a notification and he advised her to submit application through defendant No. 9 (Chairman of the Governing Body). Thereafter, the plaintiff collected a copy of the said daily "Sandhan" and came to know of the said notification containing order of her dismissal to her surprise. The order of her dismissal having been passed illegally without service of any show cause notice, giving her any opportunity of being heard and beyond lawful authority and in violation of Rules and Regulations of Non-Government Intermediate College Teachers Terms and Conditions of Service Regulations, 1979 she made a representation on 20-9-1998 to the Governing Body of the College unsuccessfully for reconsideration of the same. She also served a legal notice on 22-10-98 and ultimately, filed the suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1, 6, 9 and 10 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material averments of the plaint and stating, inter alia, that in response to the advertisement dated 25-8-1995 the plaintiff submitted an application on 7-9-1995 for her appointment as Lecturer in Economics in the College and on the recommendation dated 26-9-95 of the Selection Committee she was appointed and joined on 9-10-95 as Lecturer in Economics in the College. She remained absent for a long time after 28-4-1997 for which she was served with a show cause notice dated 7-3-1996 and she gave reply to the same on 9-4-96 and she was again served with show cause notice on 29-9-1997 for her absence from the College and she gave reply to the same. Thereafter, another show cause notice was issued to her on 18-2-1998 for her absence and negligence to duty and the same was sent to her by post on her refusal to receive the same which was returned unnerved. Thereafter, she went to Dhaka from Gaibandha and started living with her husband and remained absent from the College from 19-12-1997 to 13-7-1998 without any permission. The Governing Body of the College in its meeting held on 14-7-1997, 13-7-98 and 9-8-98 took a decision to constitute a 3 members enquiry committee to hold enquiry against her. The enquiry committee submitted their report on 12-8-98 recommending her dismissal from service which was approved by the Governing Body on 18-8-1998 and the relevant papers were sent to the Education Board on 14-9-1998 and the order of dismissal was published on 2-9-1998 as notification in a local daily "Sandhan". The further defence case is, that there-after an advertisement was made in national daily "Janakantha" on 30-9-98 for appointment in the said vacant post and one ATM Rasheduzzaman was appointed as Lecturer in the said post on 26-7-99 who has already joined and performing his duty drawing his salaries and Government allowances as per MPO, etc. The suit is thus not maintainable and liable to be dismissed as in fructuous and no illegality or irregularity was committed in dismissing the plaintiff from her service.

5. Trial Court framed 4 issues for decision.

6. Plaintiff examined 2 witnesses and produced some documents which were admitted into evidence and marked as Exts. 1-7 while defence examined three witnesses and produced some documents which were marked as Exhibits Ka-Sa.

7. Trial Court dismissed the suit finding that the plaintiff was a habitual absentee, a show cause notice was duly served on her, she was given the opportunity of being heard and was dismissed in accordance with law on the recommendation of the Enquiry Committee. The trial Court further held that the plaintiff did not give her Dhaka address to the college authority for contact and she remained on long unauthorized leave and that there is no mention in the prayer of the plaint as to whether the prayer was made under section 39 or 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that the appointment in her post having already been made before filing the suit with a prayer for permanent injunction, the decree passed would not be executable and, as such, the plaintiff is not entitled to the decree prayed, etc. and dismissed the suit.

8. The plaintiff filed appeal against the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The appellate Court dismissed the appeal on contest affirming the judgment of the trial Court. The appellate Court below further held in dismissing the appeal that the prayer for permanent injunction as made in prayer 'Kha' of the plaint is not maintainable since the appointment has been made before filing the suit and there being no prayer for mandatory injunction directing the authority to reinstate her in her post with salary and allowances the suit is not maintainable in its present form and nature.

9. Assailing the judgments of the Courts below Mr Md Mazibar Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule for the petitioner, submits that the judgments of the Courts below suffers from illegality and infirmity for non-consideration of the material facts and issue involved in the suit and, as such, are liable to be set aside. He argues that the appellate Court, below being the last Court of facts, has erred in law in not at all discussing and finding on consideration of materials on record, whether the order of dismissal was passed lawfully, particularly in view of the exhibits of the parties, non-service of notice of show cause and order of dismissal on the plaintiff-petitioner, passing of the order of her dismissal on the report of the Enquiry Committee held in her absence, publishing the same in a local Daily without sending to her local address available with the college authority, etc. Mr Rahman submits that the impugned order of dismissal of the plaintiff-petitioner is illegal, without lawful authority and volatile of the principle of natural justice having been passed without giving her any opportunity of being heard. Referring Regulation Nos. 11, 12 and 14 of The Recognised Non-Government Intermediate College Teacher (Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Rajshahi) Terms and Conditions of Service Regulations, 1979, Mr Rahman submits that the Courts below, particularly the appellate Court below, being last Court of facts, failed to find that the order of dismissal has been passed in violation of the mandatory provisions of the aforesaid Regulations of the Board. He also argues that no prior approval of her dismissal was taken from the Board by the college authority nor the same has yet been approved and post facto approval of the order of dismissal being illegal, the order of dismissal is liable to be set aside. He argues that Exhibits marked as Ka-Sa on behalf of the defendants amply show that the proceeding of her dismissal was not taken by the resolutions of the Governing Body of the College in its meeting held properly and in accordance with Rules of the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Governing Bodies Resolutions, 1977, but neither of the Courts below considered this vital aspect of the facts and law which is the main issue in the suit and, as such, the judgments of the Courts below are liable to be set aside. He also submits that an order of dismissal by publishing in a local daily instead of sending and serving the same to her available local address is also not proper and lawful, etc. He argues that the appellate Court's judgment is not a proper judgment under Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the same has been passed on mere surmise and conjecture.

10. Mr Hasan Foez Siddique, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendant-opposite party No. 1, opposing the Rule, submits vehemently that a suit for mere declaration without prayer for any consequential relief is not maintainable since the decree if passed in such a suit is not and cannot be executed as the same is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Referring the prayer made in the plaint and the relevant finding of the appellate Court below that the suit is not maintainable at all in absence of any prayer for mandatory injunction, Mr. Siddique submits that since the post has already been filled up the suit has rightly been dismissed by the Court below as there was no prayer in the plaint for mandatory direction on the defendants to reinstate her to her former post with arrear pay and allowances, etc. Mr. Siddique also argued that the suit is not maintainable for defect of parties and, as such, the Rule should be discharged. Substantiating his submission on section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, Mr. Siddique has refer-red the cases of Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation Ltd, and others vs Abdul Halim Chowdhury, reported in 47 DLR 173, Dhunat Degree College & ors vs Md Abdus Samad and others, reported in 49 DLR 38 and Sonali Bank and another vs Chandon Kumar Nandi, reported in 48 DLR 330. He cited the case of Jahan Ara Begum vs Md Shamsul Hoque, reported in 27 DLR (AD) 129 in support of his submission that the suit is not maintainable for defect of parties since the College has not been made party in the suit.

11. In reply, Mr Mazibar Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, strongly contends that the citations referred by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1 are not applicable in the instant case as the facts and issue of the instant case are not the same and similar with those cases and Mr Siddique has also misconceived the prayer of the plaintiff-petitioner made in sub-paragraph 'Ka' of the plaint where both substantive and consequential relief have been prayed in 2 distinct parts. Mr Rahman stoutly argues that Mr Siddique is incorrect in submitting that the decree cannot be executed and submits that the decree if passed is very much executable. He also submits that there is no defect of parties in the suit nor the same was raised before the Courts below by the defendants nor any issue was framed or any decision or finding has been given on the same by the Courts below in dismissing the suit. He submits that the Principal and Secretary of the Governing Body of the College and all the members of the Governing Body including its Chairman have been made parties in the suit.

12. In support of his submissions Mr Rahman cited the decisions in the cases of Governing Body of Kapilmuni College, represented by the Principal, Kapilmuni College vs Sheikh Roushan Ali and ors, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 31, Sheikh Roushan Ali vs Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Jessore and others, reported in 48 DLR 128, Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Syed Moazzem Hossain and others, reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 239 =1 BLC (AD) 13, Sufia Khanam Chowdhury vs Faizun Nessa Chowdhury, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46, Province of East Pakistan vs Abdul Latif Talukder and another, reported in 22 DLR 589, Sarder Ahmed Ali vs GM Ali Baksh, reported in 1984 BLD 309 = 37 DLR 7, Aziza Nilufa Begum vs Jahanara Begum reported in 3 BLC 117, Abu Bakar Siddique (Md) vs Additional Deputy Commissioner, Kurigram and others, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 154, Abdul Mazid Howlader and another vs Lahajuddin Howlader reported in 48 DLR (AD) 160 and Safaruddin and others vs Fazlul Huq and others, reported in 5 BLT (AD) 201 = 49 DLR (AD) 151.

13. Perused the judgments of the Courts below, evidence and materials on record of the case and heard the learned Advocates of both the sides.

14. Mr Hasan Foez Siddique, the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1, did not argue on merit of the suit itself. He made two-fold submissions on the maintainability of the suit as aforesaid referring section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and for defect of parties. He, however, emphasized much on his first submission with a number of citations. In that view of the matter. I like to address his submissions first. In order to properly address his submission that a suit for mere declaration without a prayer for consequential relief is not maintainable since any decree if passed in such a suit cannot be executed. I think it prudent to quote the reliefs sought by the plaintiff-petitioner in her prayer made in sub-paragraphs 'Ka' and 'Kha' of the plaint which are as follows:

“ক) মুল বিবাদীগণ কর্তৃক বাদিনীকে তাহার চাকুরী হইতে বরখাস্তের সিদ্ধান্তের আদেশ (যাহা দৈনিক স্নধান পত্রিকায় প্রকাশিত) উক্ত সিদ্ধান্ত ও আদেশ বে-আইনী, বিধি বহির্ভূত, একতরফা, যোগসাজশী, উদ্দেশ্য প্রনোদিত, beyond natural justice, without jurisdiction, ফলবলহীন মর্মে রদ রহিত করিতে এবং বাদীনি তাহার সপদে বহাল আছে মর্মে আদেশ দিতে;

খ) বাদীনির পদে মূল বিবাদীগণ যাহাতে অন্য্ কোন বেক্তিকে নিয়োগ দিতে না পারে তজ্জন্য নালিশী প্রতিষ্ঠানের প্রভাষক হিসাবে বাদিনীর কর্তব্য দায়িত্ব পালনে কোনরুপ বিঘ্নের সৃষ্টি করিতে না পারে তজ্জন্য এবং বাদীনির নামীয় সরকার কর্তৃক বরাদ্দকৃত বেতনের সরকারী অংশের ৮০% বেতন বাদিনী ব্যতীত নতুন কোন ব্যক্তিকে মাস মাহিনা হিসাবে প্রদান করিতে না পারে ত��্জন্য প্রথমে অস্থায়ী ও পরে চিরস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার ডিক্রি দিতে:

15. In sub-paragraph 'Ka' of her prayer she has prayed for declaration that the impugned order of her dismissal is illegal, inoperative, etc. and is liable to be set aside and also for a declaration that she be deemed to be in her service. In sub-paragraph 'Kha' the plaintiff prayed for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from causing any disturbance or obstruction in performing her functions/duties and also for restraining them from appointing any person to her said post.

<u>16. From plain reading of the prayer as aforesaid, I am of the opinion that the prayer made in sub-paragraph 'Ka' has two parts, first one is substantive relief and the second part is consequential relief and those made in sub-paragraph 'Kha' are mere ancillary/auxiliary relief’s sought for her protection from any mischief during tendency of the proceeding in the form of preventive order, i.e., injunction against the defendants. It seems to me that Mr Siddique has totally misread, mixed up and misconceived the prayers made in sub-paragraph 'Ka' and has been misled by the findings of the Courts below which are thoroughly misconceived, erroneous and based on misreading of the pleadings, that is, the prayer of the plaintiff as quoted above. The plaintiff has clearly prayed in the first part of sub-paragraph 'Ka' for declaration of her impugned dismissal order as illegal and inoperative and in its second part for declaration that she is in service in her post. On plain reading of the same, I am clearly of the opinion and find that the second part of her prayer is a consequential relief followed by her substantive relief prayed in its first part for declaration of the impugned order of her dismissal as illegal and inoperative. I have gone through the decisions referred by Mr Siddique and bear no disagreement with the those. But, in the instant case, the facts as well as the relief sought for are completely different from those cases. The instant suit is not a suit for simple declaration of the impugned order of dismissal as illegal and inoperative but also for a declaration that the plaintiff is in her service which is very much a consequential relief and if decree is passed by the Court, the same is very much executable.</u>

<u>17. I am also of the opinion that failure and/or frustration of the ancillary/auxiliary relief cannot frustrate the entire suit and cannot result in dismissal of the suit if the plaintiff is otherwise entitled to a decree of her substantive relief. The prayer of the plaintiff made in sub-paragraph "Kha', as quoted above, may become in fructuous due to an appointment to her post before filing the suit but for that reason her suit for declaration as prayed in sub-paragraph 'Ka' cannot fail if she is otherwise entitled to get a decree to that effect which is very much effective and executable. In that view of the matter, the findings of the Courts below that the suit is not maintainable since the prayer for permanent injunction became in fructuous and for not praying for a mandatory order for her reinstatement are erroneous, perverse, not maintainable and are liable to be set aside.</u>

18. Mr Hasan Foez Siddique, the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1, in his second and last submission urged that the suit is bad for defect of parties since the college has not been made a party as defendant in the, suit for proper and effective adjudication of the issue involved in the suit.

19. Mr Md Mazibar Rahinan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, strongly controverted the above submitting that the suit is not bad for defect of parties, inasmuch as all the necessary parties have been imp leaded in the suit.

20. Firstly, I like to mention that I fully agree with the citation reported in 27 DLR (AD) 129, the same referred by Mr Siddique is not applicable in the instant case. In the citation referred by Mr Siddique it has been held that a necessary party is one whose presence is necessary to effectively adjudicate the point of issue involved in the suit and against whom the plaintiff must have right to seek relief and in whose absence the Court cannot give an effective remedy.

<u>21. It is true that the College has not been imp leaded as a defendant but his presence in the instant case is not necessary for Court to give an effective remedy sought by the plaintiff. The Principal of the College under whose signature the impugned order of dismissal has been published as a notification in the local daily "Sandhan" and the President and Members of the Governing Body of the College, who took the relevant resolutions in its meetings relating to all matters including the proposal of her dismissal, have been imp leaded as parties in the suit as defendants No. 1-11. Defendant Nos. 1-6, 9 and 10 have filed the written statements and contested the suit. Trial Court framed 4 issues and dismissed the suit on hearing the parties and on the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by both the parties. Neither of the Courts below gave any finding that the suit is not maintainable for defect of parties nor the same was agitated before any of the Courts below by the contesting defendants-opposite parties. In that view of the matter, it cannot be said that the suit was bad for defect of parties and for that reason the Court could not effectively adjudicate the dispute in issue in the suit. I therefore, find no substance in the submissions of Mr Siddique.</u>

22. Now let us turn to the merit of the case. The learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1 has not made any submission on merit of the suit controvert the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

23. In dismissing the suit, the trial Court found that the plaintiff-petitioner was a frequent absentee since her appointment in 1995 in the college. In 1998 she was on unauthorized leave for a long time. She did not give her address while she was in the clinic and hospital in Dhaka, she was given the opportunity of being heard after issuing due show cause notice, etc. and her order of dismissal is proper and legal. The trial Court, however, found that she was absent during enquiry held by the Enquiry Committee, the proposal of her dismissal was not earlier approved by the Board as per its Rules and Regulations and appointment in her post was also made without prior sanction of the Board. The appellate Court below affirmed that judgment of the trial Court.

24. Admittedly, she was a duly appointed Lecturer in Economics in Kanchipara Mohila College, she was married, became pregnant, went on maternity leave on 12-7-1998, admitted herself into a clinic in Mirpur, Dhaka under Dr Niky Akhter, gave delivery of a boy who became sick and admitted into Shishu Hospital in Dhaka for treatment and ultimately, after discharge from hospital she came back home at Gaibandha and went to the college for joining on 15-9-98 but the defendant No. 1 refused to allow her to join informing that she has been dismissed from her service by the Governing Body of the College and her order or dismissal has been published on 2-9-98 is a local daily "Sandhan".

25. On perusal of the judgments of the Court below and the evidence and materials on record, I find that the show cause notice served on the plaintiff and her reply as mentioned in the judgment are not at all related with the alleged unauthorized absence in question covering the period from 12-5-98 to 14-9-98 but of the previous years, but the Court erroneously found that she was served with the show cause notice and she gave reply on misreading the documents produced by the defendants. The positive case of the plaintiff is that she went on maternity leave on 12-7-98 submitting an application for maternity leave to the defendant No. 1 and it is the normal practice that such application remains in his office but the Courts below erroneously found that the plaintiff failed to produce the same in Court. The Court found that the show cause notice, notice of inquiry and the order of her dismissal could not be served on the plaintiff-petitioner because she did not give her Dhaka address to the college authority. This finding is thoroughly perverse and erroneous, inasmuch as her local address at Gaibandha was very much with the record of the college and she went to Dhaka for treatment and not for residing. Admittedly, she was in a clinic and then in Shishu Hospital in Dhaka for giving birth of her son and his treatment. So, the question of giving her address of the clinic and Shishu hospital does not arise. The defendants could very well send and serve any notice, letter and her order of dismissal to her local address at Gaibandha which is available in the record of the college. But instead of doing so they sent her order of dismissal for publication in a local daily. Admittedly she was dismissed on the basis of the inquiry report submitted by the 3-member Enquiry Committee. The trial Court has found that inquiry was held in her absence, There is no evidence and finding that the show cause notice was sent to her local address nor any evidence or finding that the Enquiry Committee has sent any notice to her said address asking her to appear before them. Thus, she was denied the opportunity of being heard and, as such, her order of dismissal is volatile of natural justice. The trial Court also found that the proposal of her dismissal was not approved by the Education Board before it was sent for publication in the local daily. Therefore, it can be well said that the said order of dismissal is also vocative of Rules and Regulations of the Education Board as mentioned above and the same has not been passed in accordance with law.

26. From perusal of the judgment of the Courts below I do not find that the Courts below have made any attempt to scrutinize and consider the proceeding adopted by the defendants in dismissing her nor there is any evidence on record about holding of meeting of the Governing Body in accordance with relevant rules and regulations mentioned above relating to her dismissal nor the Courts below gave any finding on the same. On examining the documents produced by the defendants marked Exts. Ka-Sa it appears that neither proceedings and decisions of her dismissal were taken in accordance with law in properly held meeting of the Governing Body of the College nor the proposal of her dismissal was approved in accordance with the rules and regulations and, as such, on this count also the impugned order of dismissal is liable to be declared as illegal, ineffective and inoperative.

<u>27. The appellate Court below being the last Court of facts totally failed to take into consideration the above facts and his judgment is a product of non-consideration of the material facts and is not a proper judgment of affirmance. The Courts below, particularly the appellate Court below, misread the evidence on record of the case and passed their judgment on total non-consideration of material facts and on surmise and conjecture. The Court below failed to find from the materials on record that the order of dismissal of the plaintiff-petitioner is thoroughly improper and illegal. The impugned order of dismissal having been passed improperly and illegally against the rules and regulations of the Board and violating the principle of natural justice and the same being also inoperative, the plaintiff is rightly entitled to her relief as prayed in sub-paragraph 'Ka' of the plaint. The appointment in her post having been made as found by the trial Court and affirmed by the appellate Court below, without prior approval and sanction of the Appeal and Arbitration Committee of the Board as per its Rules and Regulations, she is also entitled to relief that she should be deemed to be in service in her post. I find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and merit in the Rule.</u>

28. In consideration of my above discussion and finding and the decision referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, I hold that the suit is maintainable and the plaintiff has been able to prove her case and she is entitled to the decree as prayed for in terms of sub-paragraph 'Ka' of the plaint.

29. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below are hereby set aside. The suit is decreed in terms of sub-paragraph 'Ka' of the plaint. The impugned order of dismissal of the plaintiff published under the signature of defendant No. 9 on 2-9-98 in the local daily 'Sandhan' is hereby declared illegal, ineffective and inoperative and it is further declared that the plaintiff be deemed to have been in her service in the post of Lecturer in Economics.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule arises out of an application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the judgment and order dated 22-2-95 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Second Court, Feni, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 37 of 1987 affirming the order dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1984 passed by the then Munsif, Sonagazi, under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

2. The petitioner as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1984 in the Court of the then Munsif Sonagazi, Feni, against the opposite parties for pre-emption claiming himself as co-sharer in the case-joth. The defendant opposite-parties contested the suit by filing written objection denying the material allegations of the petitioner and further asserted that they are in possession of the suit land as purchasers from the heirs of Haider Ali and the alleged deed dated 20-12-80 is not a deed of sale but in fact, it is a ''Nadabi'' deed and, as such, there is no scope for pre-emption. The further case of the defendant opposite-parties is that they purchased the suit land from the heirs of Haider Ali through different deeds in 1962, 1963 and 1965 respectively and thereafter they are in possession of the suit land and the pre-emptor petitioner knows about the same and, as such, the pre-emption application is barred by time as well.

3. The learned Munsif on review of the evidence dismissed the Miscellaneous Case holding that the alleged deed dated 20-12-80 is not a sale deed but, in fact, it is a deed of release. The learned trial Court also found that there is no evidence as to whether any consideration had passed from the vendor to the vendee in pursuance of alleged sale deed dated 20-12-80. The learned trial Court also found that the pre-emptor petitioner was in the know of the transaction made by the heirs of Haider Ali in 1962, 1963 and 1965 and the pre-emptee opposite parties were in possession of the suit land by virtue of their purchase from the heirs of Haider Ali and, as such, the pre-emptor petitioner failed to prove his case. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the trial Court the pre-emptee petitioner preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Feni, which was registered as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 37 of 1987 and the said appeal on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court. Feni and by the impugned judgment and order the learned appellate Court below affirmed the judgment and order passed by the trial Court and dismissed the Miscellaneous Case. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order of the learned appellate Court below the pre-emptor petitioner moved this Court in revision and obtained the instant Rule calling in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and order dated 22-2-95 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Feni.

4. Mr Ruhul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor petitioner, submits that both the courts below on misinterpretation of section 92 of the Evidence Act and consideration of inadmissible extraneous evidence arrived at a concurrent finding that the deed in question dated 20-12-80 is not a deed of sale, rather a deed of release. The learned Advocate further submits that both the Courts below completely erred in fact that in view of Ext.2 there is no scope for the Courts below to consider any evidence which contradicts or tries to vary, add to or subtract the terms of the contract and from the recital of the deed in question it is crystal clear that it is a deed of sale and not the deed of release, as such, there was no scope for the pre-emptee opposite parties to lead any evidence to the contrary and both the Court below committed error of law in considering those evidence and arriving at a concurrent finding that the deed in question is not a deed of sale, rather it is a deed of release. Mr Ruhul Amen further submits that DW 1 admittedly was not present at the time of execution and registration of the kabala and none else supports him at the trial and except the evidence of DW 3 there is no other parol evidence to show that no consideration was passed from the pre-emptee to the executant of the deed in question. The learned Advocate further submits that it is the positive case of the pre-emptee opposite-parties that there was dispute amongst the heirs of Elahi Baksh and Haider Ali over a suit property and there was a ''salish'' held in the house of the Chairman but the Chairman was not examined in this case, rather DW 2 was examined who claimed to be the Chairman-in-charge and he proved the alleged ''salish''. The learned Advocate further submits that it is the positive case of the pre-emptee opposite-parties that the disputed deed is not a deed of sale but a deed of release. Yet they did not examine anyone of the attesting witnesses nor examined the scribe to substantiate their contention. The learned Advocate further submits that there is nothing on record to show that, in fact, there was a talk for execution and registration of a deed of release and not a deed of sale. The learned Advocate further submits that both the Courts below also committed an error in finding that the deed under pre-emption was a ''Nadabi'' deed. The learned Advocate further submits that after finding that the transferees were the heirs of Elahi Baksh, there can be no reasons for them to execute a Nadabi deed of no consideration and there can be no reasons for the heirs of Elahi Baksh to forego their interest in the land of Khatian No. 64. The learned Advocate further submits that merely because 10 other kabalas were executed and the inadequacy of the consideration of the kabalas under pre-emption is not a ground for holding that it was not a deed of sale but a deed of release. In support of his contention he refers to the following decisions, namely 39 DLR (AD) 78. 44 DLR (AD) 270,1983 BLD (AD) 105, 43 DLR 429, 35 DLR (AD) 334, PLD 1960 (Lahore) 231.

5. Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the preemptee opposite parties on the other hand submits that sufficiency or insufficiency of the evidence is a matter to be looked into by the court of facts and in the instant case both the courts below on due consideration of the evidence and materials on record arrived at a concurrent finding of fact that the deed in question is not a deed of sale but a deed of release. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case there is no necessity of examining any attesting witness or the scribe of the deed in question in support of their case by the pre-emptee opposite parties inasmuch as attesting witnesses only prove the execution of the documents and they are not competent to prove the contents of the same and in the instant case the positive case of the pre-emptee opposite parties is that the pre-emptor in collusion with the executants of the deeds managed to write the deed as a deed of sale instead of ''Nadabi'' deed. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no bar in relying on the single testimony of a witness if it appears to be true to the Court and in the instant case both the courts below relying on the testimony of DW 3 arrived at a finding that no consideration was passed in respect of the deed dated 20-12-80 and on this is essentially a question of fact and relying on the testimony of DW 3 the learned courts below arrived at such a finding and it is a clean finding of fact which cannot be reopened before this Court unless it can be shown that the finding is based on no evidence at all but admittedly there is some evidence for the court to arrive at such finding. So, sufficiency or insufficiency of evidence cannot be the ground for interference by this Court with the impugned judgment and order. The learned Advocate then submits that the main grievance of the pre-emptor petitioner is that both the courts below relying on extraneous evidence arrived at a finding that the deed in question is not a deed of sale, rather it is a deed of release and that contravenes the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate further submits that this submission made by Mr. Ruhul Amin, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor, petitioner is not tenable in law inasmuch as section 92 of the Evidence Act prohibits a party to the agreement to lead evidence to add, vary or subtract from the terms of written instrument but in the instant case it is not a question of addition, varying or subtracting which will in the terms of the agreement rather in the instant case the question is what is the nature and character of the deed in question. The pre-emptor petitioner claimed the deed to be a deed of sale whereas the pre-emptee opposite parties claimed that it is a deed of release and in such circumstances the courts were competent to look into the nature and character of the deed in question and perfectly entitled to decide the nature and character of the documents and in support of his contention the learned Advocate relies on the following decisions, namely, 12 DLR 149, 19 DLR 17 and 654, 1988 BLD 33, 1986 BLD 85, AIR 1950 (SC) 15, AIR 1958 (SC) 448 and 1955 (Bombay) 320.

6. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned appellate Court below after taking into consideration the entire evidence and the materials on record and on due consideration of the same arrived at a positive finding tilt the alleged deed of sale dated 20-12-80, in fact, is not a deed of sale rather it is a deed of release. The learned appellate Court below also arrived at a finding that no consideration passed to the executant of the said deed and there is absolutely no evidence on record to show that the deed was a deed of sale. The learned appellate Court further observed that the pre-emptor petitioner failed to substantiate that consideration passed to the executant of the deed. The learned appellate Court below also arrived at a positive finding that the purchasers from the heirs of Haider Ali are found to be in possession of the lands since their purchase, namely, since 1962, 1963 and 1965 and the pre-emptor petitioner was in the know of the same. The learned appellate Court below also found that there was a ''salish'' in respect of the suit land wherein it was decided by the salishders'' that the heirs of Elahi Baksh would execute a deed of release in favour of the purchasers from the heirs of Haider Ali. In arriving at a finding that the alleged deed dated 20-12-80 is not a sale deed but a deed of release the appellate Court below took note of the fact that save and except the pre-emptor petitioner, his brothers and sisters along with 30 other persons executed 11 deeds in favour of the heirs of Haider Ali and the subsequent purchasers from the heirs of Haider Ali but significantly none of the executants including the brothers and sisters of the pre-emptor petitioner came before the court to challenge the contention of the pre-emptee opposite parties. On top of that the appellate Court below also noted that by the disputed deed 47½ decimals of land were rightly transferred to the pre-emptee opposite parties for a paltry consideration of Taka 500.00. Taking into consideration of these aspects the appellate Court below came to a positive finding that the deed in question although executed and registered as a deed of sale but in fact it is a deed of release. The appellate Court also found that the pre-emptees along with other purchasers from the heirs of Haider Ali were inducted into possession in 1962, 1963 and 1965 respectively and since then they are in continuous possession of their purchased land and the pre-emptor petitioner knew about the same right from the beginning. From a perusal of the trial Court judgment it appears that the findings given by the appellate Court are in fact correct findings of facts. Both the courts below arrived at the same findings. In that view of the matter I find substance in the submissions of Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed with the question of adequacy and inadequacy of consideration and sufficiency and insufficiency of evidence cannot be agitated before the revisional court and both the courts of fact, after taking into consideration and on proper scrutiny of the evidence and materials on record arrived at a concurrent findings and since Mr. Ruhul Amin could not show that the concurrent findings of facts are not based on evidence and materials on record the same cannot be assailed before this Court in its revisional jurisdiction.

7. Now the only pertinent question which calls for determination in this revisional application is, as to whether there is any scope for a party to adduce any parol evidence to show the true nature and character of the instrument in question. The main contention of Mr. Ruhul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor petitioner, is that the deed in question clearly shows that it is a deed of sale and the parties cannot lead evidence to contradict the recital and contents of the document. Since the document has been written as a deed there is no scope for the pre-emptee opposite parties to show by adducing extraneous evidence that the deed in question, in fact, is not a deed of sale rather a deed of release and for this purpose he relied mainly on section 92 of the Evidence Act and the decisions referred to above. In the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 334 the question came up before the Appellate Division to decide whether the question of Benami nature of Kabala on the basis of which pre-emption is claimed can be gone into and determined in proceeding for pre-emption. From a perusal of the decision it appears that if a pre-emption is sought to be resisted on the ground that no transfer took place under the relevant kabala in that vendor did not part with his possession but simply made a show of transfer for any purpose, such as to put away his creditors, as the case may be, then such a transaction, whether it is called ''Benami'' or colourable, may be gone into. So, in fact, this decision does not help Mr. Ruhul Amin, rather it goes against him. In the instant case it has been contended by the petitioner that the deed in question is a deed of sale whereas that contention of the petitioner is resisted by the pre-emptee opposite parties by alleging that it is in fact a deed of release and this point can be decided by a court in a pre-emption proceeding in an appropriate case like the present one.

8. In the case reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 105, it has been held that no evidence is admissible to vary'' the contents of the documents by any oral evidence and it is woll settled proposition of law and this is not disputed by anybody. The moot question in the instant case as to whether evidence adduced by the DWs tantamount to vary, add to or substract from the terms of the deed or the evidence of the DWs. in fact, explained the nature and character of the transaction in question. The evidence, in fact, established that the disputed deed is not a sale deed but a deed of release. In other words, the pre-emptees have not adduced any evidence to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from the terms of the disputed deed but to show the true nature and character of the disputed deed. In this connection it may be mentioned that in 35 DLR (AD) case it was canvassed by the pre-emptor that the question of ''Benami'' transaction cannot be agitated or gone into in a pre-emption case but the Appellate ''Division'' discussed the case reported in 51 CWN 644 and observed that it was found in that case as a matter of fact that no actual transfer took place under the kabala sought to be pre-empted and that the vendor remained all along in possession of the land and, as such, the question of pre-emption could not arise. It was further observed that this colourable transaction was referred to as a benami transaction in the pre-emption case and it is in such a case of benami where no actual transfer took place the question of benami nature of transaction could be considered in a proceeding for preemption. But the facts of 35 DLR case were altogether different and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case it was held that in the case the court was not required to entertain the question whether the vendor was benamder of the person seeking pre-emption.

9. Mr Ruhul Amin, the learned Advocate, also relied on the decision reported in PLD 1960 (Lahore) 231 but on a close reading of the said decision it appears that it has been held in that case that under section 92 of the Evidence Act, parol evidence is not inadmissible where the proceedings are between strangers or between a party and a stranger, because the rule embodied in section 92 applies to the parties to an instrument and their representative-in-interest. This does not mean that when a party to an instrument bases his claim on the instrument itself against a stranger, then the party to the instrument is entitled to give oral- evidence for the purpose of contradicting, varying, adding to or subtracting from the terms of the instrument. In such a case if it is claimed that besides incorporating the terms of the contract in the instrument, some other oral agreements have also been made, then in that case such oral agreement may be proved by other evidence and this decision, in my opinion, actually helps the pre-emptee opposite parties because in this proceedings the pre-emptor is a stranger to the document and, as such, it is a case between a stranger and a party to the document and in that view of the matter there was legal bar from the pre-emptee opposite parties to lead evidence to establish the true nature and character of the deed in question.

10. Section 92 presupposes the validity of the transaction evidenced by the document. If its validity is impeached, the court is not bound by what has been described as the paper expression of the parties, and is not precluded from entering into the real nature of the transaction between them. Section 92 does not preclude a party from showing that the writing was not really the contract between the parties, but was only a fictitious or colourable device which cloaked something else. Oral evidence is admissible to show that an agreement was only a sham or nominal transaction and was not intended to be acted upon or to show that a written agreement for the conveyance of property was only a fictitious sale to avoid execution proceedings against the property. In the case reported in AIR 1936 (PC) 70, the Privy Council observed. "section 92 only includes oral evidence to vary the terms of the written contract and has no reference to the question whether the parties had agreed to contract on the terms set forth in the document." Thus there is a material difference between an attempt to show that the terms of a contract were different from those recorded in a deed, and an attempt to show that the contract as mentioned in the deed was not the real contract between the parties but it was something different. It is the former that is hit by section 91 but the latter is not so hit. In the case reported in AIR 1931 (Orissa) 177, it has been held that where a husband admits that he executed a gift in favour of his wife, but alleges that he had no intention of giving away the property, oral evidence in proof of such defence is admissible. From the case reported in 1986 BLD 85, it appears that in that case an application for pre-emption was resisted by the pre-emptee on the ground that the deed in question though registered as a deed of sale but, in fact, it was a deed of exchange. It was contended on behalf of the pre-emptor that oral evidence is not admissible to prove that a document is not what it purports to be. But the court relying on the decisions reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 448 held that section 92 of the Evidence Act is not a bar to leading of oral evidence to prove that the document in question is not a sale deed but an exchange deed and I do not find any reason why this will not apply to the instant case although the deed is registered as a sale deed but it is contended by the pre-emptee opposite parties that it is, in fact, a deed of release and both the courts below concurrently found that the deed in question is in fact a deed of release and in arriving in that concurrent finding, in my opinion, the courts below did not commit any error of law. Similarly in the case reported in 1988 BLD 33 it has been held that admission of oral evidence of the acts and conducts of the parties in determining the true nature of the transaction does not infringe provision of section 92 of the Evidence Act. It can be shown by oral evidence that though a document in particular form was executed in fact it is different from what it appears to be. When a document is meant merely on an informal memorandum of transaction and not as a document embodying disposition of property, oral evidence is not excluded. Similarly, in the case reported in 19 DLR 17 it has been held that operation of section 92 of the Evidence Act is confined to the parties to an instrument and this decision is in line with the decision reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 448, wherein their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India held that section 92 applies only in case of parties to the contract and similar is the view reflected in the decision reported in PLD 1960 (Lohore) 231. It has further been held in the 19 DLR's case that the parol evidence of surrounding circumstances along with the contents of the relevant documents may be taken into consideration for the purpose of construing a document and holding whether the evidence so justified with the same, though couched in a particular form is really different. Furthermore, section 92 merely prescribes a rule of evidence. It does not fetter the Court's power to arrieve at the true meaning and effect of a transaction in the light of the surrounding circumstances. Yet there is another decision which contradicted in the instance case, that is, the case reported in 12 DLR 149 wherein it has been held that a recital in the document showing that the donor has given delivery of possession of the hiba land is no doubt binding on him and also on the persons claiming through him. But from that it does not necessarily follow that they are not entitled to disprove the recital. Oral evidence which goes to vary the terms of the contract may not be admitted into evidence between the parties. But if it is not related to any terms or intend to vary or add to or subtract from its terms, there is no bar of adducing oral evidence to prove matters other than those specifically mentioned in section 92 of the Evidence Act.

11. The next case relied on by Mr Ruhul Amin is the case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 270. In that case the pre-emptee made attempt to show that the deed in question was in fact not a deed of release but that contention of the preemptee was repelled by the court on the ground that the pre-emptee opposite party failed to prove his motive for acquisition of the case land in the ebenami. of Swapan Kumar: and, as such, the question of execution of deed of release by Swapan Kumar did not arise and so the impugned deed was construed as a transfer deed and on merit the contention of the pre-emptee was rejected. It was further observed in that case that the High Court Division really missed the vital point for consideration and consequently fell into an error in not construing the document with reference to the evidence on record. It thus appears from this case as well that in a preemption proceeding the court is entitled to inquire into the true nature and character of the transaction. In that case the pre-emptee tried to resist the pre-emption on the ground that it was, in fact, a deed of release and not a deed of sale but the court on scrutiny of evidence arrived at a finding that the deed in question was not a deed of release but a deed of sale. Thus this case also does not help Mr. Ruhul Amin in any way rather it helps the pre-emptee opposite parties and in the instant case their contention is that the disputed deed is not a deed of sale rather it is a deed of release and that contention of the pre-emptee opposite parties have been upheld by both the Courts of fact on scrutiny of evidence and materials record.

12. In the case reported in AIR 1962 (Madras) 360 it has been held that there is material difference between an attempt to show that the terms of the contract were different from those recorded in a deed and an attempt to show that the contract as mentioned in the deed was not the real contract between the parties but it was something different. It is the former that is hit by section 91 of the Evidence Act but the latter is not so hit. Thus where the contention of the plaintiff is that the actual contract itself was different and that for certain reasons it was made to appear in the document that it was a rectification deed, section 91 does not preclude the plaintiff from proving that the real contract was different from what is found in the deed. Thus, here the contention of the plaintiff is that the actual contract itself was different, and that for certain reasons it was made to appear in the document that it was a rectification deed, section 91 does not preclude the plaintiff from proving that the real contract was different from what is found in the deed. Similarly in the case reported in AIR 1955 (Bombay) 320 it has been held that there is no difficulty in spite of sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act in leading evidence to show, notwithstanding the recital of payment of consideration in a document, that it was actually not paid. In the case reported in AIR 1958 (50.15, it has been held that extrinsic evidence to determine the effect of an instrument is permissible where there remains a doubt as to its true meaning. Similarly, in the case reported in AIR 1938 (Nagpur) 335 it has been held that all that section 92, Evidence Act excludes is oral evidence to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from terms of a contract which has been reduced to writing. It does not preclude a party from showing that the writing was not really the contract between the parties but was only a fictitious or colourable device which cloaked something else. In the case reported in 95 Indian Cases 512 it has been held that where a person who has executed a document seeks to show that the document is a mere sham deed and represents nothing he is not seeking to vary or contradict any of the terms of the document and oral evidence is admissible to prove that there was no such agreement between the parties as is represented by the document.

13. From a review of the decisions cited above it appears that extrinsic evidence would be admissible for the purpose of showing that a document which appears on the face of it to be a deed of sale is in reality a deed of gift or that what appears to be a sale document with an agreement to re-sale was, in fact, a mortgage by conditional sale or that though a document was couched in a particular form, in fact, it is different from what it appears to be.

14. In this case I am not to resist the temptation of quoting a passage from the decision reported in 37 DLR 87 which runs as follows:

"Intention of the parties to a document is held in numerous decided cases to be not relevant in varying the terms of a concluded document by the parties on the reasoning that a party must have intended what, he had expressed in the language of the document and he cannot be allowed to go back from those and perjure in a Court, yet, the fact remains that may be the intention of a person in executing a document may not be the object in executing the said very document as there is a gulf of difference between an intention and an object. In the language of a psychologist and also of a jurist an intention is the doing and the manner of doing the immediate work and an object is the ultimate to be achieved but as human motivations are complex there may not always exist an union between the two intention and object. Hence, when they are in conflict the immediate intention would be a mere colourable device used in achieving a different end. If the intention in executing a document is colourable there is no intention as expressed but a mere pretence. This fact can be proved as an existing fact to show the manner in which the language of a document was related to existing fact, extraneous to the document at the time of contract and that would not mean leading oral evidence to vary the terms of a document. Further, as observed already the bar of sections 91 or 92 of the Evidence Act is only applicable when evidence is used in proving that the terms were different but not when used in proving that the transaction itself was different from what it purported to be and hence no contract at all as it appears to exist."

<u>15. It thus appears that both the courts below did not consider any illegality whatsoever in allowing the pre-emptee opposite parties to adduce to show the real nature and character of the disputed deed and the concurrent findings of both the courts below that the disputed deed in the instant case is not a deed of sale rather a deed of release cannot be assailed on the ground that the courts below on consideration of extraneous evidence arrived at such findings. I therefore do not find any substance in this revisional application.</u>

In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant No.1 petitioner, is directed against the order dated 5-3-1991 passed by the Assistant Judge, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 187 of 1989 by which the application filed by the defendant petitioner praying for dismissal of the suit on the ground of maintainability was rejected and at the same time the defendant petitioner was also debarred from filing the written statement in the suit.

2. The opposite party No. 1, as plaintiff, instituted the aforesaid Title Suit No. 187 of 1989 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Patuakhali on 8-11-1989 seeking declaration of title over the land described in schedule Ka to the plaint stating, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to late Jennat Khan, father of the plaintiff and on the death of Jennat Khan, the plaintiff inherited the suit land by way of inheritance as daughter and the plaintiff possessed the suit land on payment of rent to the government through the defendant No. 1 who is the son of Jennat Khan and that the defendant No. 1 got no right, title and possession on the suit land but the defendant No. 1 on the basis of a Deed of Waqf dated 31-1-1929 got his name mutated in Mutation case No. 194 PK of 1965-66 though Jennat Khan, during his life time, cancelled the said Waqf Deed and the said Waqf Deed was not acted upon and the land was not enrolled as Waqf property.

3. The defendant No. 1 petitioner appeared in this suit on 25-9-1990 and before filing the written statement he on 8-1-1991 filed an application praying for dismissal of the plaint on the ground of maintainability on the ground that the suit land belonged to Waqf Estate Jennat Khan and the suit land along with other lands were enrolled in the office of Administrator of Waqf by Enrollment case No. 8076 and thereafter in terms of the order of the Administrator of Waqf, Mutation Case No. 194-PK of 65-66 was started and the suit land was mutated in the name of the Mutwalli of the Waqf Estate Jennat Khan and since then the property is being treated as Waqf property and in terms of the provisions of section 50 of Waqf Ordinance 1962, the Administrator of Waqf has the sole jurisdiction to decide whether the suit property is Waqf property or not and so this preliminary issue as to whether the suit is maintainable or not is to be decided at first.

4. The learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment and order dated 5-3-1991 rejected the said application, and at the same time also debarred the defendant No. 1 from filing written statement and fixed 11-3-1991 for ex parte hearing of the case.

<u>5. Mr. M Quamrul Hasan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the very case of the plaintiff as made out in the plaint is that Jennat Khan executed the deed of Waqf on 31-1-1929 and subsequently on 22-3-1929 cancelled the same but even then, subsequently, the defendant No. 1 illegally showing him as Mutwalli of the said Waqf, mutated his name on the basis of the said Waqf deed dated 31-1-29 and so the suit in substance is a suit praying for declaration that the suit property is not Waqf property and so in the present suit, section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 will be attracted. Mr. Hasan further submits that Waqf Ordinance 1962 is a special law and accordingly in terms of provision of section 50 of the above Ordinance in the present case the jurisdiction of the civil Court will be deemed to have been ousted and in view of the principle as laid down in 31 DLR (AD) 251 it is only the Administrator of Waqfs who will decide the issue of maintainability and according to the principle laid down in the decision reported in 46 DLR 587 in such case the Administrator of Waqfs has the sole, jurisdiction to decide the claim and title of any person after taking evidence and accordingly, the plaintiff, for establishing his title to the suit land, can put forward before the Administrator of Waqfs, the evidence on which he relies. Mr. Hasan relying on the principle as laid down in the decision reported in 45 DLR (AD) 36 such objection regarding maintainability of the suit can be taken at any stage of the suit, but in the present case this issue regarding maintainability has been raised at the earliest possible opportunity so that time, energy and money are not wasted on a fruitless litigation and moreover, according to principle as laid down in the decision reported in 41 DLR 387, the provision of Order 11 rule, 1, CPC which provides time limit to file written statement is not mandatory but directory and so the impugned order by which the petitioner was debarred from filing written statement also suffers from illegality. Mr. Hasan submits that the petitioner raised this issue of maintainability by his application dated 8-1-1991 in terms of the provision of Order 14 rule 2 CPC and in terms of the principle as laid down in the decision reported in 40 DLR 267, it was incumbent upon the court below to determine this issue first to save unnecessary expense, time and energy of the court itself and moreover, the impugned order is also not a speaking order as it contains no reasons and in view of the principle as laid down in the decision reported in PLD 1970 (SC) 173 this order cannot be sustained.</u>

6. Mr. MA Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, submits that the current trend of law is that ouster of jurisdiction of civil Court is not to be readily inferred and according to the principle as laid down in the decision in 44 DLR (AD) 242 this question of maintainability should be exercised on the basis of evidence. Mr. Sobhan further submits that in terms of section 47 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 the Waqf should have been enrolled within 3 months from the date of its creation i.e. 31-1-1929 but the alleged order of enrollment was obtained after 37 years and since the wakif cancelled this Waqf on 22-3-29 and there was no existence of any Waqf after 22-3-29 and, in fact, there was no Waqf this could not be enrolled, the plaintiff after receiving notice of the mutation case for the first time came to know about the claim of the defendant No. 1 to the effect that the suit property was a Waqf property. Mr. Sobhan further submits that in the plaint only simple declarations have been sought regarding title of the plaintiff to the suit property and no declaration at all been sought as to whether the suit property is Waqf property or not and so the civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain the suit and accordingly, the learned Assistant Judge committed no illegality in rejecting the application dated 8-1-91 as the cause of action of the suit arose in view of the filing of the mutation case and not for enrollment of the suit property as an Waqf property.

7. It appears that the sole contention of dispute is whether in the present suit, the provision of section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 is attracted. It is a settled principle of law that in what form the plaintiff may seek declaration in the plaint but it is the substance of the plaint which has to be seen and in the present case it has to be ascertained whether the property is Waqf property so as to attract the provisions of section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance. Section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 provides as follows:

"50 Any question whether a particular property is Waqf property or not shall be decided by the Administrator.

Provided that the mutwalli or any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Administrator in this behalf may within three months from the date of such decision submit petition to the District Judge in accordance with the provision of sub-section (1) of section 35, and if such a petition is filed the provisions of section 35 will apply".

8. In the decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 249, which was cited by Mr. Hasan, the plaintiff filed a title suit challenging the enrollment of Waqf and the defendant immediately after presentation of the plaint and before filing of the written statement raised the question of bar under sections 50 and 102 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 and the Appellate Division held as follows:

"If a dispute as to the Waqf character of a property is false either before or at the time of enrollment or after the enrollment, the jurisdiction to decide the Waqf character is that of the Administrator. The Waqf Ordinance being a special statute providing a special procedure is to be followed. The cognisance of the civil Court is excluded."

<u>9. In the aforesaid decision the Appellate Division found that in substance the plaintiff is challenging the Waqf character of the property. It appears that in the present case also in the plaint the plaintiff categorically stated that an Waqf estate was created on 31-1-29 though according to the claim of the plaintiff the said Waqf was cancelled on 22-3-29 and thus the deed of Waqf was not acted upon and the disputed property was not enrolled as a Waqf property but even the defendant No. 1 on the basis of Waqf Deed dated 31-1-29 which stood cancelled, illegally filed mutation case No. 194 of 1965-66 showing him as mutawalli of the said Waqf and in the prayer portion of the plaint, the plaintiff amongst others sought decree for declaration of their title in the disputed 1.55 decimal of land. So following the principle as laid down in the above decision it appears that in the present suit also where the question as to whether the property is Waqf or not have been raised, the provision of section 50 of the Ordinance 1962 will be attracted.</u>

10. In the decision reported in 46 DLR 267, the defendant filed an application praying for settling the issues of law, namely, the issues on maintainability of the suit on the grounds of limitation, bar under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, res judicata and also defect of parties and the Assistant Judge after hearing the application by the impugned order only took up the question of res judicata and held that the other issues cannot be decided without hearing the suit on merit. Before the High Court question was raised as to whether the provision of rule 2 of Order 14, CPC is mandatory and the court at first is to decide the issue on limitation as it is incumbent upon the court to determine the issue of law at first as it saves unnecessary expense, time and labour of the court itself. It was held by the High Court Division that the failure to decide the issue on limitation on the face of Order 14 rule 2 CPC is an error of law on the part of the court and contrary to the decision consistently followed by the superior courts and the provision of Order 14 rule 2 CPC is mandatory and the trial Court is under mandate of law to decide the issue of law where an application under Order 14 rule 2 CPC is filed by the party to the suit.

11. In the case reported in 46 DLR 587, an application was filed by the mutwalli before Waqf Administrator under section 64(1) of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 for eviction of unauthorised occupants from the Waqf land. The opposite party filed a written objection to the same contending, inter alia, that he purchased land from the heirs of the alleged Waqf Aynuddin Munshi through registered deeds for valuable consideration and they have been possessing the disputed land for more then 33 years on mutation of their names on payment of rent thereof and the property in question was not at all Waqf property and the same was recorded as secular property and the opposite parties were also not at all aware of the Waqf until they received notice of show cause in respect of the application under section 64 (1) of the Waqf Ordinance from the office of the Administrator of Waqf and on enquiry they found that the Waqf deed was executed on 16-7-48 and registered on 17-7-48 by fraudulent means and the Waqf was not in its proper sense and subsequently when the wakif realised that fraudulent Waqf deed was created in his name he on 20-3-48 executed and registered the deed on cancellation of the said Waqf and the Waqif then executed deed of gift of the said property in favour of his 2 sons and the said deed of gift was registered on 15-2-49 and the said sons of Waqif transferred this land in favour of the opposite parties by different sale deeds in between 1951-1952 and since then the opposite parties have been possessing the same after completion of mutation in their names and on payment of rent and further during SA and RS operation their names were also recorded in the recent khatain and nature of the land has teen shown as secular property. The learned Administrator of Waqfs found that the Waqf deed was cancelled by registered deed dated 17-7-48 and the opposite parties were in actual possession of the property for the last 33 years on payment of rent and accordingly, rejected the application for eviction. On appeal the learned District Judge after hearing both the sides proceeded with the theory that once a Waqf is always a Waqf and so there could not be any revocation or cancellation of the Waqt deed and on the above ground allowed the appeal. However, it was held by the High Court Division that the jurisdiction of the Administrator of Waqfs and the District Judge and any civil Court are not parallel alternative or cumulative, power under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance provides for any adequate and sufficient relief in proceedings to decide whether the property is Waqf property or not, section 38 of the Waqf Ordinance empowers the Administrator of Waqfs and the District Judge to examine the witness and call for production of document and issuance of process as provided in the case of civil Court under the CPC and the High Court Division was pleased to set aside the judgment and order of the Administrator of Waqfs as well as the judgment of the District Judge in appeal and sent back the case on remand to the Administrator of Waqfs for fresh decision in accordance with law with the observation that before passing any order of eviction under section 64(1) the Administrator of Waqfs after taking and considering the evidence of both the sides should give decision as to whether the lands in question are Waqf property, whether the opposite parties are trespassers or unauthorised occupant therein and also whether the alleged Waqf is a valid and lawful one or the same has lost its character as Waqf property. In the present suit also the plaintiff asserted that though the Waqf was created on 30-1-1929 but the same was cancelled after three months and that they as daughters of Waqif inherited that suit land, accordingly the suit land enrolled as an Waqf property in terms of Enrollment case No. 8076, is not an Waqf property and accordingly in principle as laid down in the above decision reported in 46 DLR 587 is applicable in the present and the Administrator of Waqfs after taking evidence for both the sides and considering the same will decide the question as to whether the suit property is Waqf or not.

12. In the case reported 44 DLR (AD) 242, which has been cited by Mr. Sobhan, the plaintiff respondent instituted money suit states, inter alia, that the defendant, a trading company of London, offered to the plaintiff, by telexes made on 17th February 1982 and 11th March, 1982 to sell 150 metric tons of skimmed milk of Hungarian origin as per specifications and after accepting the offer the plaintiff on 12th, March 1982 opened letter of credit and the defendant by submitting documents against the letter of credit received the money and after arrival, the goods were found of inferior quality and accordingly the plaintiff rejected the goods and in the plaint it was averred that the cause of action of the suit arose on 12th March 1982 when the letter of credit was opened in favour of the defendant and when the plaintiff in effect rejected the goods after inspection by the SGS dated 6th October 1982 and on each and every time when the plaintiff and their lawyers sent telex and served legal notices upon the defendant. The defendant filed an application under Order VII rule 11 CPC for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the court had no jurisdiction since the defendant does not reside or carry on business within the jurisdiction of this court and it is ex facie evident from the plaint that no part of the cause of action arose within the jurisdiction of the court. In his written objection the plaintiff asserted that the cause of action arose within Dhaka where he accepted the defendants offer and opened the letter of credit for purchasing the goods, received the inspection report of the surveyor having their head office at Motijheel Dhaka, rejected the goods and asked the defendant to take back the consignment and refund the money. In the background of the aforesaid facts and circumstances it was held by the Appellate Division that the question of territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction can only be decide on the basis of evidence. But the facts and circumstances of the present case are completely different.

<u>13. In view of the discussion as made above and also in consideration of the principle of law that a judicial order should be a speaking order as has been held in the decision PLD 1970 SC page 173 of the view that in the present case the issue as to whether the suit property is Waqf property or not, will have to be decided at first and so section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 will be attracted in the present case and accordingly, the order dated 5-3-1991 cannot be sustained and the impugned order barring the defendant from filing written statement cannot also be sustained.</u>

In the result the Rule is made absolute and the order date 5-3-91 passed by the learned Assistant Judge Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 187 of 1989 in set aside. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
