full_judgment:
SM Ziaul Karim J: This Rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the Judgment and decree dated 28-8-2002, passed by the learned Additional District Judge cum Judge of the Special Court of Arms and Explosive Substance, in Title Appeal No. 157 of 2001, allowing the appeal and sending the suit on remand for fresh trial, by reversing the judgment and decree dated 15-7-2001, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 111 of 1998, dismissing the suit.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule, are that on 19-81998, opposite party Nos. 1-4 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 111 of 1998 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet, impleading the petitioner as defendant No. 1 and the opposite party Nos. 5-15 as defendant Nos. 2-13, for partition of the land described in the second Schedule of the plaint and also for declaration that the kabalas numbering three dated 17-9-1988 executed by defendant Nos. 2-12 in favour of defendant Nos. 1 in respect of the land described in the third Schedule of the plaint, are forged, collusive, inoperative without consideration and not binding upon them.

3. The plaintiff's case, in brief, is that Khan Bahadur Md Mosharraf was the original owner of first Schedule land along with other land who died leaving behind six sons and six daughters; that on 2-2-1941, except Mahmuda Khatun (mother of the plaintiffs) sold their respective share to Gonges Chandra Purkayesta for payment of loan, taken by their father; that on 5-8-1947 Mr Gonges sold the property to Aminur Rashid Chowdhury and Md Ali Box and they were possessing the land with email with Mahmuda Khatun; that subsequently defendant No. 1 collusively created forged deeds in favour of him shown to be executed by defendant Nos. 2-12 in respect of 49 decimals of land of Plot No. 367, which clouded the title of the plaintiffs. Hence, the suit.

4. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable for having no cause of action, the suit is barred by limitation, suffers from defect of parties, principle of estoppels, waiver and acquiescence.

5. The case of defendant No. 1 is that Mr Khan Bahadur Mosharraf was the original recorded tenant of the first schedule land, who as lonee died leaving behind six sons and six daughters; that except Mahmuda Khatun, other heirs of Md Mosharraf sold out their respective share to Gonges Chandra Purakayasta on 3-1-1941, for payment of loan who, on 5-8-1947 sold the property to Aminur Rashid Chowdhury predecessor of defendant Nos. 2-12; that Mahmuda Khatun, mother of plaintiffs, has no title and possession in respect of land described in Plot No. 367; that defendant No. 1 has been possessing the land after constructing dwelling but thereon; and that the suit is liable to be dismissed.

On the pleadings following, issues were settled

(a) Whether the suit was maintainable in the present form?

(b) Whether the suit was barred by limitation?

(c) Whether the suit was barred for defect of parties?

(d) Whether the suit was barred for, not bringing the ejmali properties into hotchpotch?

(e) Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to get separate saham in respect of third schedule land?

(f) Whether the impugned three cabalas were fraud, fraudulent, inoperative and collusive?

(g) Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to get decree as prayed?

(h) To what relief, if any, the plaintiffs were entitled to?

6. In course of trial the plaintiffs examined five witnesses in support of their case who proved their documents as Exhibit 1-8 and certified copies of the registered kabala deed numbering three as 9 series, while defendant No. 1 examined five witnesses in support of his case, who proved his documents as Exhibit Karma,

7. After hearing the learned Judge of the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 15-7-2001 dismissed the suit. Against which the plaintiffs as appellants preferred Title Appeal No. 157 of 2001 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet which was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Sylhet, who by the judgment and decree dated 28-8-2002 allowed the appeal and sent the suit on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial.

8. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the defendant No. 1 as petitioner obtained the present Rule.

9. Mr Md Mustafa, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, supports the Rule and submits that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below did not discuss the evidence on record as a last court of facts and without reversing the findings of facts arrived at by the trial Court passed the impugned judgment, thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Counsel adds that the Court of appeal below ought to have independently discussed the evidence on record and ought to have disposed of the appeal finally, without sending the same on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial. He adds that the learned Judge of the trial Court categorically held that the plaintiffs could not prove that the alleged deeds were forged. Mr Md Mustafa, lastly submits that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below failed to weigh and sift the evidence on record and evidently fell in an error in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. No one appears on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1-4 to oppose the Rule.

11. We have gone through the provisional application, the depositions of the witnesses, all exhibits proved by both the parties, impugned judgment, judgment of the trial Court, other materials on record and given our anxious consideration to the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner.

12. Now, the question calls for our consideration is whether the Court of appeal below committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court and remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial.

13. To appreciate the question involved in this Rule, the provisions of Order XLI, rules 23, 24 and 25 and section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure which deal with the remand of a case by the Appellate Court, may be extracted here:

"23. Where the Court from whose decree an appeal is preferred has disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point and the decree is reversed in appeal, the Appellate Court may, if it thinks fit, by order remand the case, and may further direct what issue or issues shall be tried in the case so remanded, and shall send a copy of its judgment and order to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, with directions to readmit the suit under its original number in the register of civil suits, and proceed to determine the suit; and the evidence (if any) recorded during the original trial shall, subject to all just exceptions, be evidence during the trial after remand.

24. Where the evidence upon the record is sufficient to enable the Appellate Court to pronounce judgment, the Appellate Court may, after resettling the issues, if necessary, finally determine the suit, notwithstanding that the judgment of the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has proceeded wholly upon some ground other than that on which the Appellate Court proceeds.

25. Where the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has omitted to frame or try any issue, or to determine any question of fact which appears to the Appellate Court essential to the right decision of the suit upon the merits, the Appellate Court may, if necessary, frame issues, and refer the same for trial to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, and in such case shall direct such Court to take the additional evidence required.

14. Section 107 of the Code runs as follows:

107(1) Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, an Appellate Court shall have power—

(a) to determine a case finally;

(b) to remand a case;

(c) to frame issues and refer them for trial;

(d) to take additional evidence or to require such evidence to be taken.

(2) Subject as aforesaid, the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein."

15. From a plain reading of the above stated Provisions of law it is clear that under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code there can be no remand unless the following conditions exist:

(a) that the entire suit and not a portion of it has been disposed of by the trial Court

(b) that the disposal must be on a preliminary point.

(c) and that the preliminary point on which the suit is decided has been reversed by the appellate Court.

16. Order XLI rule 24 of the Code enjoins that where the evidences on record are sufficient, the appellate Court is competent to determine the suit finally and there is no need for remand.

17. Order XLI, rule 25 of the Code lays down that only specific issues can be sent to the trial Court for findings and not for retrial of the entire suit and the appeal is to be heard under Order XLI, rule 26 of the Code.

18. Under section 107 of the Code, the appellate Court is vested with the power to determine a case finally and also to remand the case. Sub-section 2 of section 107 of the Code lays down that the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein.

19. We find from the record that the learned Judge of the trial Court, after considering SA Khatian (Exhibit 4) came to a specific finding that ejmali properties were not brought into hotchpotch and the plaintiff prayed for partial partition which is not at all maintainable. The learned Judge further came to a definite findings that the disputed kabala deeds as described in fourth schedule to the plaint (Exhibit 9 series) are not forged and, as such, the trial Court dismissed the suit.

<u>20. It appears that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below without reversing such findings of facts arrived at by the trial Court or without any independent finding passed the impugned judgment and decree. Moreover, the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below took notice of the evidences oral and documentary on record, but as a last court of facts failed to weigh and sift the same.</u>

21. On perusal of the record of the case it appears that in the instant case all the evidences and materials were before the lower appellate Court who itself could have disposed of the appeal finally.

22. It is settled principle of law that unnecessary order of remand entails hardship, agony of fresh hearing and additional expenditure and the same is to be deprecated and discouraged as it tends to delay the administration of justice far from advancing its course:

23. The Pakistan Supreme Court and the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court decided the question of the order of remand in a good number of cases.

24. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Pramoth Nath Chowdhury and seventeen others vs Kamir Mondal and others reported in 17 DLR 392 held:

"a remand cannot be likely ordered if the evidences on record is sufficient for the appellate Court to decide the question itself. There can be no bar to the Court doing so."

25. The Appellate Division, in the case of Probodh Ranjan Shome vs Md Easin reported in 1980 BSCR 457 observed that:

"It is well settled that remand orders are not to be made as a matter of course. When there is sufficient evidence on record, remand of a case to the trial Court for fresh hearing is not called for. "

26. In the case of Dr Razia Khatun vs Banu Guha and another reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 135 it was observed by the Appellate Division:

"The long line of judicial decisions is to the effect that the remand order should be avoided as far as possible and even the Privy Council in some cases observed that indiscriminate order of remand tantamount to shirking the responsibility."

27. In the Case of Abdul Awal Khan vs Md Sadu Mia and others reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 156 the Appellate Division held:

"when evidences on all material points are there on record, the revisional court is not justified in sending the case back to the Court below for reconsidering the matter."

28. In the case of Abdul Mannan and others vs Akram Ali and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 124 it was held by the Appellate Division:

"both oral and documentary evidences having been available on record there was no necessity for the remand as ordered by the High Court Division."

29. In the case of Haji Mustafiqur Rahman being dead his heirs Kabir Ahamed and others vs A Kader reported in 3 BLC (AD) 38 it is held:

"It is well settled that remand orders are not to be made as a matter of course, it should be avoided as far as possible. "

<u>30. In view of the discussion made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above we are of the view that the lower Appellate Court was fully competent to decide the case by itself as the evidence and other materials on record were sufficient to enable it to come to a final decision without entailing the parties in unnecessary trouble and expenses and the appellate court shirked its responsibility and thus committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial.</u>

31. Having regard to the facts, the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner prevails and appears to have a good deal of force.

<u>32. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the ends of justice will be met if the matter is remitted to the Court of appeal below for final disposal of the matter on merit and then pass whatever order or orders it thinks appropriate in the interest of justice.</u>

<u>33. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 28-8-2002 passed in Title Appeal No. 157 of 2001 is hereby silt aside and the suit is sent back on remand to the Court of appeal below for disposal on merit touching all points.</u>

34. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

<u>35. The learned Judge of the Court of appeal below is directed to dispose of the appeal expeditiously, preferably within three months from the date of receipt of this order.</u>

Send down the lower Courts record at once with a copy of the judgment for information and for taking necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule tinder section 25 of The Small Cause Courts Act at the instance of the tenant-petitioner is directed against the judgment and the decree dated 31-7-1995 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Sadar, Chittagong in SCC Suit No. 6 of 1993 decreeing the suit.

2. Relevant facts for disposal of the Rule are that the defendant No. 1 is the tenant and the opposite party as a plaintiff instituted the above mentioned ejectment suit against the tenant-petitioner alleging, inter alia, that the plaintiff let out the suit premises to the tenant-petitioner on a monthly rent of Taka 5,00 according to Christian Era which was to be paid within 15th day of the next month but the tenant-petitioner did never pay the rent according to the contract and he was a habitual defaulter and in spite of demand, he irregularly paid rents up to August, 1991 and he stopped paying rent from the month of September, 1991 and, as such, he has been a defaulter since then. It has been also alleged that the suit premises was required by the plaintiff for her bonafide use that though the suit premises was rented for stationery shop but the tenant-petitioner Sublette the same to the defendant No. 2 who has been running a hotel and restaurant business, previously in the name of "Baro Aowlia" and subsequently "Rahmania Hotel and Restaurant" without her consent and the smoke from ovens has been causing harm to the corrugated tin and the wall, as such, the tenant-petitioner is also an undesirable tenant. It has been further alleged that a notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act determining the tenancy on the expiry of the month of October, 1992 was sent upon the tenant-petitioner on 5-10-1992, one in the shop address and another in the residential address of the tenant-petitioner by registered post with A/D which came back to the plaintiff with the postal peon's remark "unnerved" But other copy of the said notice sent under certificate of posting in the residential and shop address of the tenant petitioner were duly served. To avoid legal complications another fresh copy of notice dated 24-7-1993 under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act determining the tenancy after the expiry of the month of August, 1993 was sent to the shop and residential address of the tenant-petitioner under registered post with A/D and under certificate of posting and for personal service. The notice sent under certificate of posting were duly served on the tenant-petitioner. Besides, on the photo copy of another notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act dated 24-7-1993, the tenant-petitioner by putting his signature on 1-8-1993 received the same. The other copy of notice dated 24-7-1993 sent to the shop and residential address under registered post with A/D came back to the plaintiff again with the postal peon's remark “বার বার খবর দেওয়া সত্ত্বেও প্রাপককে হাজির না পাইয়া ফেরৎ।” But in spite of service of notice, the tenant-petitioner has not yet handed over the possession of the suit premises. Ultimately, the plaintiff filed the ejectment suit along with the claim for compensation with effect from 1-9-1993 till 14-1-1993 at the rate of Taka 50 amounting to Taka 3,755 for 55 days.

3. The tenant-petitioner as defendant No. 1 by filing a written statement contended that no notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act was served upon him and he is not a defaulter and he did not sub-let the suit premises to the defendant No. 2 and that he himself has been running business in the suit shop in the name of "Rahmania Hotel and Resturant" and he has been paying rents regularly from the very beginning of the tenancy since 1955 but in the year 1991, when the suit premises was demolished by tornado, he then built up the present suit premise and decorated it by spending about Taka 90,000 on the permission of the landlady plaintiff. Subsequently, when the landlady-demanded Taka 1500 (fifteen hundred) as monthly rent, the relationship between them had deteriorated as the plaintiff refused to accept the rent from him in spite of offer, so the tenant petitioner on filing the Rent Control Case No. 32 of 1991 deposited the rents and in view of the dismissal of the said Rent Control Case he went on appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 325 of 1991 in which the appellate Court affirmed the decision of the Rent Controller and that he has been collecting necessary papers for filing revision in the High Court.

4. The learned Assistant Judge and the SCC Judge upon assessment of the oral and documentary evidence of the parties, decreed the suit on the finding that the petitioner is a habitual defaulter and notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act was duly served upon the tenant

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and the decree, the tenant as the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr Maqbul Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act determining the tenancy has not been properly served upon the tenant-petitioner. He further submits that the notice not being served upon the tenant-petitioner, the judgment and the decree are liable to be set aside. It is further submitted by him that the Court below committed an error in not finding that the rent deposit case is awaiting for adjudication before this court and in case if it is found by this court that the tenant petitioner is eligible to deposit rent with the Rent Controller, the question of petitioner's default will go. He further submits that while the monthly rent is at Taka 500, the compensation awarded by the trial Court is very high and, the learned SCC Judge committed an error of law in decreeing the suit and awarding the compensation.

7. On the other hand, Mr Mohammad Ismail, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, submits that notice has been legally served upon the tenant-petitioner in view of his receipt of the photo copy of the notice by putting his signature thereon. It is submitted by him further that by not disowning the signature specifically in the written statement, the tenant is estopped in raising the plea of non-service of notice under section 106 of The Transfer of property Act during the trial. It is further submitted by the learned Advocate that since the envelop containing the notice under section No. 106 of The Transfer of property Act was duly registered and posted in the correct address of the tenant petitioner, usual presumption is that notice was duly served. He then submits that the compensation as awarded by the trial Court is in accordance with law. He, thus, supports the judgment and decree of the learned SCC Judge and has referred to certain decisions to be discussed herein below.

8. At the time of hearing I have been taken through the judgment of the learned SCC Judge and other connected materials on record. Admittedly, the petitioner was a tenant under the landlady opposite party in respect of the suit premises. The moot question as raised before me is as to the legality of the service of notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act determining the tenancy between the tenant-petitioner and the opposite party landlady with the expiry of the month of 31st August, 1993. From the undelivered envelop Exhibit 4-4 (ka), it is evident that the plaintiff sent the notice dated 24-7-1993 under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act through registered post with A/D upon the tenant petitioner in both the hotel and the restaurant address and also in the residential address of the tenant-petitioner but it came back to the plaintiff opposite party with the endorsement of the postal peon on the back of the envelop in the following:

“বার বার তালাশে। প্রাপককে ঠিকানা স্থলে হাজিরা না পাইয়া ফেরত।”

These Exhibit 4 and 4(Ka) further transpires that the postal peon attempted to serve the notice upon the tenant-petitioner on several occasions between 25-7-1993 and 1-8-1993 and ultimately these were sent back to the addresses on 4-8-1993 with the aforesaid endorsement in the back of each of the Exhibits.

9. The tenant-petitioner has admitted in his written statement that he has been carrying on business under the name and style of Rahmania Hotel and Restaurant at 257, DT Road, Dewanhat. When the notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act was sent correctly under registered post in the said address, non-receipt of such notice, by the tenant-petitioner or any of his servants working in the aforesaid hotel and the restaurant, would indicate wilful avoidance of the same. In such circumstances, it has to be presumed under section 114(f) of The Evidence Act that the notice sent under section 106 was duly served on the tenant-petitioner. In this regard, reliance may be placed in the case of Rokeya Begum vs Shah M Yeamin and another reported in 1992 BLD 406. In the said case similar question arose. Learned judge of the Single Bench of this Court on discussing various cases of our jurisdiction including that of foreign jurisdiction held;

"Notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act posted on September 14, 1986 on pre-payment with correct address. Postal peon called at the address four times within the period from September 16, 1986 to September 22, 1986. Tenant in his written statement admitted to have been carrying on business at the address. No evidence to show that he had been away from the premises during the period and there was none who could accept the letter on his behalf. No reason why the registered letter could not be served on him."

10. In another place of the judgment the learned Judge has stated the following:

"It is manifest that section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, in clear terms, permits the sending of the notice under that section by registered post. There being no contrary intention expressed in the Transfer of Property Act the provision of section 27 of the General Clauses Act shall apply, and once it is established that a pre-paid registered notice in a document containing the correct address of the tenant was delivered to the post office it shall be presumed that the notice has been duly served on the address."

11. The learned Advocate for the petitioner refers to the case of Hajee Khabiruddin Ahmed vs Salam Kabir reported in 34 DLR (AD) 271. In this case similar question arose as to the presumption of service of notice when a registered letter was proved to have been duly addressed and posted. With regard to the question of due service of notice upon the tenant under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act, their Lordships in the Appellate Division with reference to the provisions of section 27 of the General Clauses Act, held as follows:

“The provision of section 27 did not leave any scope for drawing any adverse presumption regarding service of notice. in case of a letter sent by registered post according to these provisions, as soon as the posting by registered post of a properly addressed letter containing any notice or document to be served by post is proved, such service of notice shall, be deemed to have been effected after the lapse of a reasonable time."

<u>12. The decisions referred to above are quite applicable in this case. Upon perusal of the Exhibit 4 'Kha' a Copy of the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act dated 24-7-1993, the learned SSC Judge came to his finding that the tenant-petitioner himself received the copy of the notice by signing his name on the copy of the said notice on 1-8-1993 and on comparison with the signature of the tenant-petitioner with other documents on record, he reached to his decision that the signature of the tenant-petitioner appearing in Exhibit 4 'Kha' tallies with that of other documents on record. This finding of fact by the learned SCC Judge being based on evidence on record is not permitted to be disturbed by this court in its revisional jurisdiction.</u>

13. On the next submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party as to the question of estoppel, it may be viewed that by not refusing the specific averment of the plaint disowning the fact of signing upon the copy of the notice by the tenant petitioner in his written statement, certainly the doctrine of estoppel has come in to play and, thereby, the tenant petitioner was precluded from making any statement before the court during the trial that no notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act was served upon him.

14. In view of my above discussion and the legal position as to the service of notice under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act it appears to me that the learned SCC Judge has committed no error of law in his decision occasioning failure of justice in holding the view that the notice under section 106 was duly served on the tenant-petitioner.

15. Further, on the question of default, learned SCC Judge has held the petitioner as defaulter after assessment of the oral and documentary evidence on record. He has further held that the deposits of rent by the tenant petitioner in the above stated Rent Control Case No. 32 of 1991 are not valid deposits and in support of his decision, he has referred to the case Ramjan Ali vs Hedayetullah, 31 DLR (AD) 183. In this case their Lordship in the Appellate Division, while discussing the case of AK Fazlul Hoque vs Nibaron Chandra Saha 19 DLR 901, Mollah Mahbub Ali vs Jonah Ali, 8 DLR 448 and Aunada Sundari Karmakar vs Dr Mazammel Hoque, 12 DLR 720 observed as follows:

"A tenant is protected not withstanding the provisions of Transfer of Property Act or the Contract Act from ejectment, "as long as he pays rent" to the full extent allowed by the Ordinance and he performs the conditions of the tenancy. The expression, 'as long as the tenant pays rent' in our opinion, no 'doubt indicates that the point of default on the part of the tenant will not only be the date of filing of the suit but will continue till decree is passed. It does not, however, mean if the tenant subsequent to the filing of the suit has deposited the rent with the Rent Controller, the default incurred earlier is cured. On the contrary the tenant's liability for default even after the filing of the suit continue under the law till the passing of the decree."

16. In another place of their judgment in the said case their Lordships referring to the case of East Bengal Paper Traders vs Md Waziullah, 21 DLR, 572; Sk Md Emdaduddin vs Jasimuddin, 25 DLR 404; Zainal Abedin vs Nazira Banu, 26 DLR 221; Must Hayatunnessa vs Abdur Rahman, 26 DLR 342; Dr Md Arfan Ali vs Md Bazlur Rahman Chowdhury 28 DLR 443; Abul Layes vs Anwara Khatoon 29 DLR (SC) 13 observed as follows:

"The tenant must pay rent in terms of the contract, and in the absence of the contract within fifteen day next following month on which the rent falls due, and if the landlord refuse to accept rent tendered by the tenant, the tenant must remit the rent within the aforesaid fifteenth day of the following month by money order. If the rent remitted by money order is refused, the tenant can deposit the rent with the Rent-Controller within a fortnight from the date of the receipt of the undelivered rent sent through the postal authority and when these conditions as prescribed in the Ordinance are fulfilled by the tenant, he gets the protection, otherwise the protection from ejectment on ground of default in the payment of rent granted by the Ordinance is clearly taken away by the express language of sub-section (5) of section 18."

17. In the concluding part on the facts of the case, their Lordship stated in the followings:

"It is the concurrent finding of the courts below that the tenant failed to prove that he did tender rent for the month's of Kartick and Aswin, 1380 BS as alleged by him, and the remittance and the deposit were made beyond the time prescribed by the law. The default in the payment of rent has taken place in terms of the Ordinance. The tenant appellant before us by the clear language of sub-section (5) of section 18, is disentitled to the protection from ejectment on the ground of default in the payment of rent. The Ordinance makes no distinction between the default of one month or default for more than one month or a habitual defaulter. If the default has taken place the protection from ejectment is withdrawn and that has occurred in the particular case."

<u>18. In the instant case the tenant petitioner appears to have deposited the rents of two months September and October on 14-11-1991 in Rent Control Case No. 32 of 1991 and also deposited rents by challan beyond the prescribed period of time allowed by The Rent Control Act. Further to mention that the learned Advocate for the petitioner, fails to supply us any papers showing institution of any civil revision in this Court against the decision passed in the aforesaid Miscellaneous Appeal No. 325 of 1991 affirming the order of the Rent Controller dismissing the Rent Control Case No. 32 of 1991. In the facts and circumstances and the cited decisions stated above, the tenant petitioner in the instant case appears to have disentitled him in getting protection from ejectment for the invalid deposits as rightly found by the learned SCC Judge.</u>

19. Next, on the question of compensation, it appears that in the facts and circumstances of the case, learned SCC Judge has correctly assessed the amount of compensation in exercise of his discretion and I find no legal ground to interfere with the decision of the learned SCC Judge in this regard.

20. For the reasons stated above, I find no illegality in the impugned judgment and the decree complained of in this revision.

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged without costs.

22. The judgment and the decree of the learned SCC Judge dated 31-7-1995 passed in the SCC Suit No. 6 of 1993 are upheld.

23. The tenant petitioner is allowed to hand over the vacant possession of the suit premises to the plaintiff opposite party within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the record by the lower court, in default, he will be evicted in due process of law.

24. Stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

Send down LCR to the court concerned at once.

End.

lawyer:
MI Chowdhury, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
KS Nabi, Attorney-General with AM Aminuddin, Assistant Attorney-General — For the Respondents.
parties:
Rehana Kamal and another ------ Petitioners
Vs. 
Chairman Court of Settlement and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mahfuzur Rahman J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why listing of the building at plot Nos. 537 and 538 of Road No. 8, Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka as abandoned building, published in the ''ka'' list as item No. 31 of Bangladesh Gazette dated 23-9-86 and the order passed by the 1st Court of Settlement on 26-11-92 in Case No. 3 of 1992 dismissing the case should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

2. The short fact relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule is that, the disputed building situated at plot Nos. 537 and 538 known as "Hasan House", Holding No. 14, Road No. 8 Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka was alloted to Dr. Mahmood Hasan former Vice-Chancellor of Dhaka University and Secretary, Foreign Affairs of erstwhile Pakistan by a lease deed executed on 24-8-56 and registered on 25-8-56 by the Dhaka Improvement Trust. The said original owner namely, Dr. Mahmood Hasan after allotment constructed a building on the plots named as aforesaid. During his lifetime he rented it to the American Embassy by executing a lease deed which expired in 1970 and thereafter second lease deed was also executed in favour of the American Embassy on 18-8-70 which also expired on 15th November, 1973. Dr. Mahmood Hasan on 23-10-70 distributed of his properties to his wife, sons and daughters by Notarial deed being Notarial deed being Notarial Deed No. 911 which was accepted by his heirs. Accordingly, the aforesaid building was equally bequeathed to his daughter namely, Mrs. Rehana Kamal petitioner No. 1 and Mrs Rifat Alam mother of petitioner No.2 and this Rifat Alam made an oral gift to her minor son Syed Ayyab Alam on 27-2-71 in Dhaka and confirmed the same by a Notarial Declaration in Canada on 28-11-88. After making the gift to the heirs Dr Mahmood Hasan died on 25-12-70 in Karachi. After the death of Dr. Mahmood Hasan the tenant of the building in question ie the American Embassy on 11-10-71 before the birth of Bangladesh accepted Mrs. Rehana Kamal and Mrs. Rifat Alam as their landlady and paid them one year's advance rent amounting to Taka 24,000.00 @ Taka 2,000.00 per month less Taka 475.00 as cost of overhead water of the house in question for the period November 15th, 1971 to 14th November, 1972 and issued vouchers. The rent had been deposited in the joint SB Account of both the sisters in American Express International Banking Corporation, Alico Building, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka. The aforesaid two sisters Mrs. Rehana Kamal and Mrs. Rifat Alam mutated their names in the Dhaka Municipal Corporation and lastly paid urban Immovable tax of Taka 1,000.00 for the year 1974-75 by pay order No.041372 on American Express, Dhaka and the tax receipt was issued on 24-1-76 by the Municipal Corporation for payment on 30-8-75 vide Annexure-I to this petition. Accordingly, they paid Municipal tax, all revenues payable and bills including light charges for the house in question for the period of October, 1972 from their joint SB Account No. 8719 maintained with the American Express International Banking Corporation, Alico Building, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka. The bill was sent for payment to the Manager of the Bank by special messenger with a forwarding letter dated 22-6-73 by the Assistant Administrative Officer of the American Embassy. They also paid Urban Immovable Tax of the house in question for the year 1969-70 to 1972-73 out of their joint SB Account No.8719 maintained with American Express International Banking Corporation. The notice of demand for the tax together with TR Form No.7 was sent to the, Manager of the said Bank with a forwarding letter dated 19-9-73 by the Administrative Officer of American Embassy with a copy to Mrs. Mizanur Rahman the local Power of Attorney holder. The Assistant Administrative Officer of the American Embassy and 2 sisters Mrs Rehana Kamal and Mrs. Rifat Alam were in correspondence for the renewal of the lease agreement of the building in question and the Assistant Administrative Officer Mr.Carrol F. Wines on May 17, 1973 wrote a letter to Mrs Rehana Kamal in West Germany with a copy to Mrs Mizanur Rahman, In turn the owners of the building were in correspondence with the tenant the American Embassy. Thereafter, one Mr. Abdur Rob Chowdhury, Deputy of the Ministry of Works wrote a letter to the Embassy by Memo No. 2F-111-156/73/8 dated 23-10-73, informing the Embassy that the legal status of the house is under examination in the Ministry of Law and in this circumstances they may choose not to pay rent to the absentee owners, their attorneys and agent until further communication from this Ministry vide Annexure-M to this petition. The Assistant Administrative Officer aforesaid of the American Embassy wrote a letter on November 5th, 1973 to Mrs. Anwari Begum, Power of Attorney holder of one the sisters, informing that in the circumstances they are not in a position either to negotiate a new lease or make a further correspondence with her concerning the premises; but assured that they are continuously alert on the subject and will immediately inform her when a course is open to them. On 20-11-73 Joint Secretary of the Ministry of Works wrote to the Administrative Officer of the Embassy to the effect that he was directed to advise that pending decision of the legal status of the property in question within the meaning of the Article 2 of the President Order 16 of 1972 the Ministry allowed the Embassy to stay in the house vide Annexure-Q to the petition. Then the Administrative Officer of the American Embassy by a letter dated 31-12-75 invited personal attention of the Secretary Ministry of Works to look into the matter and to decide the legal status of the house vide Annexure-P. In the meantime Major (Retd) Mahmud Kamal, husband of Mrs. Rehana Kamal (petitioner No.1) came to Bangladesh from Germany and met the Secretary, Ministry of Works on 7-5-76 and also submitted a written representation to him vide Annexure- Q. When the decision of the legal status of the house was thus pending the Attorneys of Mrs. Rehana Kamal and Rifat Alam wanted to pay revenue, tax to the Government but the Government refused to accept it on the ground that the house had already been declared abandoned property and the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka advised them in writing on 6-1-91 to contact with the Management Board of the Abandoned Property cell vide Annexure-R. On 23-9-86 the aforesaid building was published in the Gazette Extraordinary as an abandoned building in the ''Ka'' list at page No.9762(14) against serial No.31 vide Annexure-S. In the meantime Syed Ayyed Alam, petitioner No. 2, son of Mrs. Rifat Alam came to Bangladesh from Canada and knowing that the house was declared abandoned property and a Settlement Court was established to try the abandoned cases, instructed the Attorney to apply to the 1st Court of Settlement, Segun Bagicha, Dhaka. Accordingly the Attorney filed an application on 8-4-91 before the respondent No.1 under section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1975 for exclusion of the building from the list. Both the petitioners have given general power of attorney to Mrs. Anwari Begum and Mrs Sajeda Chowdhury on 27-11-88 and 28-11-88 respectively to defend them and to file suit, petition, etc. in due course including this Hon'ble Court. The said General Power of Attorney are annexed herewith as Annexures-A and A-1.

3. Respondent No. 1 by his judgment and order dated 26-11-92 rejected 23 cases including the case No. 3 of 1992 of the petitioners filed under section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1975 for exclusion and release of the house from the list of abandoned property by one judgment in the case No. 248 of 1988 as barred by limitation.

4. Thereafter the petitioners moved this petition before this Court and obtained this Rule.

5. By supplementary affidavit the petitioners filed certain documents including the passport, etc. showing that the petitioners are Bangladesh Nationals and their whereabouts were very much known to the Government and they did not abandon their citizenship.

6. Respondent No. 2, the Government of Bangladesh, contested the petition by filing a written affidavit-in-opposition denying all material allegations but admitting that the DIT leased out the case property for 99 years to Dr. Mahmood Hasan who died in Karachi on 25-12-90 leaving behind Rifat Alam and Rehana Kamal as 2 daughters and 2 sons as his legal heirs and successors. It is further stated that during and after liberation war they never returned to Bangladesh and they ceased to occupy, manage and supervise the case property in person. They were the citizens of a state which was engaged in military operation with the People''s Republic of Bangladesh and the property was legally taken over by the Government as abandoned property under President''s Order 16 of 1972. It is further stated that the petitioner's petition before the 1st Court of Settlement was hopelessly barred by limitation and they filed the writ petition before this Hon'ble Court by creating some false, fabricated, baseless antedated papers and the petitioners are not the citizens of Bangladesh and they are not entitled to any relief sought for.

7. Mr. M I Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submitted that both the sisters namely, Rifat Alam and Rehana Kamal became the owner of the building in question according to gift by their father who died in the year 1970 in Karachi. During the lifetime their father rented it to the American Embassy, of the then East Pakistan and they were accepted as the landladies by the said Embassy on 11-10-71 and paid them one year''s advance rent amounting to Taka 24,000.00 @ Taka 2,000.00 per month and issued voucher Annexure-H. Both the sisters mutated their names in the Dhaka Municipal Corporation and they paid lastly the Municipal Tax of Taka 1000.00 for the year 1974-75 by the pay order No. 041372 of American Embassy and the tax receipts was issued on 24-1-76 by the Municipal Corporation for payment on 30-8-75 Annexure-I. He submits that one of the daughters, Rifat Alam, wife of Syed Firoj Alam, gifted her share in the property to her son Syed Ayyad Alam petitioner No. 2. They were possessed the same through tenants who used to deposit rent for the premises in Joint SB Account of the both sisters with American Express International Bank Motijheel. He submits that the property cannot be abandoned as the petitioners are Bangladeshi Nationals who acquired it by way of gift from their father in the year 1970 before the birth of Bangladesh. He submits that the building was rented by the original owner Dr. Mahmood Hasan with American Embassy by executing a lease deed and subsequently it was renewed. After expiry the lease deed was also excited on 18-8-70 which expired on 25-11-73 Annexure-E. He submits that it is also a recorded fact that both the sisters mutated their names in respect of the building with Dhaka Municipal Corporation and paid rent for the year 1974-75 and the tax receipts was issued on 24-1-76 for payment up to 30-8-75 Annexure-I. The learned Advocate submits that there is nothing to show that the petitioners ever obtained citizenship of any other country other than Bangladesh during liberation wars which were enemies of Bangladesh or the petitioners were connected with any activities in any manner prejudicial to Bangladesh. Rather, he submits that the Municipality taking them as Bangladeshis mutated their names and received all taxes, revenues, etc. They have also filed a Nationality Certificate from the local Union Parishad Chairman Annexure-B and also another Nationality Certificate from the Chairman of Ward No. 62 of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation Annexure-C. Regarding petitioner No. 2, a certificate has been given by an Advocate of this Court stating that Syed Ayyed Alam, son of Syed Fayyaz Alam, is a Bangladeshi National and Bengali speaking and serves in Canada. By the supplementary affidavit, he submits, he filed the passport issued at Dhaka on 30-11-65, the certificate issued on 3rd February 1976 of passing Intermediate Examination under Dhaka University dated 8-7-61 and the passport issued from Dhaka shows her place of birth at Dhaka. The learned Advocate further submits that the assertion of the petitioners that they are Bangladeshi Nationals is not controverted by the contesting respondents and the property in question cannot be declared as abandoned since that was occupied by their tenants and they possessed the same through their tenants. The learned Advocate referred to section 2(1), President''s Order 16 of 1972.

"Abandoned Property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including:

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People''s Republic of Bangladesh."

And contends that there is nothing to show that after 25th day of March, 1971, the petitioner were citizen of Pakistan which was at war or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh to bring the property within the mischief of abandoned property as defined under the aforesaid section and also is not supported by any document or evidence. He submits that admittedly on 25th December, 1970 Dr. Mahmood Hasan died and prior to that his two daughters inherited by way of gift the building in question which was rented to the American Embassy by Dr. Mahmood Hasan himself during his life time, subsequently renewed for 2 years and the American Embassy accepted these two sisters as their landladies and paid rent to them which was deposited in the Joint S/B. Account of the 2 sisters maintained in American Express International Bank situated at Alico Building Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka and then referred to a letter addressed to the Embassy by the Deputy Secretary Ministry of Works vide Memo No. 2F-III-156/73/8 dated 23-10-73 Annexure-M to this petition informing the Embassy that legal status of the house is under examination in the Ministry of Law and in this circumstances they may choose not to pay rent to the absentee owners, their Attorneys and agents until further communication from this Ministry. Mr. Chowdhury submits that this amply shows that Ministry was aware of the fact that both the sisters and petitioners had their possession of the properties through their tenant. Then by a letter dated 20-11-73 vide Annexure-O the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Works wrote a letter to the Assistant Administrative Officer of the American Embassy in Bangladesh stating therein that he is directed to advise that pending decision of the legal status of the property in question within the meaning of Article 2 of the Presidents Order 16 of 1972 the Ministry allowed them to stay in the house till last day of the year 1975. Since the legal status of the house was not determined the American Embassy invited the attention of the Ministry to look into the matter and decide the status vide Annexure-P. On such facts, Mr. Chowdhury submits, that it does not attract section 2(1) of the Abandoned Property as provided in President's Order 16 of 1972. He next contends that since even on the last day of the year 1975 the Government could not decide whether the property is an abandoned property. In the middle of 1976, Mahmood Kama, husband of petitioner No. 1, filed an application on 7-5-76 to the Secretary of Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh for release of the property of the petitioners but with no effect. On an application by the Attorney of petitioner No. 1 Mrs Anwari Begum a reply was given by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka vide Annexure-R informing her that the property had been taken as abandoned and leased out and to contact the Management Board. The learned Advocate further submits that as they were residing with their father from before 1971 at Karachi and during liberation war they were stranded there and Pakistan Government did not allow them to leave Pakistan officially. In October, 1972 the husband of petitioner No. 1 managed to escape from Pakistan and went to Germany. This assertion of the petitioner No. 1 has not been challenged by the Government. In support of his contention regarding citizenship, Mr. Chowdhury, referred to Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order 1972 (President''s Order 149 of 1972) which provides that

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, on the commencement of this order, every person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh-.........

(i).........

(ii)..........

Provided that if any person is a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh or its dependent is, in the course of his employment or for pursuit of his studies, residing in a country which was at war with, or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh, such person, or his dependents, shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh."

He also referred the case of People''s Republic of Bangladesh vs. Abdul Haque, reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143 paragraph 4 wherein it has been held:

"The respondent was born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh but his temporary absence is covered by the proviso quoted above and the law says "They shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh", notwithstanding his temporary residence in a country which was at war or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh."

The learned Advocate then referred the case of Bangladesh vs. ATJ Industries Ltd. and others reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120-relevant para 6, 7, 9 wherein it has been held that:

6, 7- "The questions involved in the interpretation of articles 2(1) and 4 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order may be divided into three heads. First is what on true construction of the Article 2(1) is the meaning of abandoned property Secondly whether formation of the opinion of the Government is necessary for holding or declaring property as abandoned property and its vesting under article 4 and thirdly, whether prior show cause notice is mandatory before the opinion of the Government is formed.

On the first question, a reference to the language of article 2(1) indicates that the language is not free from ambiguity. It appears that the legislative authority has employed multiple systems in the definition. It has first defined with denotation and connotation the words abandoned property, and then has employed an inclusive definition, and then an exclusion clause. It has also added an explanation. Interpretation of the definition clause no doubt creates some complexity. The best way to interpret it is to give a harmonious meaning to all the clauses of articles 2(1) so that each clause gets its own meaning and at the same time harmonizes with the meaning of the whole. The defining part denotes property owned by a person who is either not present in Bangladesh, or whose whereabouts are not known, or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property. A question may arise whether the three sub-clauses are disjunctive or conjunctive. We think they have been used disjunctively and there is no need to construe them conjunctively.

(9) Then is the exclusion clause. The first question which arises is whether the exclusion clause also qualifies the inclusion clause. Except for the fact that the exclusion clause follows the inclusion clause, there is nothing in the grammatical construction of the whole clause to indicate that it qualifies the inclusion clause. Exclusion clause contemplates two categories of property. The first is the property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The second is the property which is in possession or under the control of the Government under any law in force for the time being. The second part of this exclusion clause needs no classification for the purpose of this appeal. The first part of the exclusion clause is not only an exception but it qualifies the definition clause and this qualification is such that it is implicit with the definition and an integral part of it. Definition clause cannot be conceived without this implicit qualification. What then is the qualification? The sub-clause says that if the residence of the owner of a property outside Bangladesh is, in the opinion of the Government, for a purpose not prejudicial to the interest of the State, then the property is not an abandoned property. In this sub-clause the condition is such that the operation of the definition clause will come into effect only when the Government has formed its opinion. The definition clause with inclusion and exclusion clauses have been so framed that we do not find any other reasonable construction to bestow on entire clause of article 2(1) than we have given. On the formation of opinion of the Government the definition clause comes into operation, but once opinion has been formed the law takes effect from 28-2-72, the day President''s Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated. The Government is to form its opinion on the events as they stood on 28-2-72."

Relying on this decision he submits that to declare the property as an abandoned property the Government is to form an opinion that the owner of the property is not in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts were not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or to manage the property before declaring the property as abandoned. On the formation of opinion of the Government the definition clause comes into operation but once opinion has been formed the law takes effect from 28-2-72, the day President''s Order 16 of 1972 was promulgated. The Government is to form its opinion on the events as they stood on 28-2-72. He points out that in this particular case admittedly till the last day of the year 1975 (31 December) Government could not form any opinion as to the status of the property. In support of his contention he referred the case of Speed Bird Navigation Co and another vs. Bangladesh and others, reported in 27 DLR 170 relevant paragraph 37 wherein it has been held:

"The necessary implication of this clause appears to be that the properties of those absentee owners about whose purpose of staying outside the country the Government has not as yet formed any opinion whatsoever cannot also be regarded as abandoned properties, but the properties of those persons about whose purpose of staying abroad the Government has formed an adverse opinion, shall be deemed to be abandoned properties."

8. He next referred the case of Farida Aziz vs. Government of Bangladesh and another, reported in 45 DLR 12 wherein it has been held:

"Whenever possession of a house is taken by the Government from lawful tenant of the owner such possession for the purpose of treating it as an abandoned property is illegal, for, the owner is in possession through the tenant. The Government in such a position is not empowered to take possession of the house on plea of absence of the owner and property does not fall within the meaning of "abandoned property."

Relying on this decision, he submits that the property in question admittedly was in possession of lawful tenant of the petitioners and the property taken as abandoned from the lawful tenant was without any lawful authority.

9. He next referred the case of Nurul Hoque (Md) vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 46 DLR 601 wherein it has been held:

"To come within the definition of abandoned property a property has to be a property the owner of which is not present in Bangladesh and whose whereabouts are either not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property and whose stay abroad is, in the opinion of the Government, prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. Formation of such opinion is essentially required."

He next contends that as per sub-article 3 of Article 7 of President''s Order 16 of 1972 the notice is essentially required to be served on the person in possession of the abandoned property in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession mentioned in the notice within such period. Section 7 sub-sections 1, 2, 3 and 4 which runs as follows:

7(1) "Where any abandoned property is not in possession of any person the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate (or the authorized officer) shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed.

(2) Where any abandoned property is in possession of any person, such person shall, within seven days of the commencement of this Order, surrender such property to the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate, (or the authorized officer)

(3) Where the person in possession of any abandoned property fails to surrender such property as he is required to do under clause (2), the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate, (or the authorized officer) shall serve a notice on him in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession of the property, within seven days of the service of notice, to the person mentioned in the notice or to show cause against such surrender within the said period and, if he fails to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate (or the authorized officer) shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed.

(4) Where the person on whom a notice is served under clause (3) shows cause, within the period specified in that clause, against the surrender of the abandoned property, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate, (or the authorized officer) as the case may be, shall, after making such local enquiry as he may consider necessary and after giving the person an opportunity of being heard, pass such order as he deems fit."

The learned Advocate submits that admittedly no notice was served on any person, either on the petitioners or their tenant, American Embassy, who was occupying on behalf of the petitioners and admittedly till last date of December, 1975 (31-12-75) the status of the property was not determined, listing the properties as abandoned property and publication thereby is absolutely illegal. In support of his contention he referred the case of Amela Khatoon and others vs. Chairman Court of Settlement and another, reported in 46 DLR 18 wherein it has been held:

"Listing of property as abandoned and publication thereof in the official gazette in respect of which notices have not been issued will be per se illegal."

He also referred the case of Nurul Haque (Md) vs. Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 46 DLR 601 relevant paragraphs 21 and 22.

"If any statute takes away the right to property of any person the provision thereof has to be strictly construed and necessary formalities required under the statute have to be duly complied with."

"Since no notice for surrendering possession of the property was issued, it can hardly be said that the property has been lawfully included in the list of abandoned buildings."

The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the fundamental right of the petitioners to maintain or acquire property as guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh there can be no limitation in view of the fact that the inclusion of the abandoned property has been made without any lawful authority and in clear violation of the mandatory provision for the purpose embodied in President''s Order 16 of 1972. He submits that the Settlement Court dismissed the case of the petitioners only on the point of limitation without going into any other points in the case. The learned Advocate referred the case of Saleha Begum vs. Chairman 1st Court of Settlement and another, reported in 49 DLR 243 wherein it has been held that the "petitioner is entitled to challenge the inclusion of her house from the list of abandoned building by way of the court''s writ jurisdiction in spite of dismissal order of her application by the Court of Settlement on the ground of limitation." He also referred the case of jobon Nahar and others vs. Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 49 DLR 108 wherein it has been held:

"The right to enforce a fundamental right is another fundamental right which gives the petitioner right to move this court even though his application was rejected by Settlement Court on ground of limitation."

The learned Advocate lastly contends that on the recorded facts and circumstances the property could not be declared as abandoned and listing of it as abandon is illegal and without any lawful authority.

10. Mr. KS Nabi the learned Attorney-General for the respondents submits that this writ petition is not maintainable in view of the fact that there was a delay of 4 years in filing the case before the Settlement Court and as such the petition is liable to be rejected. He submits that Article 4 of President''s Order 16 of 1972 provides that on the commencement of this Order all abandoned property in Bangladesh shall vest in the Government. He next contends that the petitioners have got no locusstandi to file this Writ petition as because they are Pakistani Nationals.

11. We are unable to accept the submission of the learned Attorney-General. The properties in question admittedly were allotted to Dr. Mahmood Hasan and Dr. Mahmood Hasan constructed a building there on and died in December 25, 1970 in Karachi. Before death he distributed all his properties to his wife, daughters and sons, who accepted the same and his two daughters namely; Rehana Kamal and Rifat Alam were given the building in question in equal share which has been accepted by other co-sharers and there is no dispute. It appears that in the affidavit-in-opposition it is also admitted by the Government that Dr. Mahmood Hasan died in Karachi on 25-11-70 leaving behind Rifat Alam and Mrs Rehana Kamal amongst other legal heirs as two daughters. In fact there is no denial about acquiring property by two sisters by gift from their father Dr. Mahmood Hasan and there is no denial that before creation of Bangladesh Dr. Mahmood Hasan died in December, 25th, 1970 in Karachi and before his death he gifted the property in question to his 2 daughters namely, petitioner No. 1 and mother of petitioner No. 2 and also there is no denial by any affidavit-in-opposition that both the sisters were accepted as landladies by the tenant American Embassy who was inducted by their father. There is also no denial that they mutated their names with the Dhaka Municipality and paid rent and taxes, etc. Then there is no denial by any affidavit to the assertion made in supplementary affidavit that the petitioner No. 1 and her sister, mother of petitioner No. 2, were stranded in Pakistan and thereafter managed to escape to Germany and Canada in 1973 and furthermore, there is no denial by any affidavit that the tenant American Embassy paid rent to them and the rents were deposited in the Joint SB Account of the 2 sisters with American Express Bank situated at Alico Building, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka. Mr. Attorney-General simply argued on presumption that they are not Bangladeshi Nationals but could not show anything that they obtained citizenship of a country which was at war with Bangladesh, or the two sisters in any way engaged in any prejudicial activities against Bangladesh. It appears that Dr. Mahmood Hasan before his death on December 25th, 1970 gifted his properties to his heirs and the property in question fell in the share of the 2 daughters, petitioner No. 1 and mother of petitioner No. 2 and the American Embassy inducted as tenant by their father, accepted them as their landladies and none of the other heirs of Dr. Mahmood Hasan raised any objection. It appears that in the year 1970 the lease agreement was further renewed for 2 years more and the American Embassy accepting both the sisters as land ledies paid .them rent for 1 year in advance amounting to Taka 24,000.00 @ of Taka 2000.00 per month. In the meantime Rifat Alam, sister of petitioner No. 1 gifted her share to his son Syed Ayyad Alam petitioner No. 2 and to manage their properties both the sisters executed general power of attorney appointing Mrs. Anwari Begum and Mrs Syeda Sajada Chowdhury on 27-12-88 and 28-11-88 respectively. It further appears from the record of the Government annexed hereto the Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Works wrote a letter under Memo No. 2F-III-156/73/8 dated 23-10-73 to the American Embassy informing them that the legal status of the house is under examination in the Ministry of Law and in this circumstances they may choose not to pay rent to the absentee owners, their Attorneys or agents until further communications from the Ministry. From this letter it is abundantly clear that whereabouts of the owners were very much known to the Ministry and also they had attorneys, agents to manage this properties etc. vide Annexure-M. The Assistant Administrative Officer of the Embassy duly informed Mrs. Anowari Begum, constituted attorney of one of the owners, about the letter. Then again, on 20-11-73 one Joint Secretary of the Ministry of Works wrote to the Assistant Administrative Officer of the Embassy informing that he was directed to advise that pending decision of the legal status of the property in question within the meaning of Article 2 of the President''s Order 16 of 1972 the Ministry allowed the Embassy to stay in the house. But when the legal status was not decided for two years thereafter then the Embassy on 31-12-75 wrote a letter to the Secretary, Ministry of Works to look into the matter to decide the status of the house. In the year 1976 Mahmud Kamal, husband of the petitioner No. 1, came to Bangladesh from Germany and met the Secretary, Ministry of Works on 7-5-76 with a written representation to him with a prayer to hand over the property; Annexure-O and since the legal status of the house was thus pending the attorneys of Mrs Rehana Kamal and Mrs. Rifat Alam wanted to pay revenue, tax etc. but the Government refused to accept on the ground that the house has been declared as abandoned property and the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka advised them in writing on 6-1-91 to contact with the Management Board of the abandoned property as it was published in the Gazette Extra-ordinary as abandoned building in the Ka list at page 9762 dated 23-9-86. Thereafter the petitioner No. 2 came to Bangladesh from Canada knowing that his house was declared abandoned property and a Settlement Court was established to try the abandoned cases and instructed the attorneys to apply before respondent No. 1 for exclusion of the building from the list and it was numbered as 3/92 which was dismissed along with 22 other petitions on the ground of limitation. Admittedly till 31st December, 1975 the legal status of the property was not decided by the Government. The President''s Order 16 of 1972 came into force on 28-2-72 and all properties abandoned on or before 25th March, 71 vest in the Government to deal with the administrative control, management and disposal of or otherwise in accordance with the provision of this Order but admittedly from the Annexures-M, N, O, P it appears that the Government could not decide till 31st December, 1975 what will be the status of the property. Only thing they said that the legal status of the property in question was under consideration of the Ministry of Law. From such facts it appears admittedly till 31-12-75 no opinion could be formed by the Government. In the case referred above reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 and 27 DLR 170 wherein it has been held to declare the property as abandoned Government is to form an opinion that the owner of the property is not in Bangladesh his or whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage the property before declaring the property as abandoned. On the formation of opinion by the Government the definition clause comes into operation. The petitioner''s positive case is that they are in possession of the property in question through their tenants and also the assertion of the petitioners that their whereabouts were very much known to the Government have not been denied by the Government by any affidavit.

<u>12. The decisions referred above reported in 45 DLR 12 wherein it has been held that whenever possession of a house is taken by the Government from lawful tenant of the owners for the purpose of treating it as an abandoned property is illegal for the owner is in possession through the tenant and the Government is not empowered to take possession of the house on the plea of the absence of the owner and the property does not fall within the meaning of abandoned property. As per sub-Article 3 of Article 7 of President''s Order 16 of 1972 the notice is essentially required to be served on the person in possession of any abandoned property in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession mentioned in the notice. But admittedly no such notice was served upon the tenants or anybody in possession when the notice is mandatory. In the cases reported in 46 DLR 19 and 46 DLR 601 it has been held that listing of property as abandoned and publication in the Gazette in respect of which the notices have not been issued and without following the formalities strictly as required under the statute in respect of the notices the listing and publication are per se illegal. It has not been asserted or challenged by the Government that the owners of the property are nationals of a country inimical to Bangladesh or they left the property immediately after the war of liberation and acted in a manner prejudicial to the cause of liberation. Government by any affidavit-in-opposition could not place before us any materials to the effect that they were never in the management of the property either directly or by any agent or through tenant and they were in any military operation or acted in any way prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. There is nothing to revert the petitioner specific case that both the sisters stranded in Pakistan and they were resisted from coming to Bangladesh and any way the petitioners managed to escape to Germany and Canada respectively in 1973 and they never ceased to be citizens of Bangladesh. Both the petitioners by supplementary affidavit produced certain documents, nationality certificates, etc. that they are citizens of Bangladesh. But curious enough all those were not controverted by any affidavit-in-opposition and we find no reason to disbelieve those documents. Of course in any petition of certiorari nature this court is not supposed to go into the merits and factual aspect of the case but at the same time it is not debarred also from going into such materials and facts to enquire into whether fundamental rights as guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution is violated. On the findings stated above it is abundantly clear that in violation of the provision of President''s Order 16 of 1972 and Ordinance 54/75 the property was included in the abandoned list which is absolutely illegal, malafide, without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The Settlement Court rejected the application of the petitioners on the ground of limitation only without deciding the case on merit. We are of the view, that this court in such Writ Petition has ample power to look into the factual aspect where fundamental rights of the petitioners have been violated as guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution. In concurrence with the decisions referred above in 49 DLR 108 and 243, we hold, that to enforce fundamental rights the petitioners have a right to move this court though their application for releasing the property was rejected by the Settlement Court on the ground of limitation.</u>

13. In view of the discussions made and decisions referred above we are of the view that listing of the property in question as abandoned and publishing in the ''Ka'' list in the Bangladesh Gazette have been made illegally and without any lawful authority and is liable to be excluded from the list of abandoned property.

14. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The listing of the building at plot Nos. 537 and 538 of Road No. 8, Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka as abandoned building, published in the ''Ka'' list as item No. 31 of Bangladesh Gazette dated 23-9-86 is declared to have been made illegally, malafide without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The respondents are hereby directed to exclude the petitioners building at Plot Nos. 537 and 538, Holding No. 14, Road No. 8 Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka from ''Ka'' list published in the Gazette Extraordinary dated 23-9-86, and hand over vacant possession of the same to the petitioners within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of this order.

End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam with Md Musherraf Hossain Majumder and Nizamul Huq Chowdhury, Advocates—For the Petitioner.

Lutfar Rahman, with KS Salahuddin Ahmed and Md Zahirul Islam, Advocates—For the Opposite Party No. 1.
