parties:
Nasimuddin Mia  ----- Appellant
vs.
Monindra Kumar Maloo and others ---- Respondents
full_judgment:
This Second Appeal at the instance of the defendant-appellant has been preferred from the judgment and decree dated 22.9.72 and 25.9.72 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Tangail in Title Appeal No. 45 of 1970 reversing the judgment and decree dated 31-3-70 and 13.4.70 respectively passed by the learned Subordinate Judge Tangail in OC Suit No. (42 of 1969)/(10 of 1967) dismissing the suit.

2. Facts, in short, are that, the plaintiff brought the suit for cancellation of an exchange deed dated 8-3-63 on declaration that the same is void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. Plaintiff's case, in short, is that the schedule 1 property situated in Bangladesh belonged to the plaintiffs and proforma defendants. The defendant No. 1 Mangla Fakir who originally belonged to Kalihati Police Station within District Tangail left for India long ago and settled in Assam. He came back to the then East Pakistan about a year before the exchange deed in question and there was an agreement between the parties that by mutual exchange the defendant No.1 will get the schedule 1 property of the plaint in Bangladesh from the plaintiffs and proforma defendants and the plaintiffs and proforma defendants will get schedule 2 and 3 properties from the defendant No. 1 in Assam by proper documents of exchange. The plaintiffs and the proforma defendants believed the assurance of the defendant No. 1 regarding the existence of schedule 2 and 3 properties in Assam and they in good faith executed and registered a deed of exchange dated 8.3.63 Exhibit. C in favour of the defendant No. 1 in respect of schedule 1 property in Bangladesh. The plaintiffs however, remained in possession of the schedule 1 property. When they went to Assam they learned that the schedule 2 and 3 properties did not belong to the defendant No. 1. The plaintiffs also found that the defendant No. 1 executed a document in favour of his nephew Amir Hamza on 30.1.65 in respect of the land of schedule 3 property of the plaint. The defendant No. 1 also executed a Hiba deed in respect of schedule 1 property in favour of his sons and other relatives (defendant Nos.2-5) The defendant No. 1 by practising fraud upon the plaintiffs and pro-defendants obtained the deed of exchange Ext.C. He also did not fulfil his part of the contract. The plaintiffs accordingly, prayed for declaration that the deed of exchange Ext. C executed by them is void, ineffective and not binding upon them and also for cancellation of the same.

3. The defendant No. 1 did not contest the suit. The defendant Nos. 2-4 by filing written statement contested the suit. They denied the material allegations made in the plaint.

4. Their case, in short, is that the defendant No. 1 is living in Assam and he used to own and possess the schedule 2 and 3 properties in Assam. The agreement of exchange was drawn up between the parties on 16.11.62 after both the parties had verified the ownership and possession of the lands of schedule 1, 2 and 3 properties. Thereafter according to the terms of the agreement dated 16.11.62, the plaintiffs and pro-defendants executed the deed of exchange dated 8.3.63 Ext. C in respect of the schedule 1 property in favour of the defendant No. 1 and delivered possession of the land. The plaintiffs and the pro-defendants thereafter went to Assam and the defendant No. 1 transferred the schedule 2 and 3 properties in their favour by executing a registered kabala dated 18.5.64 Exhibit No. G. The defendant No. 1 thereafter came to Bangladesh and transferred the schedule 1 property in favour of his sons and relatives defendant Nos. 2-5 by a Hiba deed dated 11.5.66 and since then the defendant Nos. 2-5 are in possession of the schedule 1 property and they have also constructed homestead thereof. The defendant No. 1 was owner of 222 bighas & odd land and had transferred only 136 bighas of land to the plaintiffs and pro-defendants in pursuance of the agreement. The defendant No. 1 then went back to Assam and is possessing the remaining portion of his land in Assam. The defendant No. 1 did not transfer any land of schedule 2 and 3 property in favour of his nephew Amir Hamza who created a false and forged document in respect of schedule 3 property for which the defendant No. 1 prosecuted the said Amir Hamza by filing a criminal case. The defendant No. 1 did not practise any fraud upon the plaintiffs and the pro-defendants in the matter of execution of the deed of exchange Ext.C. The plaintiffs now came back to liangladesh and are trying to grab the schedule 1 properties on false assertion. The pro-defendants are living in Assam and possessing and enjoying the schedule 2 and 3 properties. The exchange deed dated 8.3.63 is not liable to be cancelled or declared void.

5. The learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit.

6. On appeal being OC Appeal No.45 of 1970, the learned District Judge, Tangail by the impugned judgment and decree set aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court and the plaintiffs suit was decrged on contest against the defendants and ex parte against the rest with cost. The deed of exchange dated 8.3.63 was declared to be not binding upon the plaintiffs and the same was also cancelled.

7. It is undisputed that the schedule 1 property of the plaint originally belongd to the plaintiffs and pro-defendants and these properties are situated in Bangladesh. It is also not disputed that there was an agreement between the parties for exchange of schedule 1 property belonging to the plaintiffs and pro-defendants with the schedule 2 and 3 properties of the plaintiff in Assam and belonging to the defendant No.1. Exhibit 'D' is an agreement dated 16.11.62 executed by the defendant No.1 alone. This shows that the parties agreed for exchange 53.52 acres of land described in schedule 1 belonging to plaintiffs and pro-defendant's situated in Bangladesh with 222 and odd bighas of land of schedule 2 and 3 of the plaintiff situated in Assam belonging to defendant No.1. It is also undisputed that in pursuance of this Ext. D a registered deed of exchange dated 8-3-63 Ext.0 was executed by the plaintiffs and the proforma-defendants in favour of the defendant No. 1 but in this Ext.0 an area of 59.85.5 acres of land was inserted in place of 53.52 acres of land as was agreed upon as per Ext. D.

8. Plaintiffs' case is that, the land exceeding 53.52 acres of land did not belong to them and this excess land belonged to one Narayan and another and the defendant No. 1 fraudulently inserted this land in the deed of exchange beyond the knowledge of the plaintiffs and the pro-defendants for which Narayan and another brought a suit in the court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh and got the deed of exchange Ext. C cancelled to the extent of their shares. The defendant No. 1 or defendant Nos. 2-5 did not prefer any appeal before any higher forum against the judgment and decree passed for cancellation of the exchange deed Ext. C in respect of the share of Narayan and another. It is also undisputed that the defendant No. 1 executed a kabala deed dated 18-5-64 Ext. G in favour of the plaintiffs and the pro-defendants in respect of 136 bighas of land in place of 222 and odd bighas of land as was agreed upon vide Ext. D. The plaintiffs case is that by this the terms of agreement Ext. D were violated and the plaintiffs have been deprived of 86 bighas of land and thereby fraud was practised upon them. Their next contention is that in fact this. 136 bighas of land also did not belong to the defendant No. 1 and he fraudulently exchanged the land belonging to others by Kabla Ext. G

9. Now the vital point for our consideration is whether the plaintiffs were entitled to cancel and rescind the deed of exchange Ext. C which was executed by them in favour of the defendant No. 1.

10. Mir Mahfuzur Rahman along with Mr. S. Karmakar, the learned Advocates appearing for the appellants, submits that the plaintiffs' suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. But this point was not raised before the learned trial Court as well as the court or appeal below. But this being a law point may be raised at this stage. He submits that as per Article 91 of the Limitation Act the suit is to be brought within 3 years but in the instant case as the suit has not been instituted within 3 years the suit is barred by limitation. Such a suit is governed by Article 91 of the Limitation Act which provides three years limitation. Under Article 91 time begins to run when the fact entitling the plaintiff to have it cancelled or set aside became known to the plaintiff. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the appellants referred to the case reported in 21 DLR 626.

11. In reply the learned Advocate for the respondents submits that after execution Ext. G on 18-5-64 the fraud became known to them that in place of 222 and odd bighas of land only 136 bighas of land were transferred in their favour in violation of the terms of agreement dated 16-11-62 Ext. D. and the suit is well within time from this date. He further submits that Article 91 of the Limitation Act is to be read with section 18 of the Limitation Act and he further submits that when fraud is proved there is no question of limitation as fraud vitiates everything. The learned Advocate further submits that a person cannot be allowed to take advantage of his own fraud. In the instant case the defendant No. 1 himself executed the deed of agreement Ext. D whereby he agreed to exchange 222 and odd bighas of land belonging to him in Assam with 53.52 acres of land belonging to the plaintiffs and pro-defendants situated in Bangladesh, but in violation of the terms of the deed of agreement Ext. D he executed Ext. G only in respect of 136 bighas of land. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the respondents has placed reliance on the decisions reported in 46 DLR 621, 14 DLR (HC) 119, 38 DLR (AD) 41, 32 DLR (AD) 167. In the case reported in 46 DLR 621 it was held that where fraud is alleged to have been practised and it is so found, the question of limitation will start from the date of knowledge of fraud practised.

<u>12. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case, materials on record and in the light of my above discussion I hold that the allegation of fraud has been proved and the violation of terms of original agreement Ext. D has been also proved in the matter of exchange of the property between the parties as in place of 222 and odd bighas of land belonging to the defendant No. 1 in Assam he executed Ext. G only in respect of 136 bighas of land. Accordingly, the suit is not barred by limitation.</u>

13. The learned Advocate for the respondents then submits that section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that when two persons mutually transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another, neither thing or both things being money only, the transaction is called an exchange, In the case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 86 it was held that when there is a question of title to be decided on the basis of an exchange deed, the party claiming title must prove that he had ownership in the property exchanged which had been transferred under the exchange. A party to the exchange when deprived of the thing or any part of the thing received by him in exchange because of any defect in the title of the other party has his remedy under section 119. The learned Advocate for the respondents further submits that since Ext. D is a promise expressed in writing with thumb impression of the defendant No. 1, it is a contract within the meaning of section 25(3) of the Contract Act and the defendant No. 1 is bound by the terms of the contract. In this connection he has placed reliance upon the case of Riasatulla vs. The Tripura Modern Bank Ltd., reported in 20 DLR 44.

<u>14. The learned Court of appeal below observed that under section 39 of the Contract Act a party to the contract is entitled to have it performed in its entirety and any breach of any part of the contract tantamounts to a breach of the whole contract and unless the parties waived the breach, the contract is at an end. Section 39 of the Contract Act provides that when a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from promise in its entirety, there the promise may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by word or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Thus it is clear that a contract of exchange does not become complete unless the parties to the contract performed their part of the obligation in its entirety. In the instant case as I have already pointed out that as per agreement Ext.D the plaintiffs and pro-defendants were to execute a deed of exchange for 53.52 acres of land belonging to them in Bangladesh and the defendant No.1 was to exchange 222 and odd bighas of land belonging to him in Assam. But in violation of the terms of deed of agreement, the defendant No. 1 had executed Ext.G a kabala deed only for 136 bighas of land. I have also pointed out that in Ext. C the deed of exchange executed by the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants in place of 53.52 acres of land 59.85-1/2 acres were inserted. The plaintiffs' contention is that the excess land did not belong to them rather it belonged to one Narayan and another who brought a suit in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh and got a decree in their favour and the deed of exchange Ext. C was cancelled to the extent of their share. From this it is clear that the plaintiffs and pro-defendants performed their part of the contract as per terms of agreement. Ext. D. It is also clear that for insertion of 59.85-1/2 acres of land in place of 53.52 acres of land as was originally agreed upon vide Ext. D the plaintiffs and pro-defendants were not responsible. But the defendant No. 1 by executing Ext.G in respect of 136 bighas in place of 222 and odd bighas of land as was agreed upon vide Ext. D has violated the terms of agreement Ext.D executed by him. The learned Court of appeal below further observed that section 35 of the Specific Relief Act provides that any person interested in a contract in writing may sue to have it rescinded, and such rescission may be adjudged by the Court in any of the following cases namely:</u>

<u>(a) Where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff.</u>

<u>15. In the instant case as I have already found that the plaintiff and pro-defendant have performed their part of the obligation but the defendant No. 1 did not fulfil the terms of the contract and as such the plaintiffs are entitled to rescind or cancel the exchange deed.</u>

16. The learned trial Court found the possession of the plaintiffs in the land situated within PS Shakipur as described in schedule 1 of the plaint which constitutes major portion of the land. The trial Court further held that some portion of this land in Bangladesh are being possessed by the defendants 2-5. The learned appellate Court observed that this fact also goes to show that the contract of exchange was not acted upon according to the agreement of exchange and accordingly, held that the plaintiffs appellants are not left without any remedy and the finding of the learned trial Court that the only course left for the plaintiffs-appellants are to go to Assam and enjoy 136 bighas of land given in their favour by the defendant No. 1 by kabala Ext.G is not correct. The learned Advocate for the respondents further submits that the instant suit has been brought for declaration that the exchange deed Ext C is not binding upon them and also for cancellation of the same on the ground that fraud was practised upon them by the defendant No. 1 He further submits that in such a case the question of possession is not very much material and if the plaintiffs succeed in getting a decree for cancellation of the deed of exchange he will take proper step for recovery of possession if he is found to be out of possession in any portion of the land. The learned Advocate for the appellants submits that under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act the defendant Nos.2-5 can well defend their possession against the plaintiffs and in support of his contention he has placed reliance on the case of Osman Gazi and others vs. Hemanta Kumar Haider and others, reported in 74 CWN 355.

<u>17. The learned Advocate for the respondents then submits that the settled principle of law that in view of the section 100 CPC the High Court will not interfere in Second Appeal with the findings of facts reached by the first Appellate Court when there is no allegation of gross misreading and nonreading of the evidence on record and in the instant case the lower appellate Court on proper consideration and appreciation of the evidence on record arrived at the decision. In support of his contention he has placed reliance on the case of Misri Lai Nayak vs. Musammat Surji alias Ramdulari and others reported in 9 DLR (Privy Council) 375.</u>

<u>The learned Advocate for the respondents further submits that in the cases reported in 38 DLR (AD) 201 and 37 DLR (AD) 205 the same principle has been reiterated.</u>

<u>18. Therefore in the facts and circumstances of the case, materials on record and in the light of my above discussion I am of the view that the learned court of appeal below on proper appreciation and consideration of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision and this is a proper judgment of reversal and accordingly, I have nothing to interfere with.</u>

19. In the result, the appeal fails. The judgment and decree appealed from are hereby affirmed.

No order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mohammad Ali, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Md Mosiul Alam, Advocate—For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Khandaker Mahmud Hasan ----- Petitioner
vs
Amirul Islam ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
By this Rule the opposite party was called upon to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 5-9-2000 (decree signed on 14-9-2000) passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in SCC Suit No. 3 of 1999 dismissing the suit for ejectment of monthly tenant shall not be set aside.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule are as follows:

3. The petitioner as plaintiff filed SSC Suit No.3 of 1999 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka against the defendant-opposite party for ejectment of monthly tenant. The father of the petitioner named Dr Abdul Monayem Khandaker was the owner of a tin- shed shop situated at holding No. 34 Siddeshwari New Circular Road, Police Station-Ramna, District-Dhaka. The defendant-opposite party entered into the said tin-shed shop as monthly tenant under Dr Abdul Monayem Khandaker, the father of the petitioner-Khandaker Mahmud Hasan on 1st December, 1980 by executing a monthly tenancy deed. The father of the plaintiff-petitioner during his lifetime gifted the suit holding to him and since then the defendant and other tenants of the suit holding started to pay the monthly rent to the petitioner. The last rate of rent of the suit shop has been mutually fixed at Taka 1500 per month. The plaintiff brought the suit for ejectment of the defendant from the said shop room on the grounds that the defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent and that the plaintiff bonafide required the room amongst other rooms of the suit holding which were let out to other tenants. The bonafide requirement has been stated to be for constructing a multi-storied building as per plan passed by RAJUK.

4. The defendant appeared in the suit and filed written statement denying the material allegation of the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the defendant was not a defaulter and that the plaintiff had no bonafide requirement of the suit shop room. Moreover, since the plaintiff had other rooms of the suit holding let out to other tenants, the plaintiff should not have chosen the particular room of the defendant as target of eviction for bonafide requirement.

5. At the trial the plaintiff examined 3 (three) witnesses and the defendant also examined 3(three) witnesses and both the parties filed series of documents to prove their respective claims.

6. The Trial Court on consideration of the evidence and circumstances of the case dismissed the suit by impugned judgment and decree dated 5-9-2000 (decree signed on 14-9-2000).

7. Aggrieved thereby, the plaintiff-petitioner approached this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in the course of argument, after placing the Revisional Application and other connected papers including plaint, impugned judgment and deposition of witnesses, submits that the learned SSC Judge on misconception of law and facts most illegally and mechanically dismissed the suit even though the plaintiff made out a clear case for bonafide requirement for construction of a multistoried building as per plan of RAJUK. The learned Advocate next submits that PW 1, plaintiff himself stated in his deposition that the defendant was a defaulter inasmuch as he did not pay any rent since December, 1998 to February, 1999 and thereafter, the defendant on pretext started to pay the rent through postal money order. Mr Mohammad Ali further submits that the judgment of the learned SSC Judge is not based on correct evaluation of the facts and materials on record and, as such, the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment which is liable to be set-aside. The learned Advocate in support of his submissions relied on the cases reported in 43 DLR (AD) 225, 9 BLT (AD) 69 = 53 DLR (AD) 63, 6 BLC (AD) 36 and 1985 BLD (AD) 77.

9. Mr Mohammad Ali finally, on referring Exts 4, 5, 5(ka) and 6, submits that on several occasions the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was returned as undelivered which shows that the defendant-opposite party deliberately with ill motive avoided to receive the notice and therefore, it cannot be said that no notice was served as per provision of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The learned Advocate in support of this contention relied on the cases reported in 34 DLR (AD) 271 and 2992 BLD 406.

10. On the other hand, Mr Md Mosiul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite party after placing the impugned judgment and the depositions of PWs and DWs submits that the learned SSC Judge was right in finding that the petitioner failed to prove the bonafide requirement for purposes of a multistoried building. He next submits that the trial Court was right in holding that since the advanced security money is not adjusted, the question of defaulter in respect of payment of rent does not arise at all. He further submits that the approved plan of RAJUK does not contain the area of suit shop premises and thus, the plea of so-called bonafide requirement of suit-shop is false and malafide. Mr Mosiul Alam finally submits that the findings of the SSC Judge based on correct evaluation of the evidence on record cannot be disturbed by this Court unless it is shown that the decision is based upon gross misreading of evidence or it has been founded on misapprehension of law or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to law. The learned advocate to fortify his submission relied on cases reported in 31 DLR (AD) 155, 55 DLR (AD) 63 and 46 DLR (AD) 121.

11. These are the points which were argued by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. Now, to deal with the contentions raised by the learned Advocates for the respective parties from a correct angle let me see the evidence and other materials on record.

12. PW 1, Khandaker Mahmud Hasan, as plaintiff stated in his deposition that on 1-12-1980 his late father let out the shop premises to the defendant. This witness also stated that সেপ্টেম্বর ও অক্টোবর ১৯৯৮ মাসের ভাড়া একত্রে ১৪-১০-৯৮ তারিখে এবং তজ্জন্য নভেম্বর ১৯৯৮ মাসের ভাড়া ৩০-১১-৯৮ তারিখ পরিশোধ করেন। তৎপর বিবাদী আমাকে কোন ভাড়ার টাকা প্রদান করেননি। আমি ইং ১৯৯৮ সনের ঐ ভাড়ার টাকা আদায়ের মুড়ি বই প্রদর্শনী-২ দাখিল করেছি। This witness also stated that আমি নালিশী হোল্ডিং-এ বহুতল বিশিষ্ট দালান নির্মাণের জন্য রাজউক হতে প্ল্যান পাস করাই। ঐ সেংশন লেটার এর অনুমোদিত প্ল্যানে ফটোস্ট্যাট কপি (সত্যায়িত করা) দাখিল করেছি। মূল কপিদ্বয় আছে দেখায়ে। উহা প্রদর্শনী-৩, ৩(ক)চিহ্নে চিহ্নিত করা গেল।

আমি এই প্ল্যানের বিষয় বিবাদী সহ অন্যান্য ভাড়াটিয়াগণকে জানায়েছি। বিবাদী প্রথমে একটি সমঝোতায় আসেন কিন্তু পরবর্তীতে উহা মানেননি। This witness also stated that বিবাদী একজন ডিফলটার এবং নালিশী দোকানটি উন্নয়নের জন্য আমার একান্ত আবশ্যক। তাই আমি ৭-২-৯৯ইং তারিখ আমি আমার বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবী মোহাম্মদ আলী মাধ্যমে বিবাদীর নামে ১০৬ ধারার নোটিশ দেই। আমার কথামত তিনি উহা লিখেন। বিবাদীর এগ্রিমেন্ট এর ঠিকানায় ও দোকানের ঠিকানায় ঐ নোটিশ এডি সহ রেজিষ্ট্রিকৃত ডাকযোগে পাঠাই। ঐ নোটিশের কপি প্রদর্শনী-৪ দাখিল করেছি। উক্ত নোটিশদ্বয় অবিলিকৃত অবস্থায় ফেরত আসে। দোকানের ঠিকানা পাঠানো ঐ নোটিশ প্রাপক সর্বদা অনুপস্থিত মন্তব্যে ফেরত আসে। ডাক পিওন মোট ৬ দিন যায়। এটা সেই খাম।

13. PW 2, Quayum Mohammad one of the tenant, under the same holding of the plaintiff-petitioner, stated that the plaintiff obtained plan for construction of building in the suit shop premises. This witness denied the defence suggestion that-সত্য নহে যে, আমি বাদীর অধীনে ভাড়াটিয়া নই বা বাদীর কথামত তাঁর সঙ্গে মিথ্যা সাক্ষ্য দিলাম বা বাদী নালিশী হোল্ডিং এ দালান নির্মাণ উন্নয়ন করতে চাননি বা নালিশী হোল্ডিং টিনসেড এখনও অত্যন্ত ভাল আছে বা আমার সাথে বাদীর কোন সমঝোতা হয়নি বা বাদীর অনুরোধে তাকে সমর্থন মিথ্যা সাক্ষ্য দিলাম।

14. PW 3 Md Shahid Ullah, in his deposition supported the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 in respect of all material particulars.

15. DW 1 Amirul Islam, defendant himself stated in his deposition that he took rent in the suit shop premises from the father of plaintiff on 1-12-80 by executing an agreement. This witness also stated in his deposition that the plaintiff did not give rent receipt regularly. In cross-examination, he denied the suggestion of the plaintiff that- সত্য নহে যে, নালিশী দোকান ঘরটি বাদীর বহুতল বিশিষ্ট দালান নির্মাণের জন্য প্রয়োজন আছে বা আমি অভ্যাসগত খেলাপী ভাড়াটিয়া বা নালিশী হোল্ডিংস বিল্ডিংটি পুরাতন ও জরাজীর্ণ অবস্থায় আছে বা উহা যে কোন সময় ভেংগে পড়তে পারত । In cross-examination this witness also admitted that বাদী অনেক আগে আমাদেরকে নোটিশ দিয়ে জানান যে, তিনি এখানে একটি বহুতল দালান নির্মাণ করবেন ও প্ল্যান পাস করেছেন।

16. DW 2 SM Sanwar and DW 3, AFS Abdul Hadi both of them in their respective testimony corroborated the evidence of DW 1 is respect of all the material particulars.

17. It appears from the impugned judgment that the SSC Judge dismissed the suit mainly on two counts.

-Firstly, the plaintiff could not prove his bonafide requirement of the suit premises for his own use or for the purpose of building. Secondly, the plaintiff could not prove that the defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent.

18. I have examined the averments of plaint and find in the plaint the plaintiff clearly stated that he required the suit premises for construction of a multistoried building as per approved plan of RAJUK. It also stated that বিবাদী একজন খেলাপী ভাড়াটিয়া এবং দোকান ঘরটি উন্নতি করার জন্য বাদীর একান্ত প্রয়োজন। (বোনাফায়েড নেছেছিটি) তজ্জন্য বাদী তাহার নিয়োজিত এডভোকেট জনাব মোহাম্মদ আলী মারফত বিবাদীকে সম্পত্তি হস্তান্তর আইনের ১০৬ ধারায় নোটিশে ভাড়াটিয়া স্বত্বের অবসান করিয়া দোকান ঘরটির দখল ১৯৯৯ইং সালের ফেব্রুয়ারী মাস অন্তে বুঝাইয়া দেওয়ার অনুরোধ করেন।

19. It thus, appears that the plaint does disclose clearly that the defendant was a defaulter in payment of rent and the plaintiff needed the suit shop premises for construction of a multistoried building as per approved plan of RAJUK.

20. On assessment of the evidence on record, it appears that PW 1, PW 2 and PW 3 all of them in their respective testimony stated that in order to develop the suit shop room amongst other rooms of the suit holding which were let out to other tenants the plaintiff obtained a plan from RAJUK. It also appears that the rented shop situated at 34, Siddeswari New Circular Road, Police Station Ramna, District Dhaka wherein, other adjacent holdings contained multistoried buildings. It also appears that DW 1, defendant himself in cross-examination admitted that it প্রদর্শনী-১ হচ্ছে আমার নেয়া ঐ ভাড়াটিয়া চুক্তি পত্র। উক্ত চুক্তি পত্রে লেখা আছে যে, উক্ত টিনসেড ঘরটি রিকনস্ট্রাকশন করা হলে কিংবা পাকা বিল্ডিং করা হলে আমি উহা ছেড়ে দিব।

21. Now, let me examine the legal position in this regard.

22. In the case Chand Miah Sawdagar vs AMA Rahman reported in 43 DLR (AD) 225, it has been laid down that :

"The plaintiff-appellant was not required to adopt the language of the statute to make out a case for rebuilding of the suit house. Whether "addition, alteration and renovation" of the suit house amounts to cosmetic improvement or entails reconstruction after demolition is a question of fact which must be decided on evidence. The respondent did not agitate in the Courts below that the sanctioned plan did not involve demolition. It is now too late to raise fresh issues of fact.

The only objection taken by the two Courts is that the sanctioned plan cannot be seriously considered in the absence of any averment in the plaint regarding its existence. But the fact is that the SCC suit was filed in 1980 whereas the building plan was sanctioned in 1978. There is no finding that the sanctioned plan was forged and spurious as contended by the defendant-respondent. The learned SCC Judge evidently misread the plaint when he found that the plaintiff did not state in the plaint that the suit premises was required for the purpose of rebuilding. The plaintiff-appellant was not required to state in the plaint as to what proof he had with regard to the requirement of rebuilding. A plaint contains facts, not proof. On both counts, namely, (a) bonafide requirement for his personal use and the use and occupation of his family members and (b) bonafide requirement for rebuilding, the plaintiff-appellant has adequately stated his case in the plaint and has proved the same. The two Courts below failed to apply the provisions of proviso (e) to sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Ordinance, to the facts and circumstances of the case.

For all the reasons above we hold that the learned SCC Judge and the High Court Division wrongly dismissed the appellants' suit and incorrectly applied the test of bonafide requirement."

23. In the case Zahir Ahmed vs Manik Sardar reported in 9 BLT (AD) 69 = 53 DLR (AD) 63, it has been laid down that :

"It is for the appellant to decide which premises out of many is required by him bonafide. The learned Single Judge took a wrong view that the appellant picked up the shop room let out to the respondent malafide on the plea of bonafide requirement without requiring other show rooms let out to other tenants for the reason that choice for other shop room will be confronted with the same argument leading to an absurd situation. The right of bonafide requirement is always with landlord but he is under legal obligation to prove that he needs the premises for such requirement. Expansion of existing business of a landlord run in a shop room adjacent to the shop room let out to a tenant involves element of must have and constitutes bonafide requirement. Thus, we do not find any reason to uphold the judgment and order of the learned Single Judge and accordingly we set aside the same and restore those of the learned SCC Judge and Assistant Judge and decree the suit."

24. This view gets support from the case of Abdus Salam Bapari vs Shamsun Nahar reported in 6 BLC (AD) 36.

25. From the above evidence, averment of the plaint vis-a-vis the principles as laid down in those decisions, I do not find any possible reason to agree with the finding of the SSC Judge that the plaintiff could not prove his bonafide requirement of the shop room for the purpose of building inasmuch as there are consistent evidences both oral and documentary available on record to corroborate the landlord's bonafide requirement of the suit premises. Moreover, I find that the disputed suit shop is situated at 34 Siddeshwari New Circular Road, Police Station Ramna, District-Dhaka wherein, other adjacent holdings contained multistoried buildings and if construction is raised it will be beneficial to all the parties and will meet the need of the day. Thus, 43 DLR (AD) 225 has not been correctly appreciated by the learned SSC Judge.

26. It is true Sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance protects a tenant from eviction "as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy". This protection is given "notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Contract Act, 1872". The protection is not available if he is a defaulter and/or in the contingencies mentioned in clauses (a)-(e) of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18, namely.

"(a) where the tenant has done any act contrary to the provisions of clause (m), clause (o) or clause (p) of section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, or

(b) where, in the absence of any contract to the contrary, the tenant has, without the consent in writing of landlord, sublet the premises in whole or in part, or

(c) where the tenant has been guilty of conduct which is a nuisance or any annoyance to occupiers of adjoining or neighbouring premises, or

(d) where the tenant has been using the premises or part thereof or allowing the premises or part thereof to be used for immoral or illegal purposes, or

(e) where the premises are bonafide required by the landlord either for purposes of building or rebuilding or for his own occupation or for the occupation of any person for whose benefit the premises are held of where the landlord can show any cause which may be deemed satisfactory by the Court".

27. The last clause (e) of the proviso allows the Court to order eviction of a tenant "where the landlord can show any cause which may be deemed satisfactory by the Court."

28. It is thus clear, that a bonafide requirement of the premises in suit by the owner for his own use or for the purpose of construction of building is a matter exclusively with landlord but still then he is under legal obligation to prove that he needs the premises for his own use or for construction of building through the evidence of reliable witness. In this case I have already indicated that there are sufficient corroborative evidence both oral and documentary available on record to arrive at a finding that the plaintiff-petitioner has been able to prove his bonafide requirement of the suit shop premises for purpose of multistoried building.

29. There is another aspect of the case which needs to be addressed as it involves an important question of law.

30. In the present case it appears from the materials on record (Exhibits 4, 5, 5(ka) and 6 that on several occasions the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was posted in the address of the suit-shop but at all these times the same was returned as undelivered.

31. In the case of Rokeya Begum vs Shah Md Yeamin reported in 1992 BLD 406, it has been decided that:

"In the instant case, as already indicated, the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act had been posted on September 14, 1986, on pre-payment with correct address. The postal peon called at address four times within the period from September 16, 1986, to September 22, 1986, although as per his own admission in the written statement the tenant had been carrying on business at the address. There was no evidence to show that he had been away from the premises during the period and there was none who could accept the letter on his behalf. If he was not away there was no reason why the registered letter could not be served on him. As he was in arrears, there could also be no reason why the landlord should have withheld the service. In the circumstances the failure of the postal peon to actually deliver the letter would be attributed to the tenant's conduct. In the aforesaid circumstance, the learned Small Cause Court Judge, on a reference to the principle enunciated in the cases reported in 22 DLR 664 and 31 DLR 269, took the view that there was due service of the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In my opinion, the learned Judge, in arriving at the said finding, committed no error of law which can be said to have been occasioned a failure of justice."

<u>32. On an analysis of the aforesaid decision, I am led to hold that in this case there was due service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act inasmuch as I have already noticed that in the present case it appears from the materials on record on several occasions the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was posted in the address of the suit-shop to the defendant-opposite party but all the times the same was returned as undelivered.</u>

<u>33. There is another aspect. Admittedly, the plaintiff brought allegation against the defendant-opposite party that he was a defaulter with regard to payment of rent for the period of December, 1998 to February, 1999 although, the defendant claims that the plaintiff on protest did not pay the rent receipt for that period after taking rent. In this connection on assessment of the entire evidence on record I find that the defendant did not or could not adduce any documentary or corroborative evidence to prove that he was not a defaulter with regard to payment of rent for the period of December, 1998 to February, 1999.</u>

34. In order to meet the grievance of Mr Mosiul Alam that the approved plan of RAJUK does not contain the area of suit premises, I have examined the connected papers including the approved plan of RAJUK, it appears that the plan of RAJUK contained the suit shop premises. Therefore, I do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate on this point. As to the observation given by the Trial Judge that since the advanced security money is not adjusted the question of defaulter does not arise at all to which straightforward answer is the same cannot be the basis to dismiss the suit while landlord's bonafide requirement of the suit shop premises for purposes of building has been established by sufficient corroborative evidence both oral and documentary.

35. Mr Md Mosiul Alam, the learned Advocate tried his best to convince me that the learned SSC judge has rightly arrived at a finding that the principles enunciated in the decision reported in 43 DLR (AD) 225 are not applicable in this case. In this connection I have already noticed that the principles laid down in said case are attracted in its entirety in this case and therefore, I am unable to accept the submission of Mr Mosiul Alam on this point as well.

36. The decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party is distinguishable on facts.

37. Be that as it may, the proposition of law is well settled that once a tenancy comes into an existence the tenant cannot convert his tenancy into a permanent one by doing any act adverse to the landlord.

38. Having given my best consideration to the materials on record both oral and documentary and the legal position I hold that the trial Court below committed gross illegality in dismissing the SSC suit, which calls for inter ference.

39. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 5-9-2000 (decree signed on 14-9-2000) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in SCC Suit No. 3 of 1999 is hereby set aside. The defendant-opposite party is directed to vacate the rented suit shop premises within 4(four) months from date.

Let a copy of the judgment along with LC record be send down at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Zinat Ara J: Since similar question of facts and laws are involved in Writ Petition Nos. 5962, 3876, 5963, 4894, 4893 and 4895 of 1997, these will be heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment.

2. In these writ petitions, the petitioners challenged the legality of various Staff Orders passed on different dates, described herein-after by which the petitioners were placed under suspension by respondent No. 2, General Manager, Bangladesh Bank, Khulna.

3. Facts relevant for disposal of the writ petitions, in brief, are as under:

4. The petitioners were appointed as employees of Bangladesh Bank on various dates. While the petitioners had been working in various capacities in the Bangladesh Bank two First Information Reports were lodged with the Khulna Police Station by Mr Ataur Rahman Miah, District Anti-Corruption Officer against petitioners (i) Md Abul Hossain Shah, (ii) Md A Khaleque Mollah, (iii) Shaikh Md Abul Hossain, (iv) Shahadat Hossain Mina, (v) Md Enamul Hoque Mollah, (vi) Champak Kumar Biswas, and (vii) Mirza Saifuddin Hasan and others for preparing fictitious bills by creating advice with forged signatures and thereby misappropriating a huge amount of Bank money which were recorded as Khulna Police Station Case No. 45 dated 30-9-1993 and 25 dated 19-1-1994. Thereafter on investigation charge sheets were submitted in both the cases being Charge Sheet Nos. 70 and 92 dated 5-4-1997 and 28-4-1997 respectively. In the first information reports, all the writ petitioners had been named as accused persons of the cases along with some others. In the charge sheets also, they were shown as accused. All the petitioners knowing about the aforesaid criminal cases had appeared before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Khulna and obtained bail. Since then the petitioners had /have been performing their normal duties in connection with the service of Bangladesh Bank. The petitioners were never arrested in connection with the aforesaid two cases. Prior to the lodging of the First Information Reports, departmental proceedings were also initiated against all the petitioners and they were also asked to submit their explanations by various memos for negligence of their duties. The petitioners submitted reply to the show cause notices. Thereafter, departmental charges were brought against them by various orders. The petitioners were also placed under suspension by Bangladesh Bank under the following orders:

The aforesaid orders of suspension were not in accordance with law as provided in Regulation No. 22 of Bangladesh Bank's Staff Regulations According to the Bangladesh Bank's Staff Regulations, departmental proceedings should be concluded within 4 months from the date of showing cause for disciplinary actions. The proceedings could not be completed within time in accordance with law and the departmental charges were submitted after 8 months. The order of suspension can only be passed by a person having authority to make the final order i.e. the order of dismissal and, as such, the suspension orders which were not passed by the appointing authority are without lawful authority. Actions against the petitioners under Regulation No. 22 of Bangladesh Bank's Staff Regulations should not have been taken before judgment in the criminal cases. Thus the orders of suspension are without lawful authority.

5. In the backdrop of the aforesaid circumstances, these writ petitions were filed and rules were obtained. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, Governor, Bangladesh Bank and General Manager, Bangladesh Bank, Khulna, respectively, opposed the Niles by filing affidavits-in-opposition and supplementary affidavits-in-opposition denying the allegations made in the writ petitions contending inter alia, that the petitioners while discharging their duties in various capacities of Bangladesh Bank, they, in total violation of the established practice, made payment of Taka 7,25,400 and Taka 7,69,144 against 8 forged bills for which Khulna Police Station Case Nos. 45 dated 30-9-1993 and 25 dated 19-9-1994 were lodged against them; that after investigations Charge Sheet No. 70 dated 5-4-1997 and Charge Sheet No. 92 dated 28-4-1997 under sections 409/467/468/471/472/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 were also submitted against them: that due to the fact that criminal cases were pending against the petitioners for misappropriation of money through the forged bills, the petitioners were suspended by various staff orders (described earlier) in accordance with the provision of Regulation No. 22 (IV) of the Bangladesh Bank (Staff) Regulation read with Rule 73 of the Bangladesh Service Rules that charges have been framed by Bangladesh Bank for making payment of Taka 7.69,144 and Taka 7,25,400 in total Taka 14,94,544 against 8 forged bills in violation of section 424 of the Banking Department Manual (BD Manual) and other established practice; that the inquiry officer of Bangladesh Bank has also submitted his inquiry report; that since criminal cases are pending against the petitioners, Bangladesh Bank did not take any further action on it and after the disposal of criminal cases by competent court of law, the departmental proceedings would be concluded; that the departmental proceedings and criminal proceedings being pending against the petitioners, the writ petitions challenging interim orders like suspension are absolutely misconceived and the writ petitions are not maintainable against the same; that the petitioners' remedy lies with Administrative Tribunal and on that count also these writ petitions are not maintainable; that the petitioners were found guilty in Special Case No. 33 of 1997 and Special Case No. Al of 1997 arising out of the police station cases by the Divisional Special Judge, Khulna and they were convicted and sentenced to suffer “দন্ডবিধির ৪০৯/১০৯ ধারা মতে ৩ (তিন) বৎসর সশ্রম কারাদন্ডে এবং ১,৩০,০০০ (এক লক্ষ ত্রিশ হাজার) টাকা জরিমানা অনাদায়ে আরো ৯ মাস বিনাশ্রম কারাদন্ড এবং দন্ডবিধির ৪৭১/১০৯ এবং ৪৭২/১০৯ ধারামতে প্রতি ধারায় ৫০০ (পাঁচশত) টাকা করিয়া জরিমানা অনাদায়ে প্রতি ধারায় আরো ১ (এক) মাস করিয়া বিনাশ্রম কারাদন্ডে দন্ডিত করা হইল” in the aforesaid criminal cases; that against the said order of conviction and sentence, the petitioners moved before the High Court Division by way of filing criminal appeals and the appeals were also dismissed by the High Court Division affirming the judgment and order of conviction amid sentence passed by the Divisional Special Judge in Special Case No. 41 of 1997 and Special Case No. 33 of 1997; that the present writ petitions are not maintainable and the rules are liable to be discharged.

6. The petitioners filed affidavits-in-reply against the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondents stating that the criminal case and appeals were disposed of after the issuance of the impugned orders of suspension and so that result of those criminal cases and appeals should not have any bearing on the legality of the orders of suspension and that the petitioners have also filed Criminal Petitions for Leave to Appeals against the judgments of the High Court Division.

7. Mr Md Abdul Jabbar, the learned Advocate for the petitioners of Writ Petition Nos. 5962/1997, 5963/1997, 4894/1997 and 4895/1997, submits that the suspension orders are without lawful authority since it was issued without following the provisions of Regulation Nos. 22 and 33 of the Bangladesh Bank's (Staff) Regulations. He further submits that the appointing authority did not issue the suspension orders and, as such, the suspension orders are without lawful authority He next submits that the departmental proceedings must be completed within 4 months from the date of issuance of show cause notice but the proceedings against the petitioners could not be completed within time and the suspension orders are thus without lawful authority. However Mr Abdul Jabbar admits that the petitioners being employees of Bangladesh Bank and suspension being a term and condition of service, it normally falls within the jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunal since it is a statutory public authority specified in The schedule of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980. But he argues that since Administrative Tribunal has no authority to pass an interim order of stay, the petitioners had no equally efficacious remedy there as available under Article 102 of the Constitution. So, according to him, the present writ petitions are maintainable. In support of his arguments, he has referred to the decisions of the following cases:

(i) Kamrul Hasan vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 35 = 49 DLR (AD) 44.

(ii) Md Abdul Karim Khan vs Commissioner, Khulna Division, Deputy Commissioner, Jessore, Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar, Dist. Jessore, Ershad Ali Gazi, reported in 16 DLR (SC) 624.

(iii) MA Hai, Wazed Ali Minh & Md Moslem vs Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 84 = 40 DLR (AD) 206 .

(iv) Mujibur Rahman (Md) vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111.

(v) Govt. of Bangladesh and others vs Md Abdul Halim Minh and others, reported in 13 BLT (AD) 120 = 9 BLC (AD) 134 and

(vi) The Collector of Custom, Customs House, Chittagong and others vs Mr A Hannan, reported in 1990 BLD (AD) 216 = 42 DLR (AD) 167.

8. Mr Abul Kalam Mainuddin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition' No. 3876 of 1997 and Mr Nurul Mostafa, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4893 of 1997, adopted the submissions of Mr Md Abdul Jabbar.

9. On the other hand, Mr Md Khalilur Rahman Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for Bangladesh Bank contends that admittedly the petitioners are employees of Bangladesh Bank and suspension orders being terms and conditions of petitioners' service, the petitioners' remedy lies before the Administrative Tribunal and, as such, the present writ petitions are not maintainable. He also contends that no writ petition lies against an order of suspension because suspension is not a punishment but simply an interim order. He next contends that the impugned orders of suspension are in accordance with the Service Regulations of the petitioners and lawful. In support of his contentions, Mr Md Khalilur Rahman Bhuiyan has referred to the decisions of the followings cases :

(i) Shamsul Haque vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 1 BLC 93.

(ii) Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Establishment Division and others vs Mahbubuddin Ahmed, reported in 3 BLC (AD) 45.

(iii) Pakistan through General Manager NWR (now PWR), Lahore vs Mls. AV Issacs, reported in 22 DLR (SC) 371.

(iv) Abdul Mannan vs Bangladesh and another, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 75.

(v) Executive Engineer Public Health, Barisal Division, Barisal vs Mohammad Ali and others, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 64.

(vi) Abdul Latif vs Government represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Defence and others, reported in 43 DLR 446.

(vii) Mujibur Rahman vs Government and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111.

(viii) Junnur Rahman vs Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha and others, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 166.

(ix) De/war Hossain Mia (Md) and another vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and others, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120, and

(x) Md. Shamsul Islam Khan vs Secretary, Ministry of Communications, Roads and Highways and others, reported in 8 BLT (AD) 64.

10. In view of the above submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties, the most pertinent questions to be decided in these rules are (i) whether the writ petitions are maintainable and (ii) whether the impugned orders of suspension are with lawful authority.

11. Perused the writ petitions, affidavits-in-opposition, supplementary affidavits-in-opposition, reply to the supplementary affidavits-in-opposition and also considered the materials on records.

12. It is an admitted proposition that all the writ petitioners are employees of Bangladesh Bank, Khulna and that while the petitioners had been working in various capacities of the Bangladesh Bank, Khulna Police Station Case No.45 dated 30-9-1993 and Khulna Police Station Case No. 25 dated 19-9-1994 were lodged against the petitioners under sections 409/467/468/471/472/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of Act, II of 1947 for dishonest misappropriation of Taka 7,25,400 and Taka 7,69,144 respectively against 8 forged bills in violation of section 424 of the Banking Department Manual. Admittedly, Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Khulna after investigation submitted Charge Sheet No. 70 dated 5-7-1997 for dishonest misappropriation of Taka 7,25,400 against 4 forged bills and Charge Sheet No. 92 dated 28-4-1997 for dishonest misappropriation of Taka 7,69,144 against another 4 forged bills. There is also no dispute that the petitioners were convicted and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment of various terms and also to pay fine in Special Case No. 33 of 1997 and Special Case No. 41 of 1997, arising out of those police station cases, by the Divisional Special Judge, Khulna and that the petitioners filed criminal appeals against the said judgments and orders of conviction and sentence. Admittedly, the High Court Division dismissed those criminal appeals on contest and affirmed the judgments and orders of conviction and sentence passed by the Divisional Special Judge, Khulna. However, admittedly, some of the writ petitioners filed Petitions for Leave to Appeal before the Appellate Division against the judgments of affirmance of the 'conviction and sentence passed by the High Court Division. It is also admitted that depart-mental proceedings were also drawn up against the petitioners prior to the filing of the criminal cases whereupon the petitioners were asked to show cause and that the petitioners were placed under suspensions by the impugned staff orders which have been stated earlier. Admittedly, the orders of suspension of the petitioners who are employees of Bangladesh Bank is one of the terms and conditions of their service and that the Administrative Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine the applications of the petitioners in respect of the terms and conditions of their service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Bangladesh Bank. So, there is no dispute that suspension being one of the terms and conditions of the service of the petitioners they have remedy available before the Administrative Tribunal constituted under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980.

13. However, Mr Abdul Jabbar's main contention is that since Administrative Tribunal had no authority to pass any interim order like stay the petitioners had no equally efficacious remedy available there and so the writ petitions filed under Article 102 of the Constitution are maintainable.

14. It is well established by now that the Administrative Tribunal has no authority to grant interim relief like stay, injunction, etc in respect of a case pending before it for final adjudication.

15. On this point, Mr Jabbar has referred to the decision in the case of Kamrul Hasan vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 35. Since it is a settled principle of law that the Administrative Tribunal has no jurisdiction to grant interim relief like stay, injunction, we do not feel it necessary to discuss the aforesaid decision.

16. Our view on the other decisions referred to by Mr Jabbar are as follows:

17. The case of Md Abdul Karim Khan vs Commissioner, Khulna Division, Deputy Commissioner, Jessore, Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar, Dist. Jessore, Ershad Ali Gazi, 16 DLR (SC) 624, is relating to a removal order from membership and chairmanship by controlling authority. The facts and circumstances of this case is completely different and it has no manner of application in the present rules.

18. The case of MA Hai , Wazed Ali Miah & Md Moslem vs Trading Corporation of Bangladesh 1988 BLD (AD) 84 is relating to a criminal case and the same is not at all relevant for the purpose of deciding these rules.

19. The case of the Collector of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong and others vs Mr A Hannan, 1990 BLD (AD) 216, is not relating to any service matter and the said decision is absolutely irrelevant in deciding these writ petitions.

20. In the case of Mujibur Rahman (Md) vs Government of Bangladesh and others [44 DLR (AD) 111], it was observed by the Appellate Division as follows:-

"Within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an order for violation of

principle of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising from sub-clause (9a), but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A [See SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1937 SC 386(Para 161 and JIB Chopra vs Union of India AIR 1987 SC 357 (Para 2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging ,the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102((1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)."

21. Thus this decision clearly shows that a person in the service of the Republic who intends to challenge vires of a law on the ground of violation of the fundamental right may only seek his remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution. So, from this decision, it is rather clear that the present writ petitions challenging simply the orders of suspension are not maintainable in writ jurisdiction.

22. In the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs Md Abdul Halim Miah and others, 13 BLT (AD) 120, the Appellate Division held as follows:

"In the instant case, no vires of the Rules has been challenged but certain decisions taken at the meeting of the Standing Committee and the placement in the gradation list and publication in the official gazette have been challenged by way of an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. The right of judicial review under Article 102(2) of the Constitution is neither a fundamental right nor a guaranteed right. Similarly, the judicial review of an administrative action is neither an all weather remedy nor a remedy for all wrongs but is available only when there is no other equally efficacious remedy. The writ petitioners have challenged the impugned decisions alleged to have infringed their fundamental right guaranteed under Article 27 and 29 of the Constitution, But in view of the provision of Article 117(2) of the Constitution the Parliament has set up the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 for exercise of the functions enumerated in Article 117(1)i.e. by setting up of the Administrative Tribunal to exercise the jurisdiction in respect of matters relating or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the republic etc. Article 117(2) provides that no Court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such Tribunal. Section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act 1980 specifically provides how the jurisdiction under Article 117(1) is conferred to any other Court. In the case of 44 DLR (AD) 111 it has further been cautioned that an aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, allege contravention of some fundamental right which may ultimately turn out to be frivolous or vexatious or not even wrongly attracted in the case and asked to be a ground so that great value of the right given under Article 102(1) is not frittered away or misused on the pretext of alternative remedy. The question of enforcement of fundamental right is not available in the case as the questions involved in the impugned decisions are mere clarification of the rules for giving effect thereto and, as such, the assumption of jurisdiction under Article 102(2) of the Constitution for ventilating certain grievances regarding terms and conditions of service of the writ petitioners pursuant to the impugned decisions has never been contemplated. On our examination of the impugned order we do not think that any question of fundamental right is involved in the case so as to allege that the same cannot be extricated for exclusive consideration in the petition for enforcement of fundamental rights."

23. In the present Rules the vires of a law has not been challenged on the ground of fundamental rights. So, this decision also shows that the writ petitions are not maintainable.

24. Thus it is found that none of the decisions referred to by Mr Jabbar supports his contention that a writ petition is maintainable for violation of any terms and conditions of the service of the petitioners only on the ground that the Administrative Tribunal has no authority to grant interim relief. On the other hand, two of the decisions referred to by him and discussed earlier rather support the contention of Mr Md Khalilur Rahman Bhuiyan that writ petition is not maintainable against any matter relating to terms and conditions of the service of the petitioners without challenging the vires of a law on the ground of violation of fundamental right.

25. We have gone through the ten decisions referred to by Mr Bhuiyan, earlier noted in the judgment. Out of the ten decisions, those applicable to the present situation in our view, are discussed hereinafter:

26. In the case of Junnur Rahman vs Bangla-desh Shilpa Rin Sangstha and others, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 116 the High Court Division discharged the Rule issued in that case deciding that since there is no question of violation of any fundamental right of the petitioner, the writ petition was not maintainable, inasmuch as the relief sought for by the petitioner was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal. The petitioner went to the Appellate Division against the said decision and the Appellate Division decided as follows:

"Having regard to the relief sought for by the petitioner in his writ petition, namely, for a declaration that the aforesaid Administrative Circular and Office Order dated 1-6-96 were issued without lawful authority, etc., it is clear, and the High Court Division has rightly held, that the writ petition was not maintainable because he (petitioner) did not seek to enforce any fundamental right and further, it was within the competence of the Administrative Tribunal to entertain the grievance of the petitioner."

27. Similarly, in the case of Del war Hossain Mia (Md) and another vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and others, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120 the Appellate Division decided that seniority and pro-motion of civil servants being terms and conditions of service the Administrative Tribunal is possessed of the exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute in such matters.

28. In the case of Shamsul Islam Khan vs Secretary, Ministry of Communications, Roads and Highways, reported in 8 BLT (AD) 64 the Appellate Division decided that,

"It is laid down by this court in Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 117 that a Government servant, who intends to challenge the vires of a law on the ground of violation of fundamental right may seek his remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution, but in all other cases his remedy lies before the Administrative Tribunal under Article 117(2) thereof. In the instant case, the writ petitioner is a Government servant. He has not challenged the vires of any law. His grievance relates to the terms and conditions of his service. The High Court Division is, therefore, correct in its view that the writ petitions are not maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution."

29. Thus it appears that the Appellate Division in a series of cases has taken a consistent view that a person in the Service of the Republic who intends to challenge the vires of a law on the ground of violation of fundamental right may seek his remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution, but in all other cases he will seek remedy under Article 117(2) and that on the terms and conditions of service, the Administrative Tribunal is possessed of the exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute in such matters.

30. In consideration of all the above decisions and also the fact that the petitioners did not challenge the vires of any law on the ground of violation of their fundamental right in these writ petitions, we are of the view that the petitioners being employees of Bangladesh Bank, the Administrative Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute in relation to the impugned orders of suspension of the petitioners. When a person in the service of Bangladesh Bank is suspended he is to follow that order of suspension. If by the order of suspension any of the terms and conditions of service is violated his remedy lies before the Administrative Tribunal. But it cannot be a ground of maintainability of a writ petition only on the ground that the Administrative Tribunal, had no authority to pass an order of stay.

31. This view of ours is also supported by the decision in the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs SM Fariduddin, reported in 2001 BLD (AD) 155, wherein it was decided by the Appellate Division as under:-

"It may be argued that the Administrative Tribunal has no authority to pass any order of stay or injunction but when a person is transferred from one place to another he is to follow or abide by that Order. If by the order of transfer any terms and conditions of service is violated his remedy lies before the Administrative Tribunal. But it cannot be a ground to issue an order of stay by the High Court Division only on the ground that the Administrative Tribunal has no authority to pass any such order. This has been well settled by this Division in the aforesaid decision In view of the clear decision by this Division we hold that the High Court Division committed gross illegality in passing the aforesaid orders.

The appeals are accordingly allowed without cost. The impugned orders passed by the High Court Division on 16- 8-2000 and 21-8-2000 in Writ Petition Nos. 4165 and 4380 of 2000 respectively are hereby set aside and the writ petitions are found to be not maintainable."

32. In view of the above, our answer to the question No. (i) is negative i.e. the writ petitions are not maintainable.

33. Since it is found that the writ petitions are not maintainable, we do not like to embark further on question No. (ii) i.e. on legality of the suspension orders touching the merit of those orders.

34. Accordingly, all the six Rules are discharged with a cost of Taka 5000 to be paid by each of the petitioners in favour of Bangladesh Bank.

The orders of stay in all the writ petitions stand vacated.

End.
