Md Umbar Ali, Advocate ---For the Applicant. 
Mahbubey-Alam, Attorney-General with Mahfuza Begum, Assistant Attorney-General, Abdur Rahim Bhuiyan, Assistant Attorney-General--For the Respondent.
parties:
Glaxo Smith Kline Bangladesh Ltd.  ----- Applicant
vs
Commissioner of Taxes ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J: This reference application is at the instance of the assessee applicant against order dated 11-1-2007 passed by the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Division Bench, Chittagong (Circuit Bench) in Income Tax Appeal No. 2174 of 2006-2007 and Income Tax Appeal No.2213 of 2006-2007 (Cross Appeal).

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the reference application are that the applicant is a Multinational Public Limited Company incorporated under the Company Act and derived income from (I) manufacturing and sale of medicine; (II) house property; and (III) from other sources (Bank Interest). The assessee-applicant regularly maintained account under the mercantile system of accounting and a regular income tax payee.

3. The assessee-applicant filed return for the assessment year 2004-2005 showing income of Taka 8,99,93,911 along with books of accounts duly audited and certified by a qualified chartered accountant in compliance with section 35(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. Pursuant to notice under sections 79 and 83(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, an authorised representative of the assessee-applicant appeared before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (hereinafter called the 'DCT') along with ledger, bank statements, bills, vouchers and other details in support of the audited accounts and explained about the return submitted earlier. The DCT after examining the accounts and other details furnished by the assessee-applicant accepted the sales estimate, gross profit (GP), house property income and income from other sources (Bank interests) shown by the assessee-applicant but disallowed the expenditures in the trading account, going beyond the accounts of the assessee-applicant, and thus computed the total income of the applicant at Taka 12,35,66,158.

4. The assessee-applicant, being aggrieved by the assessment order of the DCT, preferred appeal before the Appellate Additional Tax Commissioner (hereinafter called the 'AACT') contending inter alia that the DCT did not compute income of the assessee in accordance with law and further contending that the DCT disallowed trading expenses without considering the audited accounts and without verifying the evidences produced before the DCT. After hearing the parties the 'AACT' partly allowed the appeal modifying assessment order of the DCT but without assigning any reason.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order of the 'AACT' the assessee-applicant preferred a second appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Division Bench, Chittagong being ITA No. 2174 of 2006-2007. The DCT also filed an appeal against the order of the 'AACT' which was registered as ITA No.2213 of 2006-2007. Both the appeals were heard and disposed of by one judgment by the Taxes Appellate Tribunal. The Taxes Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the department and allowed the appeal of the assessee-applicant in part vide order dated 11-1-2007.

6. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the assessee-applicant filed the instant reference application under section 160(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 for answering the following questions:

(i) Whether the learned Taxes Appellate Tribunal can disregard the accounts maintained following a regular method of accounting, duly audited and certified as per requirements of section 35(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, when due to transparency of the accounts maintained by the applicant-company, its accounts had been accepted in full in all the preceding assessment years?

(ii) Whether the learned Tribunal was legally justified to confirm the disallowances from expenses claimed under section 29(1) of the ITO 1984, when those were all vouched and verifiable, but disallowed by the DCT on the basis of surmise and conjecture, ignoring orders passed in earlier years (paragraph 13 supra), when accounts were directed to be accepted in full?"

7. The learned Advocate for the applicant submits that if the question No.1 is answered then the question No. II as formulated in the reference application will automatically get its result.

8. Mr Md Umbar Ali, the learned Advocate, appearing for the assesse applicant took us through the order passed by the income tax authority and submits that in the instant case the DCT himself has found that the method of accounting employed by the applicant is correct and estimated sales, GP, income from house property and Bank interest as per books of account audited by the chartered accountant pursuant to section 35(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance but disallowed the trading expenses and additions in the profit and loss account on omnibus grounds of want of supporting evidence without specifically pin pointing what kind of evidence are wanted or what kind of defects are found in the books of accounts and thus the DCT resorted to estimate under the proviso of section 35(4) of the Ordinance. In estimating the income under the proviso to the said section, there is no finding on the part of the DCT that the method of accounting which has been employed by the assessee-applicant is not regularly employed or the method was such that, in his opinion, the income of the assessee could not be deduced therefrom. The learned Advocate, also submits that the disallowances and deductions made by the income tax authority on omnibus grounds without pinpointing any defect whatsoever in respect of the audited accounts and without rejecting the books of accounts of the assessee-applicant are not at all sustainable in law. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate referred the case of Eastern Hardware Store vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 54 DLR 125; the case of Bangladesh Steels Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes (2000) BTD 113 and also referred some other cases of different jurisdictions.

9. On the other hand, Mr Abdur Rahim Bhuiyan assisted by Mr Mahfuza Begum, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, entered appearance on behalf of the respondent and filed affidavit-in-opposition contending inter alia that Chapter V of the Income Tax Ordinance deals with computation of income and section 35 of the said chapter provides method of accounting and section 35(4)(c) provides that if a company failed to comply with the requirements of sub-section 3 of section 35 of the Ordinance, in that case the DCT can compute the income according to his own discretion. Further contending that section 35 deals with the correctness of arithmetical calculation and genuinely of the same is certified by the chartered accountant. On the other hand, Chapter IX which contains sections 81 to 94, deals with assessment and section 83 provides 'production of evidence.' In the present case, the DCT allowed expenditures where bills and vouchers were produced in support of the expenditures on different heads but the DCT disallowed some expenditures where the assessee failed to produce evidence in support of the said expenditures. Some of the disallowances made by the DCT were upheld by the 'AACT' and Taxes Appellate Tribunal. Further contention of the respondent is that the assessee-applicant submitted return along with an audited statement of accounts under section 75(2)(d)(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. The DCT issued statutory notice under sections 79 and 83(1) of the Ordinance and the assessee submitted its books of accounts for verification and examination by the DCT and accordingly, the DCT made his assessment under section 83(2) after giving an opportunity of being heard and thereby, made disallowances under different heads of accounts in profit and loss accounts specifying reasons in each and every item due to verifiability and lack of bills and vouchers and, as such, assessment was made in accordance with law. Further contention of the respondent is that the disallowances made in the profit and loss accounts or in the trading accounts are questions of fact which cannot be resolved in this jurisdiction.

10. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney-General, in support of the affidavit-in-opposition, submits that Chapter IX of the Ordinance will be redundant if the income tax authority accepts the return filed by the assessee in toto based on a certificate issued by the chartered accountant under section 35(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. He further submits that in the instant case, from assessment order it is evident that the DCT disallowed the expenditures in absence of verifiable bills and vouchers and though the DCT did not record any findings as to the unacceptability of the method of accounting maintained by the assessee-applicant but impliedly rejected the books of accounts of the assessee-applicant. Learned Attorney-General in support of his submission referred to the cases of (1) Commissioner of Income Tax vs Ata Hossain Khan reported in 28 DLR (AD) 141, (2) Commissioner of Taxes vs Harendra Kumar reported in 34 DLR (AD) 298, (3) Commissioner of Taxes vs EM Chettyar firm (SB) Rangoon, reported in AIR 1930 page 4, (4) Laxmi Narayan Chunni Lal vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 140 ITR 837 and also referred to some other cases decided on several jurisdictions of the Sub-continent.

11. In view of the submissions made by the learned Attorney-General and the points raised by him, this bench felt the necessity to take an expert opinion, and, as such, requested Mr MA Noor, a leading lawyer in this field, to assist this Court. Accordingly, Mr MA Noor appeared and took us through section 35 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 and submits that in the instant case, the income tax authority, without taking into consideration any of the legal aspects of the case and true import of section 35 of the Income Tax Ordinance, most illegally disallowed the expenditures in the profit and loss accounts without any material basis and without arriving at a positive finding that the income, profit and gain of the assessee-applicant cannot be computed in accordance with the method of accounts employed by the assessee-applicant and, as such, disallowances made by the income tax authority in the trading expenses is beyond the scope of law. He further submits that it is only when the Revenue Authority is of the opinion that the method of accounting employed by the assessee do not reflect the true profit, income or gain of the assessee company then and only then, the department resorted to estimate upon rejecting the audited accounts expressly. In this connection, he submits that assessee-applicant is a company incorporated under the Company Act. While submitting its return, the assessee has complied with the provision of section 35(3) of the Ordinance, 1984 and a legal presumption is attached to the certificate issued by the chartered accountant and in the instant case, there is no material on record to rebut the legal presumption as to the correctness of the audited accounts of the applicant and this aspect of the case has lost sight of the Income Tax Authority. Mr MA Noor submits that there is no doubt that the taxing authority can resort to the proviso of section 35(4) but only when it finds that the method of accounting by the assessee is not regular or do not reflect the correct picture of profit, income or gain of the assessee Company. But in the instant case, there is no such finding. He further submits that the finding of the Income Tax Authority on this matter is not to be a subjective or an arbitrary decision but a judicial decision and cannot be accepted if there are no materials to support his findings. In support of his submission Mr MA Noor referred to the cases of Sagorica & Co (Pvt) Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes 1999 BTD 87 = 52 DLR 484; Friends Corporation vs Commissioner of Taxes 1975 BTD 221 = 27 DLR 566; Commissioner of Taxes vs Friends Corporation 1978 BTD (AD) 140; Titas Gas Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes 2000 BTD 77 = 53 DLR 209 and other cases of our jurisdiction.

12. Heard the learned Advocates, perused the reference application, Annexures, affidavit-in-opposition, decisions cited by the learned Advocates and the relevant provisions of law.

13. We have perused the assessment order of the DCT which runs in the following manner:

করদাতা কোম্পানী মোট টাকা ৮,৯৯,৯৩,৯১১ পদর্শন করতঃ নীতিক্ষিত হিসাব বিবরনীসহ আয়ের রির্টান দাখিল করা হয়। আয়কর অধ্যাদেশ ১৯৮৪ এর ৮৩(১) ও ৭৯ ধারার নোটিশের জবাবে করদাতা কোম্পানীর আইনানুগ প্রতিনিধি জনাব শওকত হোসেন এফসিএ হিসাবের খাতাপত্র, ব্যাংক ষ্টেটমেন্ট, বিল/ভাউচার ইত্যাদিসহ শুনানীর জন্য হাজির হন এবং এই সকল হিসাবের খাতাপত্রের সাহায্যে আয়ের রির্টান ব্যাখ্যা করেন। তিনি দাবী করেন যে, করদাতা কোম্পানী শুধুমাত্র ব্যবসা (ঔষুধ উৎপাদন ও বিক্রয়), গৃহ সম্পত্তি এবং অন্যান্য উৎস (ব্যাংক সুদ) খাতে আয় অর্জন করিয়া থাকে, তাঁহার বক্তব্য শুনিলাম। উপস্থাপিত হিসাবের খাতাপত্র পরীক্ষ-নিরীক্ষা করিলাম। কর মামলাটি তাঁহার সহিত বিস্তারিত আলোচনা করিলাম। আয়কর অধ্যাদেশ ১৯৮৪ এর ৮৩(২)/৮২ সি ধারায় নিম্নরুপে করদাতা কোম্পানীর ২০০৪-২০০৫ কর বর্ষের কর নির্ধারনী কার্য সম্পন্ন করিলাম।

14. On perusal of the aforesaid order, it appears that the DCT examined the aforesaid documents placed before him but did not record any findings as to the unacceptability of the method of accounting or rejected the books of accounts maintained by the assessee-applicant. Admittedly, the assessee-applicant is a multinational company and derives its income from manufacturing and sale of medicine, house property and from other sources (Bank interest) and maintained accounts regularly under mercantile system of accounting as provided under section 35(3) of the Income-Tax Ordinance, 1984. The assessee-applicant filed its return with profit and loss accounts, trading accounts and balance sheets duly audited and certified by a chartered accountant. It appears from the order of the DCT that he disallowed trading expenditures and deducted additions claimed by the assessee-applicant in its audited books of accounts without recording any findings that the audited accounts are not acceptable nor did he reject the accounts maintained by the assessee-applicant. It also appears that the 'AACT' though modified the dis-allowances made by the DCT on different heads but did not assign any reason. The Taxes Appellate Tribunal also partially allowed the appeal without holding and considering the legal aspect of the law that the DCT and the AACT made the disallowances and deducted additions ignoring audited books of accounts without recording any findings as to the unacceptability of the method of accounting maintained by the assessee-applicant or pointing out any defect in the method of accounting. In a series of decisions this Division and the Appellate Division of this Court observed that without pinpointing any defect in the method of accounting or recording any findings as to the unacceptability of the method of accounting maintained by the assessee-applicant, the Income Tax Authority has no power to make disallowances or deduct additions claimed in the account of the assessee under the Ordinance. The apprehension of the learned Attorney-General that 'Chapter IX of the Ordinance will be redundant if the audited accounts under section 35(3) of the Ordinance are accepted in toto' has no basis because in all the cases decided under several jurisdictions of the sub-continent their Lordships consistently held that the Taxing Authority can resort to the proviso of section 35(4) but in that case the assessing officer is only required to record with reasons that the method of accounting employed by the assessee company is not regular or from such method of accounting true income of the asses-see cannot be properly deduced or that an assessee Company has not complied with the requirements of sub-section 3 of section 35 of the Ordinance. In the case of Commissioner of Taxes vs Harendra Kumar reported in 34 DLR (AD) 298, referred by the learned Attorney-General, it is categorically held:

"In such a case the assessing officer is only required to record with reasons that the system of accounting employed by the assessee does not reflect true income and, therefore, true income cannot be properly deduced therefore."

15. In the said case, the DCT recorded its finding as follows:

"Above defects in cash book itself suggest that the books of accounts were not maintained in course of day-to-day, trading but were manufactured afterwards. In view of all the above defects I reject the books of accounts and take recourse to estimate."

16. Apart from the decisions cited by the learned Advocates, we have gone through some other decisions, such as the case of Commissioners of Taxes vs Rathna Tea Estate reported in 19 DLR (SC) 538, the case of Mark Builders vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 59 DLR 463 and also the case of Chand Textile (Spinning) Mills Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes, (judgment of which has been delivered on 23-11-2008 by this Bench).

17. All the cases from Messrs Rathna Tea Estate vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 19 DLR (SC) 538 fill the very recent case of Chand Textile (Spinning) Mills Ltd, it has been consistently held that the DCT can resort to the proviso of section 35(4) of the Ordinance upon rejecting the books of accounts of the assessee but he must record a finding that no method of accounting has been regularly employed by the assessee or method in such, that the income of the assessee cannot be properly deduced therefrom or that an assessee company has not complied with the requirement of sub-section 3 of section 35 of the Ordinance, 1984. In the case of Mark Builders vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 59 DLR 463, their Lordships held:

"Under sub-section (4) of section 35 of the Ordinance, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes has got power to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he thinks fit only where (a) no method of accounting has been regularly employed by an assessee being a company, or if the method employed is such that in the opinion of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes the income of the assessee cannot be deduced, or (c) a company has not complied with the requirements of sub-section (3). So, in the absence of any of the above grounds the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes has got no power to compute the income on any basis or in any manner he thought best."

18. In the said case, their Lordships observed that :

"The latitude available to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes under section 35 is no doubt very wide but cannot be thought to be without any restraint in the process of assessment of the total income of an assessee under sub-section (2) of section 83 of the Ordinance. Discretion of statutory authority in the exercise of statutory power, particularly in taxation matter if thought to be unlimited, then exercise of such discretion may result in arbitrariness and selectivity"

19. In the case of Commissioner of Income Tax vs Ata Hossain Khan Ltd, on which the learned Attorney-General relied, their Lordships held :

"This opinion of the Income Tax Officer, as has been referred to in the second part of the proviso, cannot be a mere subjective or arbitrary one, but it has to be formed judicially that is to say, there must be some material basis for such an opinion. It is now a well established principle of law that if any person or administrative body is in vested with a power to do an act which may affect certain individual or his rights such a person or body has the concomitant duty to exercise that power judicially. The opinion of the Income Tax Officer that the computation of the taxable income of an assessee cannot be properly deducted from the account submitted by the assessee may affect the assessee very much so as to augment his financial burden by increasing his tax liability. The formation of such an opinion should therefore, have an objective foundation which is amenable to judicial scrutiny."

20. As such, the submission of the learned Attorney-General that 'the assessment order "effects impliedly" that the DCT rejected the books of accounts' has no legal basis. It is well established canon of interpretation of fiscal statutes that the language employed in the section has to be strictly construed and given its plain and natural meaning. In a Taxing Status, one has to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment. In fiscal law nothing is to be read in, nothing is to be implied. In the process of assessment, the Income Tax Authority may reject any allowance and/or deduct any addition claimed under the Ordinance but he must record reason for such rejection or deduction. Such recording of reason is now a statutory obligation after insertion of section 30A of the Ordinance, 1984. Section 30A reads as follows:

30A. Provision for disallowance—Notwithstanding anything contained in sections 28, 29 and 30, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall not make any disallowance or deduction for any year from any claim made by an assessee in the trading account of profit or loss account without specifying reason for such dis-allowance or deduction.

21. Thus, after the insertion of the above provision of law the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes including the Appellate Authority, under the Ordinance, is also under the statutory obligation to specify reasons in maintaining or upholding any disallowances or deductions made by the DCT.

<u>22. Where section 35(4) of the Income Tax Ordinance is clear that the DCT can discard the audited accounts of the assessee only when no method of accounting has been regularly employed by the assessee or when, in his opinion, the taxable income cannot be properly deduced from the account submitted by the assessee, the Tribunal totally ignored this legal aspect and, as such, the order of the Tribunal being inconsistent with the provision of law, we are of the view that the question raised in this reference application is completely a question of law and not a question of fact as contended by the respondent. Furthermore, in the case of Chand Textile (Spinning) Mills Ltd vs Commissioner of Income Tax, this Bench held:</u>

<u>"Thus, the legal position is that in computation of income, profit and gain of company the DCT is entitled to reject the books of accounts if he is of the opinion that no method of accounting has been regularly employed by the assessee or if the method employed is such, that the income of the assessee cannot be properly deduced therefrom or that a company has not complied with the requirement of sub-section (3) of section 35 of the Ordinance".</u>

23. It is further held in the said judgment.

"Thus in the absence of any such finding of the DCT the authority was not at all authorised in law to reject the accounts of the assessee and affirming the order of the DCT. The Tribunal totally ignored the legal aspect of the case. So, where the law i.e. section 30A of the Ordinance, is clear that without specifying any reason for such disallowance or deduction the DCT shall not make any order and the decision referred above being in consonance with the provision of law, we are of the view that the question raised is completely a question of law and the same can be determined in this reference application answering the same in the form of negative."

24. We do not find any reason to depart from the view taken in the above referred cases.

<u>25. In the instant case, there is no observation given by the DCT that he has found any defect in the method of accounting employed by the assessee-applicant or there is any defect in the account itself. He simply opined that the expenditure was not fully supported by evidence and on that account he has resorted to assess under the proviso of section 35(4) of the Ordinance but he has not arrived at any positive finding that from the accounts submit-ted by the assessee he is not in a position to properly deduce the income therefrom nor has he rejected the books of accounts of the assessee. This legal aspect is totally ignored by the Tribunal. Here it may further be mentioned that the first appellate order of the AACT is extremely an unhappy one and the same is not a speaking order.</u>

<u>26. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove and considering the aforesaid several cited decisions and the provisions of law, we are of the view that the Income Tax Authority acted beyond the scope of section 35(4) read with section 30A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. Accordingly, we find substance in the reference application.</u>

27. Therefore, it is ordered that the question raised in the reference application is answered in the form of negative and in favour of the assessee-applicant.

28. The Registrar of the Court is directed to take necessary steps to communicate the result of this reference application under section 161(2) of the Ordinance, 1984.

However, there will be no order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
MA Rahim, Advocate — For the Appellant. 
M Moazzem Hossain with AH Mahfoozur Rahman, Advocates — For the Respondents.
parties:
Arifan Nessa ----- Appellant
vs.
Haroon-or-Rashid and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
M.M. Ruhul Amin, J: This is an appeal from the judgment and order dated 31-12-81 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Jhenidah in Miscellaneous Judicial Case No. 96 of 1979 under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (shortly the Act) dismissing the case.

2. Facts, in short, are that the appellant-petitioner filed the case under section 96 of the Act for pre-emption of the case land on the allegations inter alia that the appellant-petitioner is a co-sharer in the disputed holding by inheritance and the opposite party No. 5 transferred the case land to opposite party Nos. 1-4 (Ka) who are strangers by a kabala executed on 25-8-78 and registered on 21-5-79. No notice of the said transfer under pre-emption was served upon the appellant-petitioner as a co-sharar and the appellant-petitioner filed the case for pre-emption within the statutory period of limitation and prayed for pre-emption of the case land.

3. The respondent-opposite party Nos. 1, 3 and 4 and 4(Ka) contested the case by filing written objection contending inter alia that the case is not maintainable and the case is barred by limitation. They also denied the other material allegations made in the Misc. Petition.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the pre-emption case as being time-barred.

5. Being aggrieved the petitioner has preferred this appeal. It is not disputed that the appellant-petitioner is a co-sharer by inheritance in the disputed holding and the opposite party Nos. 1-4 (Ka) are stranger-purchasers. It is also admitted that no notice of the kabala under pre-emption was served upon the petitioner as a co-sharer. The kabala under pre-emption was executed on 25-8-78 and the same was registered according to the provisions of section 60 of the Registration Act on 21-5-79. The Misc. Case under section 96 of the Act was filed on 3-7-79. So the case is well within time.

6. It is also undisputed that 5 persons including opposite party No. 4(Ka) are purchasers of the case land by kabala under pre-emption and opposite party No.4 (Ka) was not made party at the time of filing the pre-emption case and opposite party No.4(Ka) one of the admitted transferees was made party in the case on 24-1-81 i.e. long after the institution of the pre-emption case on 3-7-79.

7. Mr. MA Rahim, the learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that this was a mistake on the part of the learned Advocate who drafted the Misc. Petition and by subsequent amendment dated 24-1-61 one of the admitted purchasers was made opposite party No.4(ka). He submits that the amendment of pleading can be allowed at any stage of the proceeding. He then submits that the opposite party did not point out the omission and as such, the learned trial Court rightly added the opposite party 4(ka) as a party in the proceding and further submits that subsequent addition of party will not make the case defective.

8. In reply the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents submits that the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 96 of the Act are mandatory and sub-section (2) of section 96 of the Act provides that the transferees shall be made parties in an application under section 96 of the Act and such an application must be made within four months of the service of the notice given under section 89 of the Act or if no notice has been served under section 89 of the act within four months of the date of knowledge of the transfer. The learned Advocate for the respondents further submits that the opposite party No.4(Ka) was added as party long after the expiry of four months. In fact, he was added as a party after a lapse of 1-1/2 years from the date of filing of the pre-emption case and as such, the pre-emption case became time barred. The learned Advocate further submits that the opposite party No. 4(Ka) was not added as party at the time of making the application under pre-emption. Subsequent addition of party out of time will make the pre-emption application time barred.

9. He further submits that under section 96 of the Act partial pre-emption is not allowable and even if the pre-emption case is found to be maintainable in absence of opposite party No.4(Ka), then the question of partial pre-emption will arise and it is not allowable under section 96 of the Act.

10. It is not disputed that the opposite party No.4(ka) is a necessary party and a proper party in the application for pre-emption and as such, the case is bad for defect of parties for non-joinder of a necessary party namely, opposite party No.4(Ka).

11. The learned Advocate for the respondents next submits that the point for consideration is whether such joinder of opposite party No.4(ka) after a lapse of 1-1/2 years from the date of institution of the pre-emption case shall make the pre-emption case itself barred by limitation as against the aforesaid added party. He further submits that section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that the procedure provided in the Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction. He further submits that an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act is governed by the provisions of The Code of Civil Procedure. He also submits that sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that subject to the provisions of section 22 of the Limitation Act, the proceedings as against any person added as opposite party shall be deemed to have begun only on the service of the summons/notice upon him. Section 22 of the Limitation Act provides that where after the institution of the suit if a new defendant is added, the suit shall, as regards him, be deemed to have been instituted when he was not made a party, provided that such addition has not been made owing to an assignment or devolution of any interest during the pendency of the suit. The learned Advocate for the respondents further submits that since the opposite party No. 4(ka) was added after a lapse of 1-1/2 years from the institution of the case under section. 96 of the Act, the case is hopelessly barred by limitation and must fail on this count alone. In support of his contention he has relied upon the case of Girl Bala Das vs. Vasudev Dey and others, reported in 32 DLR 68. In that case it was held:

"Considering the provisions of section 141 and sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 22 of Limitation Act as aforesaid it clearly appears that in a pre-emption case either under the State Acquisition Act if a proper and necessary party like an heir of transferee is added as a party to the proceeding evidently after the statutory period of limitation such pre-emption case must be held to be barred by limitation at least against such party added after the period of limitation as such".

12. In the instant case the opposite party No. 4(Ka) was one of the purchasers of the case land by kabala under pre-emption but he was not made party when the case under section 96 of the Act was filed and he was impleaded as opposite party No. 4(Ka) after 1-1/2 years from the date of filing of the case. In that case it was further held that in such a case the pre-emption case is barred by limitation at least against the party added after the expiry of period of limitation. I am of the view that the facts of the case referred to above are similar to the facts of the present case and accordingly, the decision referred to above is applicable in the present case.

13. The learned Advocate for the respondents next submits that if the pre-emption case is barred by limitation against opposite party No. 4(Ka), the case against the other opposite parties namely, opposite party Nos. 1-4 who are on record within the period of limitation cannot be allowed, for partial pre-emption is not allowable under section 96 of the Act.

14. In the case reported in 32 DLR 68, the cases reported in 38 CWN 654, 49 CWN 242, 19 DLR 659, 13 DLR 323, 14 DLR 847 and 28 DLR 400 were considered on this point and it was held that partial pre-emption is not allowable in view of the language imported in sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act, as partial pre-emption cannot be allowed both under law and equity.

<u>15. Mr. MA Rahim cited the case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 110 and submits that if an amendment is allowed it will relate back to the date of the institution of the pre-emption. This amendment refers to an amendment under Order 6 rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But in the instant case there was no such amendment. On the other hand, there was addition of party under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case the appellants have been able to show that a valuable legal right had accrued in their favour for not impleading opposite party no.4(Ka) within the statutory period of limitation. For not impleading the opposite party No. 4 (Ka) within time, the pre-emption application has become time-barred. In the case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 110 it was held that as a rule no amendment is allowed where its effect will take away any legal right which might have accrued by lapse of time. In the instant case, as I have already pointed out that a valuable legal right has already accrued in favour of the opposite parties for non-impleading opposite party No.4(Ka) within time.</u>

<u>16. The learned Advocate for the respondents then submits that in the case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 1, it has been held that impleading of a co-sharer, whether by inheritance or by purchase, in an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act is mandatory and omission to implead a co-sharer in the application renders the pre-emption application liable to be dismissed for defect of party. He further submits that as the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 96 of the Act are mandatory any omission to implead the transferee in the application for pre-emption within time will render the pre-emption application liable to be dismissed for defect of party.</u>

<u>17. In view of the discussion above, I am of the view that the pre-emption case is barred by limitation at least as against the opposite party No. 4(Ka) for not impleading him within the statutory period of limitation and even if the case is found to be maintainable against opposite party Nos. 1-4 who were brought on record within time, the case must fail, as partial pre-emption is not allowable under section 96 of the Act. Accordingly, I find no substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellant.</u>

18. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The judgment and order appealed from are hereby affirmed.

Send down the LC Record at once.

End.

caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 325 of 2008 with Civil Rule No. 500(FM) of 2008.
lawyer:
Syed Mainul Haque with MG Mahmud (Shaheen) Advocates—For the Appellant. 
M Enayetur Rahim with Zahangir Alam, Advocates —For the Respondents.
parties:
Shahidul Islam Reza (Md) ----- Appellant
vs
Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Roumari, Kurigram and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam J: At the instance of the plaintiff-appellant this First Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the order dated 18-8-2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Kurigram in Other Suit No. 09 of 2008 rejecting an application for temporary injunction.

2. On an application for temporary injunction the Rule was issued by this Court giving rise to Civil Rule No. 500 (FM) of 2008 wherein order of injunction was also passed by this Court.

3. Sole plaintiff has filed Other Suit No. 9 of 2008 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Kurigram against the defendants-respondents for a declaration that the resolution dated 10-7-2008 passed by the governing body of the Jadur Char Model College suspending the appellant is illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the appellant.

4. In that suit the appellant filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for an order of temporary injunction so that his peaceful functioning as the Principal of the Jadur Char Model College has not been disturbed. In that application for temporary injunction the appellant contended that he was appointed as the principal of the aforesaid college on 1-4-99 and had been serving the college diligently to the satisfaction of others. Subsequently on 10-7-2008 a meeting of the governing body was held and in that so-called meeting the plaintiff was shown to be suspended. By letter dated 16-7-2008 issued by the defendant-respondent No. 1. The Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Roumari, who is the president of that college, the order of suspension dated 10-7-2008 was effected. Stating all these facts the appellant prayed for temporary injunction. The learned Joint District Judge by his order dated 24-7-2008 issued a show cause notice upon the defendant respondent Nos. 1 to 10 asking them why the order of temporary injunction should not be passed restraining them from disturbing the plaintiff-appellant in functioning as principal of the said college. The said application for temporary injunction was contested by the defendant-respondent Nos. 1 to 5 by filing written objection bringing some allegations, in particular, that the plaintiff-appellant misappropriated the money given by the defendant respondent No. 2 to deposit the same with bank as FDR.

5. After hearing the parties the learned Joint District Judge by the impugned order dated 18-8-2008 disallowed the application for temporary injunction filed by the appellant against which the appellant has preferred the instant First Miscellaneous Appeal.

6. Mr Syed Mainul Hoque appearing with Mr MG Mahmud, the learned Counsel after taking us through the impugned order appealed against has mainly argued that the governing body of the college acted without jurisdiction in suspending the plaintiff-appellants inasmuch as in so doing no inquiry was ever held and the suspension order is malafide which is not at all in keeping with the Recognised Non-government Intermediate College Teachers (Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Rajshahi) Terms and Conditions of the Service Regulations, 1979. The learned Counsel after taking us through Annexure-A to the application for Temporary Injunction points out that without serving any show cause notice and without affording the appellant to defend him the order of suspension dated 10-7-2008 was passed which has clearly violated section 14 of the said Regulation, 1979. He submits that before makings an order of suspension it was incumbent upon the managing body of the college to issue a show cause notice upon the appellant giving 7 days' time so that he could give reply to such notice. Therefore, it is in clear violation of said regulation as mentioned above. The learned Counsel in support of his contention placed reliance in the decision of BN Khan College vs Md Abdul Rahim 7 BLT (AD) 153, (Bijoy Kumar Shaha vs DC, Chuadanga) 55 DLR 550.

7. Mr M Enayetur Rahim, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the defendants-respondents, submits that the order appealed against is absolutely justified under the facts and circumstances of the case. His contention is that the suspension order of the appellant was passed pending enquiries against the appellant which was absolutely in accordance with law and on that score the learned Joint District Judge rightly refused the prayer for temporary injunction. He submits that the order of suspension is not a measure of punishment and in the main suit the legality or validity of the order can be looked into. For the reasons stated the learned Counsel submits that in all fairness this appeal should be dismissed.

8. Be that as it may, we have heard the learned Counsel for both the sides at length and considered their respective submissions carefully. From Annexure-'A' filed with the application of temporary injunction before this Court, which is the application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial Court, we found that the appellant made a positive assertion that the order of suspension dated 10-7-2008 without issuing prior show cause notice upon him was done absolutely against the specific provision of law and for that reason the order of suspension was void ab initio. Further Annexure-'C' to the application for temporary injunction which is 'the written objection filed by the defendants-respondents before the learned Joint District Judge, this positive assertion of the appellant had not been adverted to, rather Annexure-11 of the supplementary affidavit filed before this Court on behalf of the respondents applicants for vacating the order of ad-interim injunction we found that 26-7-2008 proceeding was drawn up against the appellant and he was asked to show cause within 3 days. From which it is clear that the proceeding against the appellant was drawn up after the order of suspension and only 3 days time were given to the appellant for showing cause.

9. Let us now see the Regulation 14 which reads as follows:

14. Procedure for drawing up proceedings—(1) When a teacher is to be proceeded against for offences specified in Regulation 11, he shall be called upon by a notice to submit a written explanation within seven days as to why the penalty or penalties specified in the notice should not be imposed on him for the alleged offences and asking him if he desires to be heard in person.

10. An order of suspension of a teacher pre-supposes that the procedures laid down in Regulation 14 have been duly complied with. If it is not so complied with, the same is certainly tainted with malafide. This view finds support in the decision of Bijoy Kumar Shaha vs Deputy Commissioner, Chuadanga 55 DLR 550. Similarly Justice GG Shaha observed:

"Although suspension is not a punishment and it can be restored to in connection with a departmental proceeding already drawn up or about to be drawn up, yet it cannot be restored by way of punishment. When the Court finds the move malafide and arbitrary, it is not only competent to look into the legality and propriety of the impugned action but is also called upon to act decisively to administer even-handed justice."

11. In the case of BL Khan College vs Md Abdul Rahim the said proposition of law was held up by the Appellate Division itself in the following manner:

"From the averments in the plaint, it is found that the suspension order was passed without prior show cause. The plaintiff having been adversely affected by the suspension order has filed the suit and, as such, it cannot be said that he has no cause of action to file the suit."

12. In the case of Sheikh Abdul Kuder vs Bangladesh reported in 30 DLR (SC) 96 Justice DC Bhattacharya while interpreting Regulation 21 of the Service Regulations of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation in connection with the suspension order of an employee observed:-

"Although an order of suspension which was made by an employer of public character pending enquiry for the purpose of facilitating such enquiry and also for maintaining discipline and efficiency in the service, might not amount to a penalty but was certainly an order, adverse to the interest of the employee concerned, and, as such, the affected employee was, in the ordinary course, entitled to a prior notice to explain the allegation against him before such an order was passed.

<u>13. Admittedly, as it has been already discussed, the suspension order appealed against has been passed without giving any prior notice to the appellant and for that reason the order of suspension has certainly been passed in violation of Regulation 14 of the Recognised Non-Government Intermediate College Teachers (Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Rajshahi) Terms and Ccnditions of Service Regulations, 1979. The respondents in passing such order of suspension indeed, had indulged in accesses as discussed.</u>

<u>14. On the conspectus, we are of the view that under the facts and circumstances plaintiff-appellant had succeeded in proving that he had prima facie case that warranted an order of injunction by the trial Court and the trial Court without granting the relief has committed illegality.</u>

<u>15. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The order appealed against is set aside. The application for temporary injunction is allowed.</u>

16. Defendants are hereby restrained by an order of temporary injunction from disturbing the plaintiff-appellant in performing as principal of Jadur Char Model College till disposal of the suit.

17. Connected Civil Rule No. 500(FM) of 2008 is also discharged.

Communicate this order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Choudhury Md Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellant. 
Mahbub Ali, Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent No. 1. 
Not represented—Respondent Nos. 2-11.
parties:
Aslam Khan (Md) ----- Appellant
Vs.
Abdur Rahim and ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: This is plaintiff's appeal by leave against the judgment dated August 23, 2001 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 526 of 2000 discharging the same. The Rule was obtained against the judgment and decree dated June 29, 1999 of the Court of Additional District Judge, Moulvibazar in Title Appeal No. 54 of 1995 allowing the same and thereupon dismissing the suit being Title Suit No. 32 of 1993. The trial Court by the judgment and decree dated February 23, 1995 decreed the Title Suit No. 32 of 1993 which was filed seeking declaration that the kabala described in the schedule attached to the plaint is forged, fraudulent and void.

2. The suit was filed on September 8, 1993 having been served on September 28, 1992 with the summons of Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1992 filed on September 20,1992. The Miscellaneous Case was filed seeking pre-emption as contiguous land holder of the land transferred by the kabala sought to be declared as forged, fabricated and void.

3. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that the land in suit was owned by plaintiff's father Osman Khan who died leaving two sons, one of whom is the plaintiff, and a daughter, that upon amicable partition amongst the heirs of Osman Khan plaintiff got the land in suit and possessing the same, that on September 28, 1992 plaintiff received the summons of Miscellaneous Case (preemption) No. 18 of 1992 and thereby came to know that the defendant Nos.1-5 upon using the name of the plaintiff have created the kabala in question in respect of the land mentioned therein, that the plaintiff obtained the certified copy of the kabala from the office of the Sub-Registrar, Srimongal, that the plaintiff has not executed and registered the kabala in question, that though in the kabala value of the land has been mentioned Taka 10,000 but, in fact, the market price of the land in suit is Taka 1,00,000, that the plaintiff has never received any money in connection with the alleged kabala from the defendant Nos.1-5, that the deed was never acted upon and the said forged and fabricated kabala as has created cloud on plaintiff's title in the land in suit hence the suit.

4. The pre-emptor of the Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1992 got himself impleaded in the plaintiff's suit i.e. Title Suit No. 32 of 1993 as defendant No. 11 and contested the suit by filing written statement. It is the case of the defendant No. 11 i.e. respondent No.1 herein, that plaintiff being in need of cash money sold the land in suit by the kabala impugned in the suit for Taka 10,000 to the defendant Nos. 1-5, of whom defendant No. 5 is the maternal aunt of the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 1-4 are the close relations of the defendant No. 5, that plaintiff pursuant to the said act made over possession to the defendants, that at the time of transfer many elites of Srimongal Town were present and in presence of them plaintiff received Taka 10,000, that the plaintiff executed and registered the kabala impugned in the suit, that the plaintiff put his left hand thumb impression in the Thumb Impression Register of the office of the Sub-Registrar, that the suit has been filed in collusion with defendant Nos.1-5 who are close relations of the plaintiff to frustrate the claim of pre-emption.

5. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff's suit is not barred by limitation, that the suit is quite maintainable as per provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, that the plaintiff proved his possession in the land in suit by his evidence as well as by the evidence of PWs 2-6, that the defendant has not proved that the plaintiff executed and registered the kabala, nor the defendant has established that plaintiff received the consideration, Taka 10,000, that although it has not been established who had brought into existence the kabala but it has been established by the plaintiff that the same is a forged one.

6. The defendant No. 11, respondent No.1 herein, went on appeal. The appellate Court allowed the appeal and thereupon reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the finding that the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 1-5 in collusion with each other have filed the suit to frustrate the claim of preemption of the defendant No. 11 for which he has already filed Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1992. Thereupon, the plaintiff moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule.

7. The High Court Division discharged the Rule on the finding that the trial Court decreed the suit wrongly placing onus upon tile defendant to prove the kabala in question forged and fabricated although under the law it was the duty of the plaintiff or, in other words, onus was on the plaintiff to establish that the kabala in question is forged, fabricated and fraudulent, that the plaintiff did not take any step for calling the Thumb Impression Register from the office of the Sub-Registrar and for examination of the thumb impression appearing in the Thumb Impression Register of the office of sub-registrar by a Hand Writing Expert to establish that the kabala in question was forged, fabricated and fraudulent one, that the plaintiff failed to prove his case by reliable evidence and the plaintiff has filed the suit solely for the purpose of defeating the claim of pre-emption of the defendant No. 11 for which he has already filed Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1992, that the findings and decisions of the appellant Court as to that plaintiff could not prove his case are based on due considerations of the evidence and, as such, no error was committed by the lower appellate Court in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court which was made upon placing the onus wrongly on the defendant for proving the deed in question as forged as well as reliable evidence being nil.

8. Leave was granted to consider the contention that plaintiff having had denied to have executed the alleged kabala the onus was upon the recipients of the document to prove the same as genuine but he recipients having had not proved the same the trial Court quite legally decreed the suit and thereby cancelled the impugned deed, bur the appellate Court wrongly set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and the High Court Division was in error in affirming the judgment of the lower appellate Court, that the recipients of the alleged kabala having not contested the claim of the plaintiff, the appellate Court was in error in dismissing the suit on the basis of the contest of the added defendant No. 11 who had no locus standi to challenge the claim of the plaintiff, that the plaintiff having had prayed before the Court to call the Thumb Impression Register to show that the kabala in question is forged and fabricated and, as such, there having had no laches on the part of the plaintiff in proving his case, the appellate Court was in error in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff and the High Court Division committed an error in affirming the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court.

9. The last contention of the appellant relating to calling of Thumb Impression Register from the office of the Sub-Registrar for the purpose of establishing the fact that the kabala in question was forged and fabricated is not correct. In fact, as seen from the judgment of the High Court Division, the plaintiff filed application for calling volume wherein the kabala in question was entered into from the office of the sub-registrar instead of calling for the Thumb Impression Register. In the background of the fact that the original kabala was not filed before the Court and, as such, the plaintiff ought to have take step for calling thumb impression register from the office of the sub-registrar and to get the thumb impression examined by a Hand Writing Expert for the purpose of establishing his claim that the kabala in question is forged and fraudulent.

10. The learned Counsel for the appellant took us through the judgment of the High Court Division and the courts below. In the background of the facts and circumstances of the case and the findings made by the last Court of fact as well as by the High Court Division, the learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that for the interest of justice the case may be sent back to the trial Court to enable the plaintiff to call for the thumb impression register from the office of the sub-registrar and to get the thumb impression appearing in the said register in connection with the deed in question as well as the plaintiff's thumb impression examined by the Hand Writing Expert for ascertaining the genuineness or otherwise of the kabala in question.

11. The learned Counsel for the respondent seriously took exception to the aforesaid submission of the learned Counsel of the appellant and submitted that the plaintiff and the recipients of the kabala in question, who are the defendant Nos. 1-5, are closely related to each other and the plaintiff and the said defendants in collusion with each other have filed the suit much long after the filing of the Miscellaneous case claiming preemption of the land transferred by the kabala with the sole object of frustrating the defendant's, i.e. the preemptor's, claim of preemption. The learned Counsel also submitted that the High Court, Division as well as the lower appellate Court in the background of the materials on record, have quite correctly held that the plaintiff has filed the suit in collusion with the defendant Nos. 1-5 to frustrate the claim of the defendant No. 11 who has already filed the Miscellaneous case for pre-empting the land transferred by the kabala in question. The learned Counsel, further submitted that collusive character of the suit is very much apparent from the fact that the summons of the Miscellaneous Case. which was filed on September 20, 1992 was served on the plaintiff on September 28, 1992 and long thereafter the plaintiff filed the suit on September 8, 1993. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel that the entries in the kabala has the presumption of correctness under the provision of section 60 of the Registration Act as well as in view of the provision of section 114(e) of the Evidence Act. It has also been submitted that the suit as framed was not maintainable in that plaintiff being a party to the kabala he was required to seek for consequential relief by way of cancellation of the kabala but the plaintiff has filed the suit seeking merely declaration that the kabala in question is forged fraudulent and void. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 that evidence on possession of the land had no relevancy since matter of possession is not an issue in the suit in the background of the relief sought in the suit.

12. The learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 in support of his contention that when the plaintiff is a party to a document and if he seeks relief for avoiding the document he is to ask for cancellation of the same and a suit for mere declaration that the questioned kabala is forged, fabricated and fraudulent is not maintainable without seeking cancellation has referred to the case of Sree Chitta Ranjan Chakraborty being dead his heirs Ashish Chakraborty and others vs Md Abdur Rob alias Mvi Md Abdur Rob reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 126 = 49 DLR (AD) 96 wherein it has been observed "that where a written instrument is ab initio void the transaction is a nullity and the plaintiff is not required to have it cancelled or set aside and if, on the other hand. the instrument is only voidable, then it would be essential for the plaintiff to have it cancelled or set aside". In the instant case, the document in question is voidable at the best and, as such, the plaintiff was required to seek for consequential relief in the form of cancellation of the document in question or for setting aside the same. The other contention that the document being a registered one has the presumption of correctness because of the certificate attached thereto by the Sub-Registrar and thereupon signature put and the seal affixed by the registering officer and thus has the presumption that the said official acts have been regularly performed and that there is presumption under section 60 of the Registration Act that the document was duly registered and in support of the said contention the learned Counsel also referred to the case of Abani Mohan Saha vs Assistant Custodian (SDO) Vested Property, Chandpur and others reported in 39 DLR (AD) 223.

13. The High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court upon due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record have held that the suit has been filed to frustrate the claim of pre-emption of the respondent No. 1 who for the enforcement of right of preemption has filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1992 and long thereafter the plaintiff filed the suit. The trial Court decreed the suit wrongly shifting the onus on the defendant for establishing the fact that the document for setting aside whereof suit has been filed, was executed by the plaintiff. The plaintiff filed the suit seeking declaration that the document in question was fraudulent and forged. Since the plaintiff is urging upon the Court to declare the document in question forged and fraudulent, it was the obligation of the plaintiff to establish the said fact. The plaintiff in support of his case that the document in question is forged and fabricated has examined himself alone. He being interested for getting the kabala declared fraudulent and fabricated or for that matter forged, there was necessity of corroboration of his evidence to that effect but the same was nil. In that state of the matter, the appellate Court and the High Court Division dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff failed to establish his case. The learned Counsel for the appellant, in the background of the materials on record, felt difficulty to assail the finding of the High Court Division and the lower appellate Court that the plaintiff failed to prove his case or, in other words, failed to prove that the impugned document was forged and fabricated. The undenied position is that the plaintiff and the recipients of the document in question i.e. respondent Nos. 1-5, are closely related to each other and at one stage plaintiff tried to place a case before the Court that defendant Nos. 1-5 in collusion with the defendant No. 11 i.e. respondent No. 1 herein, created the document in question only to deprive the plaintiff of the land sought to be pre-empted. The aforesaid contention of the plaintiff was not accepted by the Court of appeal and the High Court Division, being in the background of the facts and circumstances of the case, something absurd.

14. The High Court Division and the appellate Court below in the facts and circumstances of the case have held that plaintiff's suit is collusive one. The finding so made, in our view, was quite correct in view of the fact that the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 1-5 are closely related and there is no reason for the defendant Nos. 1-5 to bring into existence the document in question fraudulently or resorting to forgery. The fact of non-contesting the suit by the defendant Nos. 1-5 has highlighted the allegation of the respondent No. 1 that the suit is a collusive one and the same has been filed by the plaintiff in collusion with the defendant Nos. 1-5 only to defeat the right of pre-emption of the contesting defendant No. 11. In the background of the materials on record, it is seen that plaintiff purposely did not produce the evidence before the Court to establish that the document in question is a fraudulent one. The plaintiff tried to obtain a decree in collusion with the defendant Nos. 1-5 making untrue statements but the said attempt has been frustrated because of the contest made by the defendant No. 11 i.e. respondent No. 1 herein.

15. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that plaintiff filed an application for calling the volume wherein the deed in question was copied from the office of the Sub-Registrar instead of calling for the thumb impression register for getting the thumb impression appearing in the said register and the thumb impression of the plaintiff examined by the Hand Writing Expert. In the background thereof, the learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that the case may be sent back on remand for enabling the plaintiff to get the thumb impression examined by a Hand Writing Expert upon calling for the thumb impression register and thereupon, if the case is adjudicated, then ends of justice would best be served.

<u>16. The submission so made is not a merited one, first, the High Court Division as well as the Court of appeal below, on consideration of the materials on record, have held that the suit is a collusive one. Since the findings so made by the High Court Division and the appellate Court is based on materials on record no purpose would be served in remanding the case back for enabling the plaintiff to get the thumb impression in the thumb impression register examined for the purpose of ascertainment whether the same is of the plaintiff. Secondly, the suit has not been disposed of on preliminary point or that without framing and trying the issue which should have been framed and adjudicated or that without determining any question of fact which was required to be determined for a correct decision in the matter involved in the suit.</u>

<u>17. The law is now settled that order of remand cannot be passed by a Court as a matter of course [41 DLR (AD) 124] and in a case where the party/parties is/are negligent in producing evidence or to fill up the lacuna [7 BLT (AD) 7].</u>

18. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore we do not find any merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the same is dismissed with costs.

End.
