Hazrat Ali Bhuiyan ----- Petitioner
vs
Md Chunnu Sikder and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the legality and property of the judgment and decree dated 17-8-12002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Patuakhali, in Title Appeal No. 167 of 2000 sending the suit on remand to the trial Court for holding retrial by setting aside the judgment and decree dated 30-7-2000 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mirjagonj, Patuakhali, in Title Suit No. 89 of 1994 decreeing the suit. Short facts leading to this Rule are that on 19-11-1994 the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 89 of 1994 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Mirjagonj, Patuakhali, impleading the opposite parties as defendants for declaration of title in respect of 4.29 acres of land out of 8.35 acres described in the schedule of the plaint and also for cancellation of the order dated 2-11-1992 passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) in Miscellaneous Case No. 3 M/91-92 being illegal void, malafide, collusive.

2. The plaintiff's case put in a nutshell is, that the suit property had originally belonged to Zaher Bhuiyan and Malancho Bibi in equal share. After the death of Zaher Bhuiyan his son Aroj Ali Bhuiyan inherited his share. Malancho Bibi died leaving behind her three daughters. Subsequently their successor settled the property in favour of Asmat Ali Bhuiyan and Ruhul Amin by a registered deed dated 12-4-1945, and also handed over the possession thereof. After the death of Asmat Ali his son the plaintiff inherited the property, but his share of the property was not correctly recorded. The defendants fraudulently recorded their names vide Order dated 2-11-1992 in Miscellaneous Case No. 3M of 1991-1992 from the office of Assistant Commissioner (Land), Mirjagonj. Hence the suit.

3. The opposite party Nos. 1-10, as defendants along with defendants Nos. 15-19 contested the suit by filing joint written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia that on 12-4-1945 Asmat Ali and Ruhul Amin got property through kabuliat. Subsequently the suit land was auctioned in Rent Execution Case No. 155 of 1954. On 10-4-1954 defendant Nos. 1-2, wife of the plaintiff and one Chand Banu purchased the same in auction. The defendant Nos. 15-19 on 12-4-1990 purchased some land from them. Thereby they have right, title, interest and possession in the suit property.

4. On the pleadings different issues were settled including, whether the plaintiff has right, title interest, and possession in the suit land and whether he is entitled to get relief as prayed for.

5. In course of trial the plaintiff examined four witnesses and defendants examined five witnesses in support of their respective case.

6. After hearing, the learned Judge of the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 30-7-2000 decreed the suit in part.

7. On appeal, the learned Judge of the Court below by the judgment and decree dated 17-8-2002 passed in Title Appeal No. 167 of 2000 allowed the appeal and remanded the suit for retrial.

8. Feeling aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below, the plaintiff as petitioner preferred the instant application and obtained the present Rule.

9. Mr AKM Jahirul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, seeks to impeach the impugned judgment and decree on the ground that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below, considering the application filed by some non contesting defendants, sent back the case on remand for retrial to fill up the lacuna, which is not permissible under law.

10. In support of his contention the learned Counsel refers the case of Abu Sayeed Sheikh vs Md Majibur Rahman reported in 51 DLR 289 wherein it has been held :

"For the laches of the indolent defendants the petitioner cannot be made to suffer for facing a new trial after the suit has been disposed of on merit;

11. The learned Counsel next refers the case of Akitullah vs Zafala Begum reported in 54 DLR (AD) 74 wherein it has been held:

"Remand as contemplated under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not a matter of course or to fill in the lacuna in any party's pleading."

12. He also refers the case of Madinullah Miah vs Md Abdul Mannan reported in 54 DLR 507 wherein it has been held:

"When the trial Court, after framing the issues and giving the parties opportunity to adduce evidence, disposes of a suit on merit, the appellate Court in the subsequent appeal therefrom, cannot remand the case back to the trial Court for its disposal on merit anew."

13. Mr Md Yunus Meah, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1-10, opposes the Rule and submits that some of the land virtually diluvated into the river long before. So, on the basis of non existence of such land a suit for declaration of title is not maintainable. He adds that the plaintiff instituted the suit against some co-sharers and it is well settled that suit for declaration against co-sharers is not maintainable. In support of his contention he refers the case of Enjaheruddin Mia vs Md Hossain reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 77 = 50 DLR (AD) 84 wherein it has been held:

"The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act provides that no Court shall make any declaration as to plaintiff's legal character or his right to any property where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration omits to do so In the instant case, the plaintiff prayed only for declaration of his title in the suit land and did not ask for either joint possession or partition as a co-sharer of the defendants in the disputed land. Although the plaintiff's possession was found in some portion of the suit property, the learned Courts below committed no error of law in dismissing the suit for declaration of title simpliciter."

14. He adds that the plaintiff in trial Court did not furnish any plot index so it was impossible to determine his land and on the basis of such unspecification of land the suit for declaration of title is not maintainable.

15. He refers the case of Chand Mia vs Md Shamsuddin reported in 5 BLC (AD) 163 wherein it is held:

"The suit was found not maintainable by the trial Court for want of possession of the plaintiff in accordance with the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act when the appellate Court found fault with the finding of possession arrived at by the trial Court holding that the reasons of the trial Court suffered from discrepancy and the appellate Court also found that the Assistant Custodian was a necessary party and thus the appellate Court did not give any independent finding on possession or decided the matter impleading the party in the suit itself and the said Court had sent back the case on remand to the trial Court for deciding it on all points after holding the trial afresh which has not occasioned any miscarriage of justice and, as such, it was not proper for the High Court Division to interfere with the order of remand while exercising revisional jurisdiction."

16. He next refers the case of Md Hossain vs Monowara Begum reported in 2 BLC (AD) 124 wherein it has been held:

"The suit was instituted by the plaintiff-respondents claiming themselves to be government servants and challenged the order directing them to apply for giving their appointment afresh Although the defendant contested the suit but could not prove his case as the prayer for shifting the date of hearing was refused and the suit was decreed and on appeal the appellate Court sent the case on remand to the trial Court giving the defendant a chance to prove his case holding that civil Court had jurisdiction to try the suit and the High Court Division endorsed the said view in civil revision. Since the petitioner could not get any opportunity to adduce evidence before the trial Court, it is the trial Court who will decide the case afresh after giving an opportunity to the defendant to adduce evidence and will also consider afresh the issue as to the maintainability of the suit in civil Court because of the plea of bar under the provision of the Administrative Tribunal Act."

17. The learned Counsel then submits that the contesting defendants wanted to furnish some documents in respect of auction and the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below should have accepted the same as additional evidence. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel refers the case of Superintendent Engineer (Distribution), PDB, Jangalia, Comilla vs Madhumati Cinema Hall Ltd Comilla reported in 7 MLR (AD) 254 = 54 DLR (AD) 170 wherein it has been held:

"Remand can be allowed in appropriate case to adduce additional evidence under Order XLI, rule 23 and rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the interest of justice but not to fill up lacuna of any party's case."

18. In this regard he also refers the case of Abu Taher vs Taleb Ali reported in 6 MLR (AD) 87 wherein it has been held:

"Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 provides for adducing additional evidence at the appellate stage in certain circumstances. But it does not provide for compulsory recording separate finding on an application under Order XLI, rule 27, CPC. Disposing the application and the appeal by the same judgment without recording separate order on the application does not constitute any illegality warranting interference therewith."

19. The learned Counsel lastly refers the case of Abdul Karim Abu Ahmad Khan vs Allahabad Bank, Ltd reported in AIR 1917 (Calcutta) 44 wherein it has been held:

"Court may order remand in cases other than those covered by Order XLI, rule 23, if justice so requires it."

20. So, according to him, the Court of appeal below has an ample jurisdiction to send back the case on remand for retrial to enable the parties to produce their respective documents and adducing evidence.

21. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels I have gone through the revisional application, impugned judgment and decree, evidences, other material on record and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

22. Now, the question which calls for consideration whether the Court of appeal below committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing the appeal and remanding the suit to the trial Court for retrial.

23. To appreciate the question involved in this Rule, the provisions of Order XLI, rules 23, 24 and 25 and section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure which deal with the remand of a case by the Appellate Court, may be extracted here:

“23 Where the Court from whose decree an appeal is preferred has disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point and the decree is reversed in appeal, the Appellate Court may, if it thinks fit, by order remand the case, and may further direct what issue or issues shall be tried in the case so remanded, and shall send a copy of its judgment and order to the Court from whose decree appeal is preferred, with directions to readmit the suit under its original number in the register of civil suits, and proceed to determine the suit; and the evidence (if any) recorded during the original trial shall, subject to all just exceptions, be evidence during the trial after remand.

24. Where the evidence upon the record is sufficient to enable the Appellate Court to pronounce judgment, the Appellate Court may, after resettling the issues, if necessary, finally determine the suit, notwithstanding that the judgment of the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has proceeded wholly upon some ground other than that on which the Appellate Court proceeds.

25. Where the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has omitted to frame or try any issue, or to determine any question of fact, which appears to the Appellate Court essential to the right decision of the suit upon the merits, the Appellate Court may, if necessary, frame issues, and refer the same for trial to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, and in such case shall direct such Court to take the additional evidence required. Section 107 of the Code runs as follows:

107(1) Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, an Appellate Court shall have power—

(a) to determine a case finally;

(b) to remand a case;

(c) to frame issues and refer them for trial;

(d) to take additional evidence or to require such evidence to be taken.

(2) Subject as aforesaid, the Appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein."

24. From a plain reading of the above stated provisions of law it is clear that under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code there can be no remand unless the following conditions exist:

(a) that the entire suit and not a portion of it has been disposed of by the trial Court;

(b) that the disposal must be on a preliminary point;

(c) and that the preliminary point on which the suit is decided has been reversed by the appellate Court.

25. Order XLI, rule 24 of the Code enjoins that where the evidence on record are sufficient, the appellate Court is competent to deter-mine the suit finally and there is no need for remand.

26. Order XLI, rule 25 of the Code lays down that only specific issues can be sent to the trial Court for findings and not for re-trial of the entire suit and the appeal is to be heard under Order XLI, rule 26 of the Code.

27. Under section 107 of the Code, the appellate Court is vested with the power to determine a case finally and also to remand the case. Sub-section 2 of section 107 of the Code lays down that the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein.

<u>28. It appears that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below sent back the suit on remand for fresh trial but I find that the learned Judge took notice the evidence oral and documentary on record but as a last court of facts failed to weigh and sift the same and to decide the same finally and should not send the suit back on remand for fresh trial.</u>

29. On perusal of the record of the case it appears that in the instant case all the evidences and materials were before the lower appellate Court who itself could have disposed of the appeal finally.

<u>30. It is settled principle of law that unnecessary order of remand entails hardship, agony of fresh hearing and additional expenditure and the same is to be deprecated and discouraged as it tends to delay the administration of justice far from advancing its course.</u>

31. The Pakistan Supreme Court and the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court decided the question of the order of remand in a good number of cases.

32. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Pramotha Nath Chowdhury vs Kamir Mondal reported in 17 DLR (SC) 392 held:

"a remand cannot be lightly ordered if the evidence on record is sufficient for the appellate Court to decide the question itself. There can be no bar to the Court doing so."

33. The Appellate Division, in the case of Probodh Ranjan Shome vs Md Easin reported in 1980 BSCR 457 observed that:

"It is well-settled that remand orders are not to be made as a matter of course. When there is sufficient evidence on record, remand of a case to the trial Court for fresh hearing is not called for."

34. In the case of Dr Razia Khatun vs Banu Guha reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 135 it was observed by the Appellate Division:

"The long line of judicial decisions is to the effect that the remand order should be avoided as far as possible and even the Privy Council in some cases observed that indiscriminate order of remand tantamounts to shirking the responsibility."

35. In the case of Abdul Awal Khan vs Md Sadu Mia reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 156 the Appellate Division held:

"when evidences on all material points are there on record, the revisional court is not justified in sending the case back to the Court below for reconsidering the matter"

36. In the case of Abdul Mannan vs Akram Ali reported in 43 DLR (AD) 124 is was held by the Appellate Division:

"both oral and documentary evidence having been available on record there was no necessity for the remand as ordered by the High Court Division."

37. In the case of Haji Mustafiqur Rahman vs A Kader reported in 3 BLC (AD) 38 wherein it is held:

"It is well settled that remand orders are not to be made a matter of course, it ,should be avoided as far as possible."

<u>38. In view of the discussions made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above I am of the view that the Court of appeal below was fully competent to decide the case by itself as the evidence and other materials on record were sufficient to enable it to come to a final decision without entailing the parties in unnecessary trouble and expenses and the appellate Court shirked its responsibility and thus committed an error of law resulting in an error in remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial.</u>

39. Having regard to the facts I hold that the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1-10, may hold good before the Court of appeal below at the time of disposal of the appeal.

40. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case I am of the view that the ends of justice will be met if the matter is remitted to the Court of appeal below for final disposal of the matter on merit and then pass whatever order or orders it thinks appropriate in the interest of justice. However, the petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 1-10 are at liberty to place their respective case, on merit in the Court of appeal below.

41. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 17-8-2002 passed in Title Appeal No. 167 of 2000 is hereby set aside and the suit is sent back on remand to the Court of appeal below for disposal on merit touching all points.

42. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

43. The learned Judge of the Court of appeal below is directed to dispose of the appeal expeditiously preferably within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of this order.

Office is directed to send down the record of this case at once with a copy of judgment for information and taking necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: This Rule was issued on an application under Article 102(1),(2)(a) of the Constitution calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the recruitment notice (নিয়োগ বিজ্ঞপ্তি) issued by the respondent No. 5, Director General of the Directorate of Primary Education vide its memo No. প্রশিঅ/সাধারণ প্রশাসন/ওএম-৪/৯৫ (অংশ-১)/৯২০ dated 30-9-2008 as published in the 'Daily Amadersamay' on 8-10-2008 so far it relates to its item No. 5 inviting application for recruitment in the permanent posts of Car Drivers for the Directorate of Primary Education and its subordinate Offices and Educational Institutions under the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education as contained in 'Annexure-A' to the writ petition shall not be declared to have been issued with-out lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the respondents shall not be directed to absorb the service of the drivers including the petitioners under the two erstwhile projects namely, “ঢাকা, রাজশাহী ও খুলনা বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” and “চট্ট্রগ্রাম বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” on Seniority Basis in the vacant posts of Drivers under the revenue budget.

2. The facts as stated in the writ petition are that the petitioner Nos. 1-4 were appointed as driver by the Office Order issued under the Memo No. 1 আর-৩৭ (নিয়োগ)/৯২-প্রাই/১০৭৫/৩৫ dated 10/5/1993 by the Director General of the Directorate of Primary Education with reference to the order of the Ministry of Education vide its Memo. No.শাঃ ৯/৯-৩/৮৯/১২৭-শিক্ষা dated 17-3-1991 for the DPE. Unit of the erstwhile project namely “ঢাকা, রাজশাহী ও খুলনা বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” financed by Asian Development Bank (ADB) and petitioner Nos. 5-6 were appointed as drivers by the appointment Orders vide its memo Nos. পিআইএমইউ/প্রাশিউ/১-১৩/৯১/১৭(১৪) dated 8-1-1994 and পিআইএমইউ/প্রাশিউ/১-১৩/অংশ-১/৯১/১৫৯(৯)dated 15-2-1995 respectively under the project namely “চট্ট্রগ্রাম বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প”, that after expiry of the project period on 30-6-1997, only 16 drivers out of total 40 drivers were posted to the vacant posts of drivers on Seniority Basis and the remaining 24 drivers including the petitioners were posted as MLSS (which is one grade lower to the post of driver) in different offices and educational institutions under the Directorate of Primary Education at the same scale of salary paid up to date of expiry of the period of the said project (30th June, 1997) by the office order vide its Memo No.৭-এ/৫-প্রাই(সাঃ)/৯৭/৫০০৮/১২০ dated 25-8-1998 as there was no other vacant post of driver, that the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education and the Ministry of Finance vide its Memo No.আম/অবিিউঃ-৮/প্রাঃশিঃ১/৯৭/(অংশ) dated 3-12-1998 awarded its consent for creating only 466 posts under the revenue budget including the said 16 posts of senior drivers out of total 40 drivers under the said two projects. Subsequently, the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education by its Memo No.প্রাগবি/প্রশা ১/১৫(২)/১৩৬/জিইপি/২০০০/৪০৬ dated 5-4-2000 awarded grant for creating 466 posts including the posts of drivers and placement thereof under the revenue budget and those posts are to be treated as absorbed/placed in the revenue budget temporarily with retrospective effect from the 1st July, 1997 and the service of man-power under the said 2 projects are to be regularised in accordance with the memo No. SRO No. 65-Ain/95/ সম/বিধি-১/ও/৬/৯৪ dated 2-5-1995 of the Ministry of Establishment and the said posts shall have to be included in the Organogram of the Directorate of Primary Education and if the posts under the said Directorate are reorganised in future while the manpower under the said two projects shall also be included therein and in this way the Government has taken the responsibility of absorption of the service of the employees under the said two projects. Subsequently, the service of 184 3rd-Class and 4th-Class employees including the petitioners placed under the said two projects were regularised by the office order vide its Memo. No. প্রশিঅ/সাঃপ্রশাঃ/ওএম-১/২০০২/৯১০২/(৭০৫)dated 12-10-2002 (Annexure-F); that the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education by its Memo No. প্রাগম/প্রশা ১/৮(১৯)/৯৩(অংশ-২)/১০৯৩ dated 20-1-2004 asked the said Director for necessary particulars and papers for obtaining opinion of the Rule section of the Ministry of Establishment on further placing the service of the MLSS who were drivers of the 2 projects under the revenue budget; that the said Directorate by its Memo No. ও,এম/১৪-প্রাই(যাপু)/২০০৩/৫০ dated 13-5-2004 sent the said particulars and papers as asked for by the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education.

3. In this backdrop, the Director General of the said Directorate published a recruitment notice (নিয়োগ বিজ্ঞপ্তি) vide its memo No.-প্রশিঅ/সাধারন প্রশাসন/ওএম-৪/৯৫ (অংশ-১)/৯২০ dated 30-9-2008 in the 'Daily Amadersamay on 8-10-2008 inviting application (item No. 5) for recruitment in the permanent post of car-drivers for the Directorate of the Primary Education and its subordinate offices and Educational Institutions under the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education instead of absorbing the similar car drivers under the said two erstwhile projects namely, “ঢাকা, রাজশাহী ও খুলনা বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” and “চট্টগ্রাম বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প”.

4. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the said recruitment notice dated 30-9-2008 (Annexure-A) so far it relates to recruitment of car drivers (item No. 5) the petitioners have come before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

5. Respondent No. 5, the Directorate of the Primary Education, Dhaka, entered appearance in compliance with the Rule and filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the claim of the petitioners and contending, inter alia, that the writ petition is not maintainable in its present form and manner mainly on the ground that the writ petitioners are being Government servants.

6. Mr Gobinda Chandra Tagore, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, has taken us through the writ petition, supplementary affidavit and other connected papers including the impugned recruitment notice and then he submits that the petitioners are citizens of Bangladesh, they must be treated equally within the meaning of Article 29 of the Constitution but in this case the respondents without absorbing 24 car drivers out of 40 drivers most illegally and mechanically published the impugned recruitment notice which is not only per se illegal but perverse in the sense that it militates against common sense and natural justice. He next, referring to the provisions of Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution, submits that the recruitment notice (Annexure-A) inviting application for recruitment in the permanent post of drivers instead of absorbing the service of the petitioners and other drivers is violative of the petitioner's fundamental rights as guaranteed under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution and, as such, the impugned requirement notice, so far it relates to recruitment of car drivers, is liable to be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The learned Advocate further after placing the supplementary affidavit dated 19-3-2009 submits with force that the petitioners and 18 other drivers are surplus public servant in the sense that they are admittedly car driver but due to want of vacant posts they could not be posted as driver earlier and, as such, they were surplus to the existing posts of driver at that relevant time. He further adds that all 40 drivers under the said projects were equal in respect of their status and nature of service but the respondents having absorbed the service of 16 drivers out of the said 40 drivers in the vacant post of drivers and, in such view of the matter, the respondents have been constitutionally and legally bound to take the responsibility of absorption of the service of the remaining 24 drivers including the petitioners on seniority basis in order to maintain the constitutional mandate of equality of opportunity in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic and, in view of such legal position, the petitioners and other 18 similar drivers are surplus public servant as defined in section 2(e) of the Surplus Public Servants Absorption Ordinance, 1985 and hence they should be absorbed in the available vacant post of drivers on Seniority Basis.

7. Mr Md Nazrul Islam Talukder, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government-respondents, on the other hand, after placing the affidavit-in-opposition, supplementary affidavit-in-opposition and other connected papers, at the very outset submits that by any means the petitioners are purely Government servants and therefore, on such count the present writ petition is not maintainable. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that admittedly at the first instance the petitioners were appointed as drivers for the two projects namely, “ঢাকা, রাজশাহী ও খুলনা বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” and “চট্টগ্রাম বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” along with other drivers and subsequently, 16 drivers out of 40 drivers were appointed under the revenue budget since there was no other vacant post of driver, the rest 24 drivers were appointed as MLSS fixing there basic salary as like as drivers and in this way 40 drivers including the petitioners were appointed under the revenue budget in two categories and they became Government servant under the revenue budget and, as such, it cannot be said that some of the drivers out of 40 drivers were appointed under the revenue budget and some drivers were left out from the list of 40 drivers. Besides, admittedly the petitioners and other drivers after expiry of project period accepted the post of MLSS on 25-8-1998 and have been drawing salary of the post of drivers and, in such view of the matter there is no logic to say that petitioners have not been treated with equality in the service of the Republic or their fundamental rights have been violated. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further referring to "Annexure-C" and section 5(2) of the Surplus Public Servants Absorption Ordinance, 1985 submits that the present petitioners were posted (Dr M) to the post of MLSS and they well accepted the same and hence, it cannot be said that the petitioners are surplus employees of the various departments under the Directorate of Primary Education. He finally adds that appointment is a matter of policy of the government therefore, this court should not interfere with the government's decision. Mr DAG on the question of maintainability of the writ petition relied on the decisions reported in 4 BLC (AD) 216, 44 DLR (AD) 111, 51 DLR (AD) 148, 52 DLR (AD) 120 and 1 MLR (AD) 32 = 1 BLC (AD) 99 .

8. These are the points which were argued by the learned Advocate and the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respective parties. To deal with the contentions raised by the parties before us it would be convenient for us to decide first of all the question of maintainability of the writ petition. Mr Deputy Attorney-General, on this point to fortify his argument, heavily relied mainly on 3/4 decisions which we have already noted above.

9. It is found that respondent No. 3 recruited 40 Drivers for 2 Development Projects namely “ঢাকা, রাজশাহী ও খুলনা বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” and “চট্টগ্রাম বিভাগের শিক্ষা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প” and the aforesaid two Development Projects were expired on 30-6-1997. Subsequently, 16 posts for the Drivers were created in the organogram of respondent No. 5 under the Revenue Budget and at which 16 drivers were appointed as drivers on Seniority Basis under the Revenue Budget and rest 24 drivers including the petitioners were appointed to the post of MLSS under the Revenue Budget keeping their basic salary intact. In this way all 40 drivers were appointed under the Revenue Budget in two categories and became Government servants.

10. In the case of Chairman, Bangladesh Telegraph and Telephone Board vs Md Shafiul Alam reported in 4 BLC (AD) 216, it has been held as follows:

"We hold that the respondent became an employee of the Government by reason of section 18(2)(f)(ii) of the Ordinance of 1979 and his service was lent to the Board and therefore he squarely qualified to be a person in the Service of the Republic so that it naturally followed that the writ petition filed by him was not maintainable."

11. In the case of Delwar Hossain Miah vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120, it has been held as follows:

"It has been answered by this Court in Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 111 in the following terms, "Within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising out of sub-clause(a), but such Tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1987 (SC) 358 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India, AIR 1987 (SC) 357 (Para 2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the Service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)." We find no reason to revise our earlier view. The gravamen of the writ petitioner's grievance is that by the impugned order of promotion their seniority has been affected. Seniority and promotion of civil servants being terms and conditions of service the Administrative Tribunal is possessed of the exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute in such matters. The case is thus fully covered by our decision in the cited case. No substantial question of law has been made out for grant of leave in this case."

<u>12. On an analysis of the aforesaid decisions it appears that a person in the Service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(i), but in all other cases he will be required to seek the remedy under Article 117(2) of the Constitution.</u>

<u>13. It is true that in this writ petition the petitioners did not challenge the vices of law, they challenged the recruitment notice dated 30-9-2008 as published in the 'Daily Amadersamay' on 8-10-2008 so far it relates to item No. 5 inviting application for recruitment in the permanent posts of Car Drivers (Annexure-A) on the sole ground that the respondent No. 5 most illegally issued the recruitment notice without absorbing them in the available vacant post of drivers. Therefore, we have no hesitation to hold that the instant writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution is not maintainable on the ground that the petitioners are Government servants. Further, it may be observed that the petitioners took a wrong way to ventilate their grievances, other than the recourse prescribed by specific provisions governing the issue. Law is well settled that except on the limited scope a writ petition involving determination of matters relating to terms and conditions of service of a person in the Service of the Republic is not entertainable by this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

14. Referring to section 5 of the Public Servant Absorption Ordinance, 1985, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, at the fag end of the hearing, agitated that the present petitioners are surplus servants and, as such, they must be absorbed.

15. To meet this branch of argument, we have carefully examined the relevant papers and the relevant provisions of Surplus Public Servant Absorption Ordinance, 1985 and find that the petitioners are not surplus servants as we have already indicated that the petitioners have accepted the service in the post of MLSS under the Revenue Budget on 25-8-1998. Therefore, we are unable to see eye to eye on such submission made on behalf of the petitioners.

16. Mr Gobinda Chandra Tagore, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, to fortify his submissions relied on the decisions reported in 51 DLR (AD) 148, 50 DLR 31, 50 DLR 396, 1981 BLD 1 = 33 DLR 16, 12 MLR (AD) 25 = 59 DLR (AD) 54, AIR 1962 (SC) 36 and AIR 1959 (SC)149.

17. We have studied the cases to the best of our ability. It appears that the facts of the case in hand are different from the facts of the cases referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioners and, as such, the principles enunciated in those reported cases have no manner of application to the instant case.

18. Here it may be mentioned that in the facts and circumstances of the present case, we find some substance in the submission of the learned Advocate Mr Gobinda Chandra Tagore for the petitioners with regard to absorbing the petitioners who have been left out cannot be discriminated from those who have already been absorbed, but we are unable to help the petitioners mainly on 2 counts as we have already observed that: (1) the writ petition is not maintainable, (2) the petitioners are not surplus public servants but still then to meet the ends of justice the concerned authority (respondent No. 5) may consider the grievances of the petitioners in all fairness when vacancies are available for the post of drivers keeping the view in mind that the petitioners are still drawing basic salary as like as drivers.

19. Since the petitioners have failed to cross the first hurdle as to the question of maintainability of the writ petition, we need not embark upon detailed discussion as to the legality or otherwise of the impugned notice (Annexure-A).

20. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs with the above observation.

Communicate this judgment at once.

End.

Ajmalul Hossain with ABM Siddiqur Rahman and Affan Ahmed Siddiqui, and Mamun Chowdhury and Sayed Afzal Hossain, Advocates---For the Petitioner. 
Mir Md Joynul Abedin Advocate---For Respondent No. 5. 
Md Mamunur Rashid Advocate---For Respondent No. 6. 
Mirazul Hossain Khan Advocate---For Respondent No. 3. 
Sufia Ahammed, Assistant Attorney-General---For Respondent No. 8.
parties:
AKM Mayeedul Islam ----- Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh Bank and others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Zinat Ara J: In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution, the petitioner challenged the legality of the Credit Information Bureau Report of Bangladesh Bank, so far as it relates to linking the petitioner as a loan defaulter in relation to Kashem Cotton Mills Limited for its liabilities to Janata Bank, Local Office, Dhaka, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, Dhaka and Pubali Bank Limited, Principal Branch, Dhaka.

2. The case of the petitioner as narrated in the writ petition, in a nutshell, is as follows:

3. The petitioner, AKM Mayeedul Islam is a businessman and an industrialist. Respondent No. 9, Quasem Cotton Mills Limited is a public limited company (hereinafter referred to as the Company) incorporated under the Companies Act and engaged in the business of manufacturing cotton yarn and selling/ supplying the manufactured yarn in the local market. The Company was nationalised and placed under Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation (shortly, BTMC) for running the Company till 1982. Thereafter, it was denationalised under a tripartite agreement and returned to the original shareholders on 10-2-1983. Under the said agreement, the advances taken from PICIC was transferred to respondent No. 5, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (BSRS) created under President's Order No. 128 of 1972 and it was finally paid off in February, 1991 which was Taka 34.66 lac. After denationalisation, the shareholders of the Company spent their own money in the Company. The investment of the petitioner and others were Taka 1 crore and 83 lac till filing of the writ petition. On 2nd March, 1983, the former Managing Director of the Company approached respondent No. 6 for raw cotton LC/CC and this respondent sanctioned Taka 1 crore and Taka 1.20 crore in favour of the Company under certain terms and conditions. The previous Managing Director of the Company also applied for loan to respondent No. 3 for Taka 5 crore CC(Pledge) and Taka 2 crore CC(Hypo) and it was sanctioned on 13 October, 1992 in favour of the Company with certain terms and conditions. The Company availed the loan facilities from respondent Nos. 3, 5 and 6 i.e. Janata Bank, Local Office, Dhaka, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (BSRS), Dhaka and Pubali Bank Ltd, Principal Branch, Dhaka respectively. The petitioner, the Company and others executed deed of mortgage, irrevocable power of attorney for various properties in favour of those respondents and also executed personal guarantee for the loan in favour of the respondents. The Company by a letter dated 16th August, 1999 requested respondent No. 3 to enhance the working capital for Taka 1.30 crore in CC(Hypo) and Taka 3 crore in CC (Pledge) for smooth production of the Company. The Company again on 27th September, 1999 made a formal application for the aforesaid working capital enhancement which was not considered by respondent No. 3. However, again on 9th April, 2000 the Company requested respondent No. 3 for working capital without any result. The Company then requested respondent No. 5 to enhance its CC(P) limit from Taka 5 crore to Taka 7 crore and CC(H) from Taka 2 crore to Taka 3 crore. On the prayer of the previous Managing Director, further loan of Taka 50 lac was sanctioned by respondent No. 3. The former Managing Director mortgaged some properties at Mymensingh for releasing this sanctioned loan. The Company on several occasions asked for payment of the sanctioned loan of Taka 50 lac in favour of the Company but, it was not implemented. Rather respondent No. 3 served a notice upon the Company for Khelapi Rin and asked to pay the outstanding debts within 20th October, 2002. However, in December 2002 the petitioner, i.e. the Managing Director of the Company, declared closure of the Company (Mill) by a notice for an indefinite period due to acute financial crisis. Respondent No. 3 by a letter dated 9-12-2002 condemned the actions of the Company in selling the goods without authority and without consent of respondent No. 3. Respondent No. 3 instructed the Company to either replace the pledged goods removed from the premises of the Company or alternatively, deposit the sale proceeds of the pledged goods. Respondent No. 3 also informed the Company that it would be sending its officials to the Company (mill premises) to inspect the remaining pledged goods and carry out a physical inventory to ascertain the amount of pledged goods removed from the Mill premises. On 15th December, 2002, a joint physical inventory was carried out by the officials of the Company and the respondent No. 5 BSRS (why BSRS and not respondent No. 3 Janata Bank ?) and the shortfall of the pledged goods were determined. By a letter dated 24th December, 2002 by the Company, they agreed to repay the value of the shortfall items as determined in the physical inventory carried out on 15th December, 2002 at the present rate. Respondent No. 3 was aware about the closure of the Company since 8th December, 2002. Respondent No. 3 by a letter dated 2-2-2003 instructed the Company to deposit the sale proceeds and in the event of non-compliance, legal action would be taken against the Company. The petitioner, by a letter dated 5th February, 2003 informed respondent No. 3 that steps were being taken to pay the sale proceeds for the pledged goods removed and asked respondent No. 3 not to initiate any legal proceeding. In the meantime, respondent No. 5 by a letter dated 9th July, 2002 sanctioned a fresh loan of Taka 50 lac in favour of the Company. The petitioner failed to supply an NOC from BSRS and/or collect a clean CIB report from Bangladesh Bank. In the CIB report dated 17th May, 2006 under borrower Code No. 1328444 and 13619, the Company was shown as a defaulting borrower and the petitioner as a Director of the Company, was also shown as a defaulting borrower. The petitioner came to know by a letter dated 26th June, 2006 from First Lease International Limited that the petitioner has been classified as a loan defaulter in the CIB report of Bangladesh Bank which resulted in refusal of First Lease International Ltd to extend any financial support to the petitioner. Hence, this writ petition.

4. Respondent No. 3 i.e. Janata Bank contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition dated 14-5-2007 denying the material averments made in the writ petition contending, inter alia, that the petitioner filed this writ petition by suppressing the material facts and the Company/petitioner hopelessly failed to fulfill the terms and conditions of the new loan sanctioned and thus failed to avail the loan due to their own fault. The alleged joint inventory with respondent No. 5 has nothing to do with the petitioner's unlawful removal of goods from the respondent No 3's pledged godown. The petitioner in order to avoid loan repayment and to suppress the facts of unlawful removal of the goods from the pledged godown and to frustrate the legal actions against the petitioner, has filed this writ petition with false excuses. The petitioner had no legal right to sell the pledged property. The petitioner executed personal guarantee for the loan availed by the Company. The Company as well as the petitioner failed to repay the same. Therefore, the petitioner and the Company are both loan defaulters. The Company failed to avail the further loan sanctioned due to their own failure in fulfilling the conditions of the loan sanctioned. The Company was classified in the CIB report under borrower Code No. 1328444 and 13619 with its Managing Director i.e. the petitioner along with other directors legally. The petitioner is a loan defaulter and, as such, there is no scope to delete his name from the CIB report and thus, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

5. Respondent No. 5 i.e. Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (BSRS), also contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition dated 3-5-2007 stating that the present writ petition is misconceived and not maintainable. The petitioner admitted in paragraph 7 of the writ petition that the Company availed the loan facilities from respondent Nos. 3, 5 and 6 and the petitioner executed personal guarantee in respect of the said loans and the loans have not been repaid till to date. The Company is a defaulter borrower to many banks/financial institutions. The petitioner is a guarantor for the loans obtained by the Company and he admitted the same. The borrower and guarantor are jointly liable for the loan liability for the borrower Company and, as such, the name of the petitioner is not liable to be deleted from the CIB report. The name of the petitioner has been rightly and legally included in the CIB report. The petitioner has alternative remedy in the civil Court and so, the present writ petition is liable to be discharged.

6. Respondent No. 6 i.e. Pubali Bank Ltd, Dhaka also contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition dated 27-11-2008 as well as a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 2-12-2008 contending, inter alia, that the petitioner has been performing the functions as a Managing Director of the Company and in that capacity, he applied to respondent No. 6 Bank for renewal/enhancement/adjustment of the loan at different times. The petitioner also deposited Taka 4 lac in his loan account lying with respondent No. 6 through a forwarding letter written on 28-5-2005. The petitioner also executed charge documents and personal guarantee on 28-5-2005 as security against the loan in favour of the Company. The petitioner's full brother AKM Mainul Islam, was one of the three directors of Company, who expired on 26-11-2000 and after his death the petitioner was appointed as Chairman and Managing Director of the Company on 24-10-2001 as per minutes of the Board of Directors of the Company. Form XII dated 28-10-2001 of the "Registrar of Joint Stock Companies" (RJSC) also show the name of the petitioner as Chairman and Managing Director of the Company and it was certified as such by RJSC on 31-12-2001. But inadvertently it was not reported to CIB of Bangladesh Bank and so the name of AKM Mainul Islam was continuing as director instead of AKM Mayeedul Islam. Subsequently, Bangladesh Bank sought for clarification of the matter vide in its letter dated 22-11-2006 written to respondent No. 6 and this respondent Bank by a letter dated 6-12-2006 clarified the matter. In respect of the loan sanctioned by the Bank, the guarantor's liability is equal to that of the borrower. To some extent the guarantor's liability is more than a borrower because the bank at the time of sanctioning the loan actively consider the guarantee of the guarantor in order to sanction the loan. Had there been no guarantor, the Bank would not have sanctioned any loan in favour of a borrower Company. The name of the Company and its directors have been legally included in the CIB Report. The writ petition is misconceived and the Rule is liable to be discharged.

7. The petitioner filed a supplementary affidavit dated 15-12-2008 stating that respondent No. 6 has acknowledged that the Board of Directors of the Company have been reconstituted by a board meeting dated 28 October, 2001 by which the petitioner has become Managing Director of the Company. The petitioner cannot be legally considered as the Managing Director of the Company as all the legal formalities have not been complied with for his appointment as a director in accordance with the provision of the কোম্পানী আইন, ১৯৯৪ (shortly, the Act, 1994). Since the petitioner was the mortgagor and the third party guarantor, he cannot be referred to as a loan defaulter. The Company is the principal borrower and it has provided sufficient security to cover the outstanding loan liabilities. Hence, the petitioner should not be considered as a defaulter in consideration of section 6(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

8. Respondent No. 6 i.e. Pubali Bank Ltd, also filed another supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 13-1-2009 stating that at the time of hearing of the Rule, the petitioner filed the supplementary affidavit narrating some new facts which were never stated before the Court either by way of statement or by oral submission. The statements made in the writ petition were normal facts but finding that those statements of facts were against the petitioner as per law, the petitioner as an after thought prepared the supplementary affidavit to divert his position from the actual position for illegal gain by misleading the Court. The petitioner was appointed as the Managing Director of the Company by unanimous decision. The petitioner has been conducting all businesses of the Company since his appointment as a Managing Director of the Company. According to section 98 of the Act, 1994, the petitioner cannot claim that he is not the Managing Director of the Company, Article 146 of the Articles of Association of the Company provides that nothing shall prevent the petitioner from seeking reappointment on the expiry of the term. In continuation of the same legal process, the petitioner was appointed as Chairman and Managing Director of the Company with effect from 24-10-2001 and he has been working in the said capacity till today. The Company informed respondent No. 6 Bank about appointment of the petitioner as Managing Director vide its letter dated 15-5-2002 and also informed RJSC of the same. Furthermore, the petitioner is debarred from raising this plea at this stage as per provision of section 115 of the Evidence Act. The petitioner is continuing as a Managing Director of the Company and so, the petitioner's name was legally included in the CIB report as a director of the Company and thus, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

9. Ms Sufia Ahammed, the learned Assist-ant Attorney-General, appeared for the respondent No. 8 by filing vokalatnama and opposed the Rule without filing any separate affidavit-in-opposition.

10. The petitioner has submitted three affidavits-in-reply on 11-1-2009 against the affidavits-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit -in-opposition filed by different respondents contending, inter alia, that it has been established by several judgments of the High Court Division that a person, who executed personal guarantee for the loan cannot be treated as loan defaulter under section 5(GaGa) of the ব্যাংক কম্পানী আইন, ১৯৯১ (hereinafter referred to as the Act, 1991). The petitioner was not legally appointed as the Managing Director on 24-10-2001 and he has 12.50% share out of the total share of the Company and therefore, the Company cannot be treated as his “স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান” for inclusion of his name in the CIB report and thus, the Rule is liable to be made absolute.

11. Mr Ajmalul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr ABM Siddiqur Rahman Khan, for the petitioner, forwarded before us the following arguments:

(i) The petitioner was not a director when the loan was sanctioned and so, he cannot be treated as a defaulter.

(ii) The petitioner, as a guarantor for the loan, is liable to pay the loan but he being a guarantor cannot be termed as “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” and, as such, the inclusion of the name of the petitioner as “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” in CIB report is without lawful authority.

(iii) The Company was taken over by BTMC after liberation and during that period the petitioner was not a director.

(iv) Though the Board of Directors of the Company have been reconstituted by the board meeting dated 28th October, 2001 by which the petitioner has become Managing Director of the Company but the petitioner cannot be legally considered as Managing Director of the Company as all the legal formalities have not been complied within his appointment as a Managing Director of the Company.

(v) According to section 98 of the Act, 1994 the director of the Company shall be elected by general share-holders in the general meeting but the petitioner was not appointed as a Managing Director of the Company by any resolution in the general meeting.

(vi) The petitioner has not given consent to his appointment as a Managing Director as per section 93 of the Act, 1994 and therefore, he cannot be legally treated as a Managing Director of the Company.

(vii) Under section 110 of the Act, 1994 the Managing Director cannot be appointed for more than 5 years at a time. Therefore, the term of the petitioner has expired during the pendency of this Rule.

(viii) Even if the petitioner is treated as a Managing Director of the Company, it has been decided in many cases that a director shall not be responsible for loan liability of the Company and he cannot be treated as “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” under section 5 (Ga Ga) and section 27 Ka Ka of the Act, 1991 as the Company cannot be treated as his “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” and thereafter, the name of the petitioner in the CIB report is without lawful authority and therefore liable to be deleted from there.

12. In support of his arguments, Mr Hossain, has relied upon the following decisions

1. Boschoek vs Fuke (1906) 1 Ch 148 @ 159;

2. Nelson vs James Nelsen (1914) 2 KB 770 @

3. Glossop vs Glossop (1907)2 Ch. 370.

4. Shekhar Mehra vs Kilpset P. Lte (1986)3 Comp. Li 234,

5. Shishu Rajan Dutta vs Bhola Nath Paper House Ltd (1983) 53 Comp. Cas. 883 Cal.

6. Jenner's Case (1877)7 Ch. D.p. 132,

7. Spencer vs Kennedy, (1926)1 Ch.125,

8. Dean vs Hiesler (1942)2 All ER 340,

9. Morris vs Kanseen (1946) AC 459.

10. Hindustan Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd 65 CWN 79,

11. Dira Dockyard & Engineers Ltd Vs Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Shangstha 1995 (III) BLT (AD)207,

12. Habibulla, Director of National Bank Limited vs Bangladesh Bank 2 BLC in Paragraph 12 of the judgment, page 523;

13. Mr Mostafa Kamal vs Bangladesh Bank,11 MLR 377.

14. Mahmudur Rahman vs Bangladesh Bank 59 DLR 540;

15. IFIC Bank Ltd vs Beximco Holdings Ltd, 57 DLR 154;

16. Major Manjur Quader (Retd) vs Bangladesh Bank 59 DLR 451;

17. Mahbub Alam vs Bangladesh Bank Ltd (Writ Petition No. 7158 of 2003);

18. Quazi Nasibul Hassan (Sunnu) vs Bangladesh Bank, (Writ Petition No. 2944 of 2005) (Larger Bench Decision).

13. Mr Mirajul Hossian Khan, the learned Advocate appeared for respondent No. 3, Mr MM Joynal Abedin, the learned Advocate appeared for respondent No. 5, Mr Md Mamunur Rashid, the learned Advocate appeared for respondent No. 6 and Mrs Sufia Ahammed, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared on behalf of respondent No. 8. The sum and substance of the submissions placed before us by the above named learned Advocates for the contesting banks, BSRS and the Government are more or less similar and so, to avoid unnecessary repetitions, their submissions are summarized below:

(a) The petitioner was the Managing Director of the Company when the Company was incorporated in 1969.

(b) In the writ petition the petitioner admitted that at the time of sanction of loan in February, 1992, the petitioner executed personal guarantee in respect of the loan.

(c) The petitioner, as a director of the Company executed personal guarantee and other documents in favour of the Bank and BSRS for taking loan.

(d) The petitioner was again appointed as a Managing Director of the Company on 24-10-2001 and since then he has been functioning as a Managing Director of the Company till date.

(e) It has been admitted in the writ petition that the Company obtained loan from respondent Nos. 3, 5 and 6 but did not repay the loan amount and therefore, the Company is admittedly a loan defaulter.

(f) Admittedly, the Company is a public limited company and therefore, according to section 5(GaGa) of the Act, 1991 the petitioner being the Managing Director of the Company, the Company is to be treated as his “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” and the Company admittedly being a “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” within the meaning of section 5(GaGa) of the Act, 1991 the name of the petitioner-director of the Company was correctly included in the CIB report as a loan defaulter.

(g) The petitioner himself admitted to be the Managing Director of the Company in paragraph 33 of the writ petition and he wrote various letters to the bank and accepted loan liability of the Company by executing promissory notes, letter of guarantee as a Managing Director of the Company and therefore, the petitioner is estopped from claiming that he is not legally appointed as Managing Director of the Company.

(h) In view of the provision of section 115 of the Evidence Act, the petitioner is estopped by the principle of estoppel from claiming that he is not a legally appointed Managing Director of the Company as the banks /BSRS on his representation as a Managing Director sanctioned loans.

(i) The petitioner is still functioning as a Managing Director of the Company and therefore, he is not entitled to get any relief in the writ jurisdiction.

(j) The petitioner, after submission of the affidavit-in-opposition by respondent No. 6, by filing a supplementary affidavit claimed that he is not a legally appointed Managing Director of the Company which is an afterthought and a cunning device to avoid inclusion of his name in the CIB report.

(k) In this writ petition, there is no scope to decide whether the petitioner is a legally appointed Managing Director or not in absence of submission of the proper documents by the petitioner.

(l) The petitioner did not claim that he is not functioning as a Managing Director of the Company till date. So he is not entitled to take the plea that he is not a legally appointed Managing Director of the Company and, in the above circumstances, the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

14. In support of their submissions, the learned Advocates for the contesting respondents referred to the decisions in the followings cases:

(1) Government of Bangladesh, represented by Secretary, Housing and Settlement, Bangladesh Secretariat vs ASM Firojuddin Bhuiyan, 53 DLR 522;

(2) MM Ispahani vs Sonali Bank Ltd, 37 DLR (AD)1;

(3) Md Ebadal Ali vs Ismail Hossain, 1989 BLD, 304 = 41 DLR 490;

(4) Director General, Bangladesh Jute Research Institute (BJRI) vs ASM Serajuddin, 2003 BLD (AD) 18;

(5) Abdur Rouf (Md) vs Power Development Board, 60 DLR 292;

(6) Khan Md Firoj Kabir vs Rupali Bank Ltd 12 MLR (AD) 186 = 59 DLR (AD) 206;

(7) Pronob Kumar Chakraborty vs Bangladesh, 46 DLR 268.

15. In view of the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the contending parties, the moot questions to be decided in this Rule are—

(1) Whether the name of a director of a Public Limited Company may be included in the CIB report where the Company is a “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা”

(2) Whether the name of a guarantor/ mortgagor may be included in the CIB report if the principal loanee is a “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা”

(3) Whether the petitioner's name was included in the CIB report legally.

16. We have examined the writ petition, supplementary affidavit, affidavits-in-opposition filed by respondent Nos. 3, 5 and 6, supplementary affidavits-in-opposition filed by respondent No. 6 and affidavits-in-reply filed by the petitioner as well as the connected materials on record.

17. At the outset, we would like to mention that on examination of the writ petition and supplementary affidavits it is found that many facts were suppressed by the petitioner in it, such as the date of the incorporation of the Company, the names of the directors at the time of its incorporation, the names of subsequent directors of the Company after it was returned to the original share-holders by BTMC by a Tripartite agreement and the names of the present directors of the Company, etc. However, at the time of hearing, Mr Hossain admits that the Company was incorporated in the year 1969 and at that time the petitioner was the Managing Director of the Company and he was again appointed as a Managing Director of the Company on 24-10-2001.

18. Be that as it may, it is an admitted proposition that the Company availed loan from respondents Nos. 3, 5 and 6 at different times. It is also admitted that the petitioner at the time of obtaining loan for the Company in the year 1992 and at different dates, has executed personal guarantee and other documents in favour of respondents Nos. 3, 5 and 6 as a security for the loan. It is not also disputed that the Company did not repay the loan of the aforesaid respondents and it is a “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” which resulted in inclusion of the name of the Company, the petitioner as well as other directors of the Company, as a loan defaulter in the CIB report published by the Bangladesh Bank.

19. The petitioner in paragraph 33 of the writ petition admitted himself to be Managing Director of the Company by stating" the Managing Director of the Company, Mr AKM Mayeedul Islam, by a notice dated 8 December, 2002, announced the closure of the Company ... ...".The notice dated 8-12-2002 (Annexure-1 to the writ petition) under section 61 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 declaring closure of the Company's Mill also shows that the petitioner, as a Managing Director of the Company issued the said notice. Furthermore, from letter dated August 20, 2002 (Annexure-G to the writ petition) filed by the writ petitioner, it appears that the petitioner, AKM Mayeedul Islam has written this letter to the Managing Director of Janata Bank as a Managing Director of the Company for implementation of the loan sanctioned. Similarly, the petitioner wrote a letter dated December 8, 2002 (Annexure-H to the writ petition) to the General Manager, Janata Bank as a Managing Director of the Company admitting sale of some stocks from the godown without approval and the management took full responsibility of the stocks disposed of. From this letter, it is clear that the Company also sold out some goods illegally pledged in favour of respondent No. 3 without permission. From letter dated 15th May, 2002 (Annexure-Y to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 13-1-2009 filed by respondent No. 6) addressed to Pubali Bank, it is found that the present petitioner as a Managing Director of the Company informed this bank about the reconstitution of the Board of Directors of the Company. In this letter, it has been clearly stated that the petitioner is the Managing Director of the Company. From Form XII (Annexure-"Y" to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 13-1-2009 filed by the respondent No. 6) it appears that the petitioner was appointed as a Managing Director on 24-10-2001. The petitioner, in his affidavit-in-reply has also filed the same Form XII wherefrom it appears that the petitioner was appointed as Managing Director of the Company on 24-10-2001. From the letter dated 28 June, 2005 (Annexure-X to the supplementary affidavit dated 2-12-2008 filed by respondent No. 6) it appears that the petitioner as a Managing Director of the Company prayed to extend the re-payment period upto 30 June, 2006, etc. The petitioner also executed the demand promissory note dated 28-6-2005 to pay Taka 4,54,60,513/76 with interest @ 16% per annum and he also executed the letter of guarantee for the aforesaid loan in favour of Pubali Bank. (Annexure-X-1, X-2 to the supplementary affidavit dated 2-12-2008 filed by respondent No. 6).

20. Therefore, from the series of the documents filed by the petitioner with the writ petition and the series of documents filed by respondent No. 6, it is found that the petitioner represented himself as the Managing Director of the Company. All these documents as discussed above clearly prove that the petitioner is the Managing Director of the Company.

21. When respondent No. 6 by filing supplementary affidavit-in-opposition stated that the petitioner was appointed as a Managing Director of the Company on 24-10-2001 and it was apparent during the course of arguments that the directors of Public Limited companies are liable to be included in the CIB report if the companies are loan defaulters, such companies are to be treated as their “স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান” The petitioner introduced a new case for the first time that he is not legally appointed as a director of the Company in accordance with the provision of the Act, 1994. Therefore, it is clear that the claim of the petitioner as Managing Director in paragraph 33 of the writ petitioner is the actual fact but, the subsequent assertion is an afterthought with ill motive for the purpose of this case only.

22. Let us now examine the provision of section 115 of the Evidence Act which is quoted below:

"115. Estoppel—When one person has, by his declaration, act or omission, intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true and to act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed, in any suit or proceeding between himself and such person or his representative, to deny the truth of that thing."

23. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs ASM Firojuddin Bhuiyan reported in 53 DLR 522 it was observed by this Division as under:

"19. Promissory Estoppel is a principle evolved by Courts on the principles of equity and to avoid injustice. Where one party by his words and conduct makes the other party a clear promise, that promise would be binding upon the former who would not be entitled to go back from it."

"Estoppel" in Black's Law Dictionary is indicated to mean that a party is prevented by his own acts from claiming a right to the detriment of other party who was entitled to rely on such conduct and has acted accordingly. Section 115 of the Evidence Act is also more or less couched in a language which conveys the same expression."

24. In the instant case, the petitioner represented himself as Managing Director of the Company in a series of documents as well as accepted the loan liabilities of the Company and therefore, in view of the provision of section 115 of the Evidence Act, he is estopped to deny the truth of him being a Managing Director of the Company. He is also estopped from disclaiming his loan liability. Furthermore, no man can take advantage of his own wrong as the same is against the principle of equity.

25. We have gone through the decisions as referred by Mr Hossain in support of his assertion that the petitioner was not legally appointed as a Managing Director of the Company. But, for the reasons discussed hereinbefore, we find that those decisions are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

26. Now let us examine whether the petitioner may be included as “মেয়াদ উত্তীর্ন ঋন গ্রহীতা” for the purpose of including his name in the CIB report in view of the provision of section 5 (GaGa) of the Act, 1991. For deciding this issue section 5 (GaGa) is quoted below:

“৫। সংজ্ঞা।–বিষয় অথবা প্রসংগের পরিপন্থি কোন কিছু না থাকিলে, আইনে------”

“(গগ) “খেলাপী ঋন গ্রহীতা অর্থ কোন ব্যক্তি বা প্রতিষ্ঠান যাহার নিজের বা স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠানের অনুকুলে প্রদম অগ্রীম ঋণ বা উহার অংশ বা উহার উপর অর্জিত সুদ বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক কর্তৃক জারীকৃত সংজ্ঞা অনুযায়ী মেয়াদোমীর্ণ হওয়ার ৬(ছয়) মাস অতিবাহিত হইয়াছে”

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা কোন পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানীর পরিচালক না হইলে অথবা উক্ত কোম্পানীতে তাহার বা উহার শেয়ারের অংশ ২৫% এর অধিক না হইলে, উক্ত পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানী স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না”

আরো শর্ত থাকে যে, পাবলিক কোম্পানী ব্যতীত অন্য কোন প্রতিষ্ঠানে এই দফার অধীন স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান বলিয়া গন্য হইবে না।”

27. In this case, it has been admitted in paragraph 6 of the writ petition that the Company is a Public Limited Company, incorporated under the Companies Act. Therefore, the Company being a Public Limited Company is to be treated as a “স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান” of the directors of the Company.

28. We have already seen that the petitioner is still functioning as a Managing Director of the Company and the petitioner failed to produce before us any iota of documentary evidence showing that he is not functioning as a Managing Director of the Company till date. Therefore, we are constrained to hold that the Company is to be treated as a “স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান”of the petitioner i.e. the Managing Director of the Company.

<u>29. In view of the above, the Company being a “স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান”of the petitioner and Company admittedly being a “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা” the name of the petitioner as a director of the Company was included in the CIB report in accordance with law.</u>

<u>30. So far the liability of the petitioner as a guarantor for loan is concerned, Mr Hossain admits the liability of the petitioner as a guarantor for the loan. However, his argument is that the petitioner's name as a guarantor cannot be included in CIB report as a “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা”</u>

<u>31. The learned Advocates for the contending parties referred to many decisions on this issue as to whether the name of a guarantor may be included in the CIB report as a defaulter borrower.</u>

<u>32. This question has been decided by this Division in favour and against such inclusion. Now the matter is admittedly pending before the Appellate Division for the final decision on this question. Therefore, we do not like to enter into the merit of question No.2. Moreover, as we have decided that the name of the petitioner is legally published in the CIB report as a director of the Company, it is not necessary to decide this question in this writ petition. Thus, we do not like to discuss the decisions as referred to by the learned Advocates for the contending parties on this question.</u>

33. In view of the discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs, it is found that the petitioner's name has been legally included in the CIB report.

34. Therefore, we find no merit in this Rule.

35. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged with a cost of Taka 5,000 (Taka five thousand) only to be paid by the petitioner through treasury chalan in favour of the Government within 60 days from date.

The order of injunction stands vacated.

End.

TH Khan with Md Halal Uddin Mollah & Md Jalaluddin, Advocates ------ For the Respondent No.1.
